parole.significato: Used to form nouns of state, condition or quality.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman -cie, ultimately from Latin -cia, -tia, Ancient Greek -κια (-kia), -τια (-tia), originally variants of Latin -ia and Ancient Greek -ια (-ia), -ία (-ía) or -εια (-eia). Original loan words like pharmacy and papacy could have formed the model.

parole.significato: Added to transitive verbs to form words meaning a person or thing that is the object of that verb (i.e., to whom or to…
parole.testo: From Middle English -ee, -ē, from Anglo-Norman and Old French -ee, French -é, -ée, endings forming past participle of verbs ending in -er. Doublet of -ate. More distantly related to inherited English -ed.

parole.significato: Instance of (the verbal action); used to form nouns from verbs.
parole.testo: From Middle English -er, from Anglo-Norman -er, Old French -er, the infinitive verbal ending.

parole.significato: Used to form abstract nouns of state, quality, or action from Latin or French roots.
parole.testo: From Middle English -our, from Anglo-Norman -our, -ur, and Old French -or (modern -eur), from the Latin accusative suffix -ōrem, from -or. parole.significato: Forming words with the sense of wholly, or utterly out.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman a-, from Old French e-, from Latin ex-.

parole.significato: To lessen (something) in force or intensity; to moderate.

parole.significato: To enter upon and unlawfully seize (land) after the owner has died, thus preventing an heir from taking possession of i…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman abatre, probably an alteration of Anglo-Norman and Middle French embatre, enbatre (“to drive or rush into; to enter into a tenement without permission”) (compare Late Latin abatare), from Middle French, Old French em-, en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + Middle French, Old French bat

parole.significato: The act of abating, or the state of being abated; a lessening, diminution, or reduction; a moderation; removal or putti…
parole.testo: From Middle English abatement, from Anglo-Norman abatre (“to abate”) (from Old French abatre), + -ment; equivalent to abate + -ment.

parole.significato: a person who, without right, enters into a freehold on the death of the last possessor, before the heir or devisee
parole.testo: From abate (“to enter without right after the owner dies and before the heir takes over”) + -or. From Anglo-Norman.

parole.significato: The act of abetting or assisting in a crime, wrongdoing etc.
parole.testo: First attested from 1350 to 1470, from Middle English abettement, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French abeter + -ment. See abet.

parole.significato: One that abets an offender; one that incites, instigates, or encourages.
parole.testo: From Middle English abettour, from Anglo-Norman abettour, from Old French abeter + -our (“-or”). See abet. By surface analysis, abet + -or.

parole.significato: Expectancy; a condition when an ownership of real property is undetermined; lapse in succession of ownership of estate,…
parole.testo: First attested in 1528. From Anglo-Norman abeiance (“legal expectation”), from Old French abeance (“desire”) from abeër (“to gape at, aspire after”), abaer, abair (“to desire”), from a (“to”) + baër (“to gape”), bair (“yawn”), from Medieval Latin batō (“to yawn”).

parole.significato: To solemnly reject (someone or something); to abandon (someone or something) forever; to disavow, to disclaim, to repud…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English abjuren (“to give up (something); to recant or renounce (something) under oath”), from Anglo-Norman abjurer, Middle French abiurer, abjurer, and Old French abjurer (“to reject or renounce (something) on oath”) (modern French abjurer), and from their etymon Latin abiūrāre, th

parole.significato: Fully sufficient; found in copious supply; in great quantity; overflowing.
parole.testo: First attested about 1380. From Middle English abundaunt, habundaunt, aboundant, from Anglo-Norman abundant, from Old French abondant, from Latin abundāns, present participle of abundō (“to overflow, to abound”). Compare abound.

parole.significato: Capable, worthy, or sure of being accepted or received with pleasure; welcome; gratifying; pleasing to a receiver.
parole.testo: From Middle English acceptable, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French acceptable, from Late Latin acceptābilis (“worthy of acceptance”). Morphologically accept + -able.

parole.significato: Pertaining to accident and not essence; thus, inessential; incidental; secondary.
parole.testo: From Middle English accidental, from Anglo-Norman accidentel, Middle French accidentel, accidental, and their source, Late Latin accidēntālis; corresponding to accident + -al.

parole.significato: Sloth, slothfulness, especially as inducing general listlessness and apathy.
parole.testo: From Middle English accidie, from Anglo-Norman accidie, Old French accide, accidie, from Late Latin accīdia, alteration of acēdia (“sloth, torpor”), from Ancient Greek ἀκήδεια (akḗdeia, “indifference”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κῆδος (kêdos, “care”). Doublet of acedia.

parole.significato: Able to be given or dispensed.
parole.testo: From Middle English acordable, from Anglo-Norman acordable.

parole.significato: A registry of pecuniary transactions; a written or printed statement of business dealings or debts and credits, and als…
parole.testo: From Middle English acounte, from Anglo-Norman acunte (“account”), from Old French aconte, from aconter (“to reckon”), from Latin computō (“to sum up”).

parole.significato: To increase.
parole.testo: From Middle English acresen, accreesen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French acreistre, from Latin accrēscere, from ad- + crēscere (“to grow”). Doublet of accresce.

parole.significato: Producing accusations; in a manner that reflects a finding of fault or blame
parole.testo: First attested in the mid 15th century. From Middle English accusative, from Anglo-Norman accusatif or Middle French acusatif or from Latin accūsātīvus (“having been blamed”), from accūsō (“to blame”). Equivalent to accuse + -ative. The Latin form is a mistranslation of the Ancient Greek grammatical

parole.significato: A purveyor of provisions; a provedore.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman achatour, Old French achateor, achateur (“buyer, provider”), derived from achater (“buy, provide”), from Late Latin accaptare, from ad (“to”) + captare (“strive for”).

parole.significato: To carry out or conclude (something, as a task) successfully; to accomplish.
parole.testo: From Middle English achieven, acheven (“to accomplish (something); to acquire or obtain (something); to carry out or finish (something); to succeed in (something); to happen, turn out”), from Anglo-Norman achever, achiever, Middle French achever, achiever, and Old French achever, achiever (“to accom

parole.significato: A state of being acquainted with a person; originally indicating friendship, intimacy, but now suggesting a slight know…
parole.testo: From Middle English aqueyntaunce, from Anglo-Norman aquaintaunce, aqueintance, Old French acointance (“friendship, familiarity”), from Old French acointier (“to acquaint”). Compare French accointance. Morphologically acquaint + -ance.

parole.significato: A writing which is evidence of a discharge; a receipt in full, which bars a further demand.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman acquitance, Middle French aquitance, from acquiter (“to acquit”). Compare later acquittal.

parole.significato: To, toward, or from the far side of (something that lies between two points of interest).
parole.testo: From Middle English acros, from early Middle English a-croiz, a-creoyz, from Anglo-Norman an (“in, on”) + croiz (“in the form of a cross”). More at cross. By surface analysis, a- + cross.

parole.significato: relating to a person's acts or deeds; active, practical
parole.testo: From Middle English actual, actuel (“active”), from Anglo-Norman actuel, actual, and its source Late Latin actuālis (“active, practical”), from Latin actus (“act, action, performance”), from agere (“to do; to act”) + -alis (“-al”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti, from the root *h₂eǵ-.

parole.significato: Synonym of adamant.
parole.testo: From Middle English adamantine, adamantyne, adamauntyn (“(adjective) of adamant; (noun) adamant”), from Anglo-Norman adamantin and Middle French adamantin (“of or resembling adamant or diamond”) (modern French adamantin), and from its etymon Latin adamantinus (“adamantine”), from Ancient Greek ἀδᾰμά

parole.significato: To share a common boundary or border with; to be physically contiguous to (a piece of land or property).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman adjoindre, from Latin adiungō.

parole.significato: To formally command or request (someone) to do something, either in the name of a deity, or to suffer a curse or punish…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English adjuren (“to bind (oneself or someone) by oath to do something; to entreat or implore (someone); to question (someone) under oath”), from Anglo-Norman adjurer, Middle French adjurer, and Old French ajurer (“to bind (oneself or someone) under oath; to entreat or implore (some

parole.significato: To measure.
parole.testo: From Middle English amesure, from Anglo-Norman amesurer, admesurer, from Medieval Latin admēnsūrō. Compare Classical Latin admētior (“measure out to”).

parole.significato: A person, group, or thing that opposes or attacks another person or group; an opponent or rival.
parole.testo: From Middle English adversarie, from Anglo-Norman aversaire (in Wace's Life of Saint Margaret) and Old French aversier, aversaire (French adversaire), from Latin adversārius, from adversus (“turned toward”). By surface analysis, adverse + -ary.

parole.significato: To give (especially public) notice of (something); to announce publicly.
parole.testo: From Middle English advertisen, from Anglo-Norman advertir (“to inform”), avertir, Middle French advertir, avertir (“to warn, give notice to”), with the French -iss- infix assimilated to -ise, -ize and probably influenced by the noun advertisement. Compare also advert.

parole.significato: The right to present a nominee to a vacant ecclesiastical benefice or church office.
parole.testo: From Middle English avowson, from Anglo-Norman avouson, from Latin advocātiō. Doublet of advocation.

parole.significato: Divination by use of atmospheric conditions.
parole.testo: From Middle English aeremance, aermancye, aaeromancye, from Anglo-Norman aermancie and Middle French aerimancie, aeromance, ayromancie (modern French aéromancie), from Latin āeromantia. By surface analysis, aero- + -mancy.

parole.significato: An eaglestone.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman aetite, aetites, Middle French aetite, and their source, Latin (lapis) āetītēs (“eagle (stone)”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek ἀετίτης (λίθος) (aetítēs (líthos), “eagle (stone)”), from ἀετός (aetós, “eagle”).

parole.significato: To make a show of; to put on a pretense of; to feign; to assume. To make a false display of.
parole.testo: From Middle English affecten, from Anglo-Norman affecter (“strive after”), Middle French affecter (“feign”), and their source, Latin affectāre (“to strive after, aim to do, pursue, imitate with dissimulation, feign”), frequentative of afficere (“to act upon, influence”) (see Etymology 1, above).

parole.significato: One who affeers.
parole.testo: Formed in English as affeer + -er, after the Anglo-Norman afferour, affoerour. Compare affeeror.

parole.significato: To startle from quiet; to alarm.
parole.testo: From Middle English affraien (“to terrify, frighten”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman afrayer (“to terrify, disquiet, disturb”) and Old French effreer, esfreer (“to disturb, remove the peace from”) (compare modern French effrayer), from Vulgar Latin *exfridāre. parole.significato: To have faith in (someone); to trust.
parole.testo: From Middle English affien (“to have faith, trust”), from Anglo-Norman afier, affier, affyer, Middle French afier, affier, affyer, and Old French afier (“to agree to marry; to believe, trust; to assure, promise; to confide in; to pledge, swear”), from Late Latin affidare (“to betroth; to pledge fait

parole.testo: From a- (intensifying prefix) + flame (verb). parole.significato: Impressed with fear or apprehension; in fear.
parole.testo: From Middle English affrayed, affraied, past participle of afraien (“to affray”), from Anglo-Norman afrayer (“to terrify, disquiet, disturb”), from Old French effreer, esfreer (“to disturb, remove the peace from”), from es- (“out”) + freer (“to secure, secure the peace”), from Frankish *friþu (“secu

parole.significato: To take to graze or pasture, at a certain sum; used originally of the feeding of cattle in the king's forests, and coll…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman agister (“to pasture for a fee”).

parole.significato: A wing of a building, notably in a church separated from the nave proper by piers.
parole.testo: From Middle English ele, from Anglo-Norman ele (“wing”) (Modern French aile), from Latin āla (whence English ala). Further from Latin axis (whence English axis, atelier). parole.testo: From Middle English algorisme, augrym, from Anglo-Norman algorisme, augrim, from Medieval Latin algorismus, from Arabic الخَوَارِزْمِيّ (al-ḵawārizmiyy), the nisba of Persian mathematician Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī and a toponymic name meaning "the Chorasmian". The spelling change (-s- > -th-)

parole.significato: Loyalty or commitment to a cause, group, nation or of a subordinate to a superior.
parole.testo: From Middle English alegiaunce, from Anglo-Norman alegaunce (“loyalty of a liege-servant to one's lord”), variant of Old French ligeance, from lige (“vassal, liegeman”). More at liege.

parole.testo: From Late Middle English allegoriese, allegorisen (“to interpret (something) in a spiritual sense”), from Anglo-Norman allegorizer and Middle French allegoriser, alegoriser (“to express or interpret allegorically”) (modern French allégoriser), and from their etymon Late Latin allēgorizāre, the prese

parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English allegorie (“symbolic interpretation; symbolism; (Christianity) one of the four methods of interpreting the Bible”) + English -y (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting a condition, quality, or state). parole.significato: A narrow street or passageway, especially one through the middle of a block giving access to the rear of lots of buildi…
parole.testo: From Middle English aleye, from Anglo-Norman aleie, feminine of alé, past participle of aler (“to go”) (French aller). Doublet of allée.

parole.significato: To let one have as a suitable share of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English allowen, alowen, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman allouer, alouer, from Medieval Latin allaudāre, merged with alouer, from Medieval Latin allocō (“to assign”). parole.significato: To unite or form a connection between (people or things), as between families by marriage, or between states by confede…
parole.testo: From Middle English allien, alien (“to form an alliance, associate, join; to become an ally; to introduce (someone) as an ally; to marry; to become related (to someone); to attack, engage in combat; to combine; (cooking) to combine ingredients, especially to bind them together”) [and other forms], f

parole.significato: A person who co-operates with or helps another; an associate; a friend.
parole.testo: From Middle English allie, alie [and other forms], probably partly: * from allien (verb): see etymology 1; and * from Anglo-Norman allié, alié, alyé, allyé, Middle French allié, alié, allyé (“associate, supporter; friend; relative; person, state, etc., associated or united with another by alliance o

parole.significato: A German.
parole.testo: From Middle English Alemaine, Almayne, from Anglo-Norman Allemaine, Almaine et al., Old French Alemaigne, from Late Latin Alamannia (“territory of the Alamanni tribe”), from Alemannī, Allemannī, of Germanic origin probably corresponding to all + men. Compare Alemannic.

parole.significato: An astringent salt, usually occurring in the form of pale crystals, much used in the dyeing and tanning trade and in ce…
parole.testo: From Middle English alum, alym, alyme, from Anglo-Norman alum, alun, from Latin alūmen.

parole.significato: To collect into a mass or heap.
parole.testo: From Middle English *amassen (found only as Middle English massen (“to amass”)), from Anglo-Norman amasser, from Medieval Latin amassāre, from ad + massa (“lump, mass”). See mass.

parole.significato: A diplomat of the highest rank sent to a foreign court to represent there their sovereign or country. (Sometimes called…
parole.testo: From Middle English ambassadore, from Anglo-Norman ambassadeur, from Old Italian ambassadore, from Old Occitan ambaisador (“ambassador”), derivative of ambaissa (“service, mission, errand”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ambahtaz (“servant”), from Gaulish ambaxtos, from Proto-Celtic *ambaxtos, fro

parole.significato: A bookcase; a library or archive.
parole.testo: From Middle English almerie, from Anglo-Norman almarie, aumer, etc., from Old French almarie, from Latin armārium. Doublet of armarium, armoire, and almirah.

parole.significato: Willing to respond to persuasion or suggestions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman amenable, amesnable, from amener (“to bring or lead, fetch in or to”) + -able (“-able”); amener is in turn from a- + mener (“to lead, conduct”), from Late Latin mināre (“to drive”), Latin deponent minārī (“to threaten, menace”).

parole.significato: To impose a fine on; to fine.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman amercier, from Old French a (“at”) + merci (“mercy”), thus “at the mercy of”.

parole.significato: A non-statutory monetary penalty or forfeiture, usually applied at the discretion of a court.
parole.testo: From Middle English amercement, from Anglo-Norman amercier + -ment, from Old French à merci. Also from Medieval Latin amerciamentum, from amerciari + -amentum, learned Latinization of Anglo-Norman amerciament, amercement, amerciment. Equivalent to amerce + -ment.

parole.significato: The reduction of loan principal over a series of payments.
parole.testo: From Middle English amortisen (“to kill, alienate in mortmain”), from Anglo-Norman amorteser, alteration of Old French amortir, from Vulgar Latin *admortire (“to kill”), from Latin ad- and mors, mortem (“death”).

parole.significato: One from whom a person is descended, whether on the father's or mother's side, at any distance of time; a progenitor; a…
parole.testo: From Middle English ancestre, auncestre, ancessour; the first forms from Old French ancestre (modern French ancêtre), from the Latin nominative antecessor (“one who goes before”); the last form from Old French ancessor, from Latin antecessōrem, accusative of antecessor, from antecēdō (“to go before”

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, derived from, or possessed by, an ancestor or ancestors.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman ancestrel, from ancestre (“ancestor”), equivalent to ancestor + -al.

parole.significato: Extreme pain, either of body or mind; excruciating distress; an emotional state caused by intense misery or suffering.
parole.testo: From Middle English angwissh, anguishe, angoise, from Anglo-Norman anguise, anguisse, from Old French angoisse, from Latin angustia (“narrowness, scarcity, difficulty, distress”), from angustus (“narrow, difficult”), from angere (“to press together, cause pain, distress”). parole.significato: A person or thing that precedes or goes before.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English antecessour, from Anglo-Norman antecessour, Middle French antecesseur, or their etymon Latin antecessor, a compound of ante + cedo + -tor; thus a doublet of ancestor.

parole.significato: Placed separately (in regard to space or time).
parole.testo: From Middle English apart, aparte, a-part, a part, from Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem (“to the side”).

parole.significato: To charge (someone) with a crime; to impeach.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman apescher, rare variant of Old French empescher, from Latin impedicō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to appeals; appellate.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French apelant.

parole.significato: A respondent.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French apelé.

parole.significato: To appropriate (for); to set apart.
parole.testo: From Middle English appropren, approprien, from Anglo-Norman approprier, from Latin appropriō; compare appropriate.

parole.significato: That which appertains to something else; a belonging, accompaniment, adjunct, appendage, attribute, or accessory ; an a…
parole.testo: From Middle English appurtenaunce, from Anglo-Norman apurtenance and Old French apartenance, from apartenir, from Latin appertineō (“to belong, to appertain”). More at appertain. By surface analysis, appertain + -ance.

parole.significato: Full of ardor; expressing passion, spirit, or enthusiasm.
parole.testo: First attested circa 14th century as Middle English ardaunt, borrowed from Anglo-Norman ardent and Old French ardant, from Latin ardentem, accusative of ardēns, present participle of ardeō (“to burn”).

parole.significato: Great warmth of feeling; fervor; passion.
parole.testo: From Middle English ardour, ardowr, ardure, from Anglo-Norman ardour, from Old French ardur, from Latin ardor, from ardere (“to burn”).

parole.significato: A fact or statement used to support a proposition; a reason.
parole.testo: From Middle English argument, from Anglo-Norman and Old French arguement, from Latin argumentum. The English word is analysable as argue + -ment. Doublet of argumentum. Displaced native Old English racu and ġeflit.

parole.significato: A protective layer over a body, vehicle, or other object intended to deflect or diffuse damaging forces.
parole.testo: From Middle English armure, armour, armor, armeure, borrowed from Anglo-Norman armure and Old French armeüre, from Latin armātūra. Doublet of armature and armure. By surface analysis, arm (“to cover or furnish”) + -or (suffix forming agent nouns or nouns of quality, state, or condition).

parole.significato: A place where arms are kept, an arsenal.
parole.testo: From Middle English armerie, armurie, armorye, from Anglo-Norman armurrie, from armure (“arms, armor”) + -ie (“-y”). By surface analysis, armour + -y.

parole.significato: A large, highly organized military force, concerned mainly with ground (rather than air or naval) operations.
parole.testo: From (1386) Middle English armee, borrowed from Old French armee (cf. modern French armée), from Medieval Latin armāta (“armed force”), a noun taken from the past participle of Latin armāre (“to arm”), itself related to arma (“tools, arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join, fit together”).

parole.significato: Clothing and ornamentation; raiment.
parole.testo: From Middle English arrayen, from Anglo-Norman arraier (compare Old French arraier, areer (“to put in order”)), from Vulgar Latin *arrēdō (“to put in order, arrange, array”), from *rēdum (“preparation, order”), from Frankish *raid or *raidā (“preparation, order”) or Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌸𐍃 (garaiþs, “ready,

parole.significato: An arrival, especially one by ship or boat.
parole.testo: From Middle English a-rivage, arryvage, aryvage, from Anglo-Norman aryvage and/or Middle French arivage; equivalent to arrive + -age.

parole.significato: The rearguard of an army or other force.
parole.testo: From Middle English arryeregarde, from Anglo-Norman arer-garde and Middle French ariere-garde, arrer-garde, arriere-garde, arrer-garde, from Old French arieregarde, from arere (“behind”) + guarde (“guard”).

parole.significato: The crime of deliberately starting a fire with intent to cause damage.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman and Old French arson, from the verb ardoir, from Latin ardeō (“to burn”). Compare ardent.

parole.significato: Someone who assails
parole.testo: From Middle English assailour, from Anglo-Norman assaillour; equivalent to assail + -er.

parole.significato: Trial, attempt.
parole.testo: From Middle English assay (noun) and assayen (verb), from Anglo-Norman assai (noun) and Anglo-Norman assaier (verb), from Old French essai. Doublet of essay.

parole.significato: One who assays, or performs chemical tests on metals.
parole.testo: From Middle English assaier, assaiour, from Anglo-Norman assaiour; equivalent to assay + -er.

parole.significato: A thing or quality that has value, especially one that generates cash flows.
parole.testo: Back-formation from assets, from Anglo-Norman asetz, from Old French assez (“enough”). Compare Middle English asseth.

parole.significato: Any property or object of value that one possesses, usually considered as applicable to the payment of one's debts.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman asetz, from Old French assez (“enough”). Originally singular, with the meaning "enough to meet liabilities"; later reanalyzed as a plural form.

parole.significato: To absolve or release (someone) from blame or sin; to forgive, to pardon.
parole.testo: From Middle English assoilen (“to absolve or release from blame or sin”), from Anglo-Norman as(s)oiler, as(s)oilier, and Old French as(s)oille [and other forms], the present subjunctive, and as(s)oil, the present indicative, of as(s)oldre, as(s)oudre (“to absolve from blame”) (modern French absoudre

parole.significato: Synonym of assoil.
parole.testo: A Scottish variant of assoil, from Scottish Middle English assolyhe, assolȝe, retaining the -le- or -li- sounds of Anglo-Norman as(s)oilier and Old French as(s)oille which were dropped in modern English spoken in England.

parole.significato: at random, without application of due thought, haphazardly or recklessly
parole.testo: From earlier at adventure, with the same meaning, from Anglo-Norman and Old French a l'aventure (“at random”).

parole.significato: To come to or reach (a place) by motion or progression.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English atteinen, atteynen (“to achieve, attain; to be adequate or sufficient; to affect; to come or get to (a place), reach; to corrupt, taint; to overcome, overpower; to overtake; to succeed; to tamper with; (law) to bring to justice, punish”), from ataign-, a stem

parole.significato: The state a prisoner entered once a death sentence (usually for treason) had been issued; the state of being stripped o…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman ataindre ("to reach"), with infinitives used as nouns being frequent in Law French. Doublet of attain and attinge.

parole.significato: The chief legal advisor to the government, overseeing legal affairs and ensuring that laws are uniformly and justly app…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman and Law French, (modern French avocat général or procureur général), hence the unusual order of adjective following noun, instead of idiomatic English *general attorney. Compare court martial, notary public, secretary general, surgeon general.

parole.significato: One who audits bookkeeping accounts.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman auditour, from Latin audītor (“hearer, auditor”).

parole.significato: Augustinian.
parole.testo: From Middle English Austin, from Anglo-Norman Aostin, Austin, similar to Old French Aostin, Austin, a popular variant of Old French Agustin, from Latin Augustīnus, from Augustus (literally “majestic”). Doublet of Augustine.

parole.significato: The originator or creator of a work, especially of a literary composition; or, one of the creators of a collaborative w…
parole.testo: From Middle English auctour, from Anglo-Norman autour, from Old French autor, from Latin auctor, from augeō (“to increase, originate”). parole.significato: A plant of the genus Geum, especially Geum urbanum, or herb bennet.
parole.testo: From Middle English avence, from Anglo-Norman avance, Old French avence, from Medieval Latin avencia (“a kind of clover”).

parole.significato: To try not to meet or communicate with (a person); to shun.
parole.testo: From Middle English avoiden, from Anglo-Norman avoider, Old French esvuidier (“to empty out”), from es- + vuidier, from Vulgar Latin *vocitāre < Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately related to Latin vacuus. Displaced native Old English forbūgan (literally “to bend away from”).

parole.significato: A judgment, sentence, or final decision. Specifically: The decision of arbitrators in a case submitted.
parole.testo: From Middle English awarden, from Anglo-Norman awarder, from Medieval Latin *exwardare, from Latin ex (“out”) + Medieval Latin wardare, guardare (“to observe, regard, guard”); see ward, guard, regard.

parole.significato: A person, especially a man, who is socially regarded as able to marry but has not yet.
parole.testo: From Middle English bacheler, from Anglo-Norman and Old French bacheler (modern French bachelier), from Medieval Latin baccalārius, baccalāris (compare Tuscan baccalare (“squire”)).

parole.significato: Cured meat from the sides, belly, or back of a pig.
parole.testo: From Middle English bacoun (“meat from the back and sides of a pig”), from Anglo-Norman bacon, bacun (“ham, flitch, strip of lard”), from Old Low Frankish *bakō (“ham, flitch”), from Proto-Germanic *bakô, *bakkô (“back”), an extension of *baką, whence English back, which see for more. parole.significato: An officer of the court
parole.testo: From Middle English baillif, baylyf, from Anglo-Norman and Old French bailif (plural bailis), probably from Vulgar Latin *bāiulivus (“castellan”), from Latin bāiulus (“porter; steward”), whence also bail. As a translation of foreign titles, semantic loan from French bailli, Scots bailie, Dutch balju

parole.significato: Any of various aromatic resins exuded from certain plants, especially trees of the genus Commiphora of Africa, Arabia a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bawme, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Middle French baume, from Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, itself from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon). Spelling modified 16th c. to conform to Latin etymology. Doublet of balsam and desman.

parole.significato: A person whose profession is cutting the hair and beards of usually male customers.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰardʰéh₂ From Middle English barbour, from Anglo-Norman barbour, from Old French barbeor, from barbe (“beard”), from Latin barba.

parole.significato: Not bearing children, childless; hence also unable to bear children, sterile.
parole.testo: From Middle English bareyne, from Anglo-Norman baraigne, baraing (“sterile; barren”), of obscure origin; probably from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *baʀ (“bare; barren”), from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare”). If so, a cognate of English bare.

parole.significato: A structure that bars passage.
parole.testo: From Middle English barrer, barrere, barryȝer, from Anglo-Norman barrere (compare French barrière), from barre (“bar”).

parole.testo: Via Middle English basynet (attested since the early 1300s), from Anglo-Norman bacynet, bacinet (“little basin”), diminutive of bacin, bassin (“basin, helmet”), but compare bassinet.

parole.significato: To place in a basket or baskets.
parole.testo: From Middle English basket, from Anglo-Norman baschet, basket, bascat, from latin bascauda. Displaced native Old English mand. parole.significato: A prefix equivalent to grand-

parole.significato: An edge that is canted, one that is not a 90-degree angle; a chamfer.
parole.testo: From Middle English *bevel, from Anglo-Norman *baivel (whence obsolete French beauveau) a diminutive of Old French baïf (“open-mouthed”), perhaps from baer (“to gape”), from Medieval Latin *batāre (“to gape, yawn, be open”), probably of imitative origin. parole.significato: A drink.
parole.testo: From Middle English bever, from Anglo-Norman bever (modern French boire), from Latin bibō.

parole.significato: A written list or inventory. (Now obsolete except in specific senses or set phrases; bill of lading, bill of goods, etc…
parole.testo: From Middle English bille, from Anglo-Norman bille, from Old French bulle, from Medieval Latin bulla (“seal, sealed document”). Doublet of bull (“papal bull; bubble”) and bulla.

parole.significato: A short informal letter.
parole.testo: From Middle English bylet, from Anglo-Norman billette (“list, schedule”), from bille + -ette, from Latin bulla (“document”).

parole.significato: To persuade someone by using flattery; to cajole.
parole.testo: From Middle English blaundishen (“to flatter; to fawn; to be enticing or persuasive; to be favourable; of the sea: to become calm”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman blaundishen, from blandiss-, the extended stem of Middle French blandir + Middle English -ishen (suffix forming verbs). parole.significato: A tumour or other malignant swelling.

parole.significato: A military document entitling a commissioned officer to hold a higher rank temporarily, but without an increase in pay.

parole.significato: A bulk quantity of precious metal, usually gold or silver, assessed by weight and typically cast as ingots.

parole.significato: To strike bluntly, particularly with the head.
parole.testo: From Middle English butten, from Anglo-Norman buter, boter (“to push, butt, strike”), from Frankish *bautan (“to hit, beat”), from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to beat, push”). Cognate with Old English bēatan (“to beat”). More at beat.

parole.significato: To lift (something) and take it to another place; to transport (something) by lifting.

parole.significato: A person who transports a load on a cart that is drawn by a beast of burden.
parole.testo: From Middle English carter, cartere, cartare, equivalent to cart + -er. Merged with Middle English careter, caretier (“coachman, charioteer”, a surname), from Anglo-Norman careter (compare French charretier).

parole.significato: The act of seizing or capturing.

parole.significato: An embankment holding in water; a dam.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman caucie, chaucee et al., from Late Latin calceāta. In Guernsey use after Guernsey Norman cauchie.

parole.significato: An ornamental container for burning incense, especially during religious ceremonies.

parole.significato: That person; the person in question.

parole.significato: One who chafes.

parole.testo: From Middle English cheker, aphetic from Anglo-Norman escheker (“chessboard”), from Latin scaccarium, thus ultimately morpheme-for-morpheme cognate to etymology 1.

parole.significato: A cheerful attitude; happiness; a good, happy, or positive mood.
parole.testo: From Middle English chere, from Anglo-Norman chere, from Old French chiere (“head, face; appearance; reception, hospitality; meal, dinner, food”) (Modern French chère), from Late Latin cara (“head”).

parole.significato: Chequered; divided into small squares (chequers) by transverse vertical and horizontal lines.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman escheké, eschequé (“chequered”), from eschec (“chess, check”). Influenced by chequ(er) + -y and check.

parole.significato: A small fruit, usually red, black or yellow, with a smooth hard seed and a short hard stem.

parole.significato: A leafy herb, Anthriscus cerefolium, resembling parsley.
parole.testo: From Middle English chervell, from Old English cerfille, from Anglo-Norman chervele (compare Jèrriais chèrfi), from Latin caerefolium, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon).

parole.significato: A cutting tool used to remove parts of stone, wood or metal by pushing or pounding the back when the sharp edge is agai…
parole.testo: From Middle English chisel, chesel, from Old Northern French chisel, cisel, from cisoir (with a change in suffix), from Late Latin cīsōrium (“cutting tool”), from Latin caedō (“cut”). Doublet of scissors.

parole.significato: Any object used as a wedge or filler, especially when placed behind a wheel to prevent it from rolling.
parole.testo: From Middle English *chokke (possibly attested in Middle English chokkefull), from Anglo-Norman choque (compare modern Norman chouque), from an Old Northern French variant of Old French çouche, çouche (“block, log”), of Celtic origin, from Gaulish *tsukka (compare Breton soc’h (“thick”), Old Irish t

parole.significato: A singer in a choir; especially a child in a church or cathedral choir.
parole.testo: Derived from late Middle English queristre, from an Anglo-Norman variant of Old French cueriste, from cuer (see Middle French cuer). Equivalent to choir + -ster.

parole.significato: A written account of events and when they happened, ordered by time.
parole.testo: From Middle English cronicle, cronycle, from Anglo-Norman cronicle, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of or concerning time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).

parole.significato: A resident of a city or town, especially one with legally recognized rights or duties.
parole.testo: From Middle English citeseyn (“inhabitant of a city or town”), citezein, citisein, from Anglo-Norman citesain (“city-dweller, town-dweller”), citesein, citezein, alteration of citeien from cite (“city”) + -ien (“-ain”) (probable variant of cithein perhaps influenced by dainzain (“denizen”), deinzein

parole.significato: An ancient Norman legal procedure, still valid in the Channel Islands, in which any person can publicly recite a certai…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman/Law French clameur de haro.

parole.significato: clary sage (Salvia sclarea)
parole.testo: From Middle English clarie, from Anglo-Norman sclaree, from Late or Medieval Latin sclarēia.

parole.significato: Transparent in colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English clere, from Anglo-Norman cler, from Old French cler (Modern French clair), from Latin clarus. parole.significato: A person who or thing that collects, or which creates or manages a collection.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English collectour, from Anglo-Norman collectour, from Late Latin collēctor, from Latin colligō (“to gather together”).

parole.significato: The spectral composition of visible light.
parole.testo: From Middle English colour, color, borrowed from Anglo-Norman colur, from Old French colour, color, from Latin color. Doublet of couleur. parole.significato: A person who comforts someone who is suffering.
parole.testo: From Middle English comfortour et al, from Anglo-Norman confortour, from Old French conforter. See comfort.

parole.significato: To begin, start.
parole.testo: From Middle English commencen, comencen (also as contracted comsen, cumsen), from Anglo-Norman comencer, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, formed from Latin com- + initiō (whence English initiate).

parole.significato: One who commissions something.
parole.testo: From Middle English commissioner, from Anglo-Norman commissionaire, from Medieval Latin commissiōnārius. Doublet of commissionaire. By surface analysis, commission + -er.

parole.significato: Spacious and convenient; roomy and comfortable.
parole.testo: From Middle English commodious (“convenient, advantageous”), from Anglo-Norman commodious, Old French commodieux, directly from Medieval Latin commodiosus (“convenient, useful”), irregularly from Latin commodus (“suitable, fit, convenient”), from com- + modus (“measure, manner”), ultimately from Pro

parole.significato: Anything movable (a good) that is bought and sold.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English commoditee, borrowed from Anglo-Norman commoditee, from Latin commoditās.

parole.significato: Mutual; shared by more than one.
parole.testo: From Middle English comun, from Anglo-Norman comun, from Old French comun (rare in the Gallo-Romance languages, but reinforced as a Carolingian calque of Proto-West Germanic *gamainī (“common”) in Old French), from Latin commūnis (“common, public, general”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom-moy-ni-s (“

parole.significato: A joining together of minds or spirits; a mental connection.
parole.testo: From Middle English comunioun, communyoun, from Anglo-Norman comunion or Middle French communion, from Ecclesiastical Latin commūniō (“communion”), from Latin commūnis.

parole.significato: Capable of working together without conflict.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English compatible, fron Anglo-Norman compatible, from Medieval Latin compatibilis (“in compatibile beneficium, a benefice which could be held together with another one”), from Late Latin compator (“to suffer with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion.

parole.significato: One who compiles.
parole.testo: From Middle English compilour, from Anglo-Norman compilour, from Old French compileur, from Latin compīlātōrem, equivalent to compile + -er.

parole.significato: The act of complaining.
parole.testo: From Middle English compleynte, from Anglo-Norman compleint, from Old French compleindre, eventually from Latin planctus (whence plaint).

parole.significato: A sexual partner, especially a woman, to whom one is not or cannot be married.
parole.testo: From Middle English concubine (first attested 1250–1300), from Anglo-Norman concubine, from Latin concubīna, equivalent to concub- (variant stem of concumbō (“to lie together”)) + feminine suffix -īna.

parole.significato: An alliance.
parole.testo: From Middle English confederacie, from Anglo-Norman confederacie, from Latin cōnfoederātiō. Doublet of confederation.

parole.significato: To admit to the truth, particularly in the context of sins or crimes committed.
parole.testo: From Middle English confessen, from Anglo-Norman confesser, from Old French confesser, from Latin confessus (Old French confés), past participle of cōnfiteor (“to confess, admit”) from con- + fateor (“to admit”). parole.significato: One who confesses faith in Christianity in the face of persecution, but who is not martyred.
parole.testo: From Middle English confessor, confessour, from Anglo-Norman confessour, and its source, Latin cōnfessor, from cōnfiteor (“confess, admit, acknowledge”). By surface analysis, confess + -or.

parole.significato: To perplex or puzzle.
parole.testo: From Middle English confounden (“destroy, ruin, perplex”), from Anglo-Norman cunfundre and Old French confondre, from Latin cōnfundō (“to mingle, mix together”). Related to found (“to melt (metals in a foundry)”) (but not to found (“to start”), nor to find) and to fusion.

parole.significato: To puzzle, perplex, baffle, bewilder (somebody); to afflict by being complicated, contradictory, or otherwise difficult…
parole.testo: Back-formation from confused, from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō.

parole.significato: unable to think clearly or understand
parole.testo: Originally from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus + Middle English -ed (past participial suffix), from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō; now equivalent to confuse (a back-formation) + -ed.

parole.significato: One who conjures, a magician.
parole.testo: From Middle English conjurer, from Anglo-Norman conjurour (“conjurer, conspirator”). Equivalent to conjure + -er.

parole.significato: The duty of directing a ship, usually used with the verb to have or to take and accompanied by the article "the."
parole.testo: Variant of cond, from Middle English conduen, condien, from Anglo-Norman conduire, from Latin condūcō (“lead, bring or draw together”), from con- (“with, together”) + dūcō (“lead”). Doublet of conduce.

parole.significato: One who conserves, preserves or protects something.
parole.testo: From Middle English conservatour, from Anglo-Norman conservatour, from Latin cōnservātor (“one who conserves”), agent noun from cōnservō (“to preserve”).

parole.significato: An agreement or arrangement between multiple parties to do something harmful, immoral or subversive; an instance of col…
parole.testo: From Middle English conspiracie, from Anglo-Norman conspiracie, from Latin cōnspīrātiō, from conspire + -acy.

parole.significato: One of a group that acts in harmony to do something unlawful and unethical; a person who is part of a conspiracy.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman conspiratour.

parole.significato: A benefactor; someone who donates to charity or some cause.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman contributour (from Latin contribuō); equivalent to contribute + -or.

parole.significato: One who controls something.
parole.testo: From Middle English countreroller, from Anglo-Norman contreroulour and Middle French contreroleur (French contrôleur), from Medieval Latin contrārotulātor, from *contrārotulāre (from which control). Doublet of comptroller. By surface analysis, control + -er.

parole.significato: The act of converting something or someone.
parole.testo: From Middle English conversion, conversioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman conversion, from Latin conversiō, from convertō.

parole.significato: To find guilty, as a result of legal proceedings, or (informal) in a moral sense.
parole.testo: From Middle English convicten, from Anglo-Norman convicter, from Latin convictus, the past participle of convincō (“to convict”). Doublet of convince. Displaced native Old English forwyrċan (“to convict, condemn”).

parole.significato: A firmly held belief.
parole.testo: From late Middle English conviction, from Anglo-Norman conviction, from Latin convictiō, from convictus, the past participle of convincō (“to convict”). Equivalent to convict + -ion.

parole.significato: A rabbit, especially the European rabbit, Oryctolagus cuniculus (formerly known as Lepus cuniculus).
parole.testo: From Middle English cony, back formation from conies (plural), from Anglo-Norman conis, the plural of connil (“rabbit”), from Latin cunīculus, of unknown origin. parole.significato: The annual herb Coriandrum sativum, used in many cuisines.
parole.testo: From Middle English coriandre, from Anglo-Norman coriandre, from Old French corïandre, from Latin coriandrum, from Ancient Greek κορίανδρον (koríandron), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: Relating to a crown or coronation.
parole.testo: From Middle English coronal, from Anglo-Norman coronal, from Latin corōnālis (“related to a crown”), from corōna (“a crown”).

parole.significato: To make something that was wrong become right; to remove error from.
parole.testo: From Middle English correcten, borrowed from Anglo-Norman correcter, from Latin correctus.

parole.significato: One who couches.
parole.testo: From Middle English coucher, from Anglo-Norman; equivalent to couch + -er.

parole.significato: In opposition to.

parole.significato: The wife of a count or earl.

parole.significato: The land ruled by a count or a countess.

parole.significato: A dog used for coursing.

parole.significato: Polite behavior.

parole.significato: A person in attendance at a royal court.

parole.significato: A first cousin.

parole.significato: A blanket used as a bed covering, usually quilted.
parole.testo: From Middle English coverlite, from Anglo-Norman cuver-lit, formed on cuvrir (“to cover”) + lit (“bed”). Cognate with Catalan cobrellit.

parole.significato: Covert, under coverture; married.

parole.significato: Distastefully desirous or keen, especially for something belonging to someone else; avaricious.
parole.testo: From Middle English coveitous, from Anglo-Norman *cuveitus, from Medieval Latin as if *cupiditosus, from Latin cupiditas (“desire”); see covet.

parole.significato: Lack of courage.
parole.testo: From Middle English cowardise, borrowed from Anglo-Norman cuardise (modern French couardise).

parole.significato: A creditor.
parole.testo: From Middle English creaunsour, from Anglo-Norman creanceour and Old French creanceor, from creancer.

parole.significato: A person to whom a debt is owed.
parole.testo: From Middle English creditour, from Anglo-Norman creditour, from Latin crēditor, from crēditum (“loan”), from crēditus, perfect passive participle of crēdō (“lend”).

parole.significato: Against the law; forbidden by law.
parole.testo: From Middle English cryminal, borrowed from Anglo-Norman criminal, from Late Latin criminalis, from Latin crimen (“crime”).

parole.significato: An old woman.
parole.testo: From Middle English crone, from Anglo-Norman carogne (compare central Old French charogne (a term of abuse, literally “carrion, carcass, old sheep, hag”), whence modern French charogne). Doublet of carrion.

parole.significato: The croup of a horse or quadruped.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English cropoun, from Anglo-Norman cropoun (continental Old French crepon), thus a doublet of Etymology 1.

parole.significato: A royal, imperial or princely headdress; a diadem.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English coroune, from Anglo-Norman corone, from Latin corōna (“crown, wreath”), from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē). parole.significato: A small bottle or container used to hold a condiment, such as oil, vinegar, salt, or pepper, for use at a dining table.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman cruet, diminutive of Old French crue (“an earthen pot”), from Old Saxon krūka.

parole.significato: A strap, looped under a horse's tail, used to stop a saddle from slipping.
parole.testo: From Middle English croper, crouper, from Anglo-Norman cruper, cropere, from Old French cropiere, crupiere, from the same Germanic root as croup. Doublet of croupiere.

parole.significato: To cover with a crust.
parole.testo: From Middle English cruste, from Anglo-Norman and Old French cruste, from Latin crusta (“hard outer covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”), related to Old Norse hroðr (“scurf”), Old English hruse (“earth”), Old High German hrosa

parole.significato: To shout out 'Havoc!'; that is, to give an army the order to plunder.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from the Anglo-Norman phrase crier havok (“cry havoc”) (a signal to soldiers to seize plunder), from Old French crier (“cry out, shout”) + havot (“pillaging, looting”).

parole.significato: The person or thing at fault for a problem or crime.

parole.significato: Inquisitiveness; the tendency to ask and learn about things by asking questions, investigating, or exploring.
parole.testo: From Middle English curiosite, variant of curiouste, from Anglo-Norman curiouseté, from Latin cūriōsitātem, accusative of cūriōsitās. By surface analysis, curious + -ity. Displaced native Old English firwitt.

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English courtelage, curtilage, curtylage (“vegetable garden; croft; gardening, farming”), from Anglo-Norman curtilage, from Old French cortillage, courtillage (modern French courtillage (obsolete); compare Medieval Latin cortilagium, curtilagium), from cortil, cortill (“small c

parole.testo: Variant of courtesy (1525) (from court + -esy), from Middle English curteisie, curtesie, from Anglo-Norman curtesie, from Old French curteisie, cortoisie.

parole.significato: One whose business is making or dealing in cutlery.
parole.testo: From Middle English coteler (“knife-maker”), from Anglo-Norman cuteler, from Old French coutelier (“knife-maker”).

parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman cy pres (“as close”) (i.e. as close as possible), equivalent to Modern French si près or aussi près.

parole.testo: From Middle English cignet, signet, from Anglo-Norman cignet, diminutive of Old French cigne (“swan”), from Latin cygnus, cycnus (“swan”), from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos, “swan”).

parole.significato: (also dairy products or dairy produce) Products produced from milk.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deyerie (“dairy, dairy farm”), from Anglo-Norman deyerie (“dairy”), from deye (“dairymaid”) + -erie (“-ery”); by surface analysis, dey (“dairymaid”) + -ry. Cognate with Scots dery, dyrie.

parole.significato: To waste time in trivial activities, or in idleness; to trifle.

parole.significato: A title of honour or respect similar to "master" or "Sir", used of historical and legendary figures of the past.

parole.significato: Exposure to likely harm; risk of death or serious injury.

parole.significato: Full of danger.
parole.testo: From Middle English daungerous (“difficult, severe, domineering, arrogant, fraught with danger”), dangerous, from Anglo-Norman [Term?], from Old French dangereus (“threatening, difficult”), from dangier. Equivalent to danger + -ous. Displaced native Old English frēcne.

parole.significato: In the names of legal actions, pleas, writs, etc.: final, last; dernier.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman derreyn, dreyn; from Old French darrein, darrain (Modern French dernier); from an assumed Late Latin *deretrānus (“to hinder”), from dē (“from, away from”) + retrō (“back, backwards; before, formerly”).

parole.significato: A senior official in a college or university, who may be in charge of a division or faculty (for example, the dean of s…
parole.testo: From Middle English den, deen (“dean”), from Anglo-Norman deen and continental Old French deien (modern French doyen), from Latin decānus. Doublet of doyen.

parole.significato: To exclude or shut out; to bar.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman debarrer.

parole.significato: Rot; any processes or result of organic matter being gradually decomposed, especially by microbial action.

parole.significato: Able to be deceived; gullible.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deceyvable (“deceptive, misleading”), from Anglo-Norman decevable; equivalent to deceive + -able.

parole.significato: To trick or mislead.
parole.testo: From Middle English deceyven, from Anglo-Norman deceivre, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive; beguile; entrap”), from dē- (“from”) + capiō (“to seize”); see captive. Compare conceive, perceive, receive. Displaced native Old English beswīcan.

parole.significato: A person who lies or deceives.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deceyvour, from Anglo-Norman decevour; by surface analysis, deceive + -er. Displaced native Old English swica.

parole.significato: Of a quantity, to become smaller.
parole.testo: From Middle English decresen, alteration of discresen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French descreistre (French: décroître), from Latin decrescere.

parole.significato: Becoming gradually less; diminishing.
parole.testo: From decressant, from Anglo-Norman [Term?], present participle of decreistre (“to decrease”).

parole.significato: To disgrace; to bring into disrepute.
parole.testo: From Middle English defamen, from Anglo-Norman defamer (verb), defame (noun), and its source, Latin diffāmō, from fāma (“fame; rumour; reputation”).

parole.significato: Destruction, defeat, overthrow.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman defeasaunce.

parole.significato: Capable of being defeated, terminated, annulled, voided or invalidated.
parole.testo: Back-formation from defeasance + -ible, from Anglo-Norman defesaunce, Old French desfaisance, a deverbal noun from desfaire (“to undo”) (Modern French défaire), from des- (“un-, apart”) + fere, faire (“to do”) + -able, reflecting Latin dis- + facere + -ābilis. Near-doublet of defeatable.

parole.significato: Someone who defends people or property.
parole.testo: From Middle English defender, deffender, defendere, defendour, defendoure, partly from Anglo-Norman defendour, from Old French defendëor; partly from Middle English defenden + -ere, equivalent to defend + -er.

parole.significato: A period of time before an event occurs; the act of delaying; procrastination; lingering inactivity.
parole.testo: From Middle English delaien, borrowed from Anglo-Norman delaier, Old French deslaier, from des- + Old French laier (“to leave”), a conflation of Old Frankish *lattjan ("to delay, hinder"; from Proto-Germanic *latjaną (“to delay, hinder, stall”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to leave, leave beh

parole.significato: Pleasing to the sense of taste; tasty.
parole.testo: From Middle English delicious, from Anglo-Norman delicious, from Old French delicious, delicieux, from Late Latin dēliciōsus (“delicate, delicious”), from dēliciae (“delights”), plural of dēlicia (“pleasure”), from delicere (“to allure, to entice”), from de- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, deceive”), fr

parole.significato: To set free from restraint or danger.
parole.testo: From Middle English deliveren, from Anglo-Norman and Old French delivrer, from Latin dē + līberō (“to set free”). Compare typologically dispatch, analyzable as dis- + impeach, from Latin impedicō (also akin to impede).

parole.significato: The act of conveying something.
parole.testo: From Middle English deliveri et al., from Anglo-Norman, from Old French delivrer.

parole.significato: To manage; to conduct; to treat.
parole.testo: From Middle English demenen, demeinen, from Anglo-Norman demener, from Old French demener, from de- + mener (“to conduct, lead”), from Latin mināre, from minārī (“to threaten”).

parole.significato: A lord's chief manor place, with that part of the lands belonging thereto which has not been granted out in tenancy; a…
parole.testo: From Middle English demayne, from Anglo-Norman demeyne, demene et al., Old French demeine, demaine, demeigne, domaine (“power”) (whence French domaine (“domain”)), a noun use of an adjective, from Latin dominicus (“belonging to a lord or master”), from dominus (“master, proprietor, owner”). parole.significato: partial
parole.testo: From Middle English demi (“half, half-sized, partial”), from Anglo-Norman demi (“half”), from Vulgar Latin *dimedius, from Latin dīmidius, from dis- (“apart; in two”) + medius (“middle”).

parole.significato: Chiefly followed by to, and sometimes by at or on: to object or be reluctant; to balk, to take exception.

parole.significato: Modest, quiet, reserved, or serious.

parole.significato: A motion by a party to a legal action for the immediate or summary judgment of the court on the question of whether, as…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman demurrer, form of Old French demourer (“to demur”), infinitive used as noun.

parole.significato: An object forfeited to the state (and supposedly to God) because it had caused the death of a person.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman deodande, from Latin deodandum, from Deo dandum (“to be given to God”).

parole.significato: A lengthy discourse on a subject.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman descaunt, from Medieval Latin discantus. Doublet of discant.

parole.significato: Senses relating to moving from a higher to a lower position.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English descenden (“to move downwards, fall, descend; to slope downwards; to go from a better to a worse condition, decline, degenerate; to be a descendant, derive from (a source); etc.”), from Anglo-Norman descendere, descendre, and Old French descendere, descendre (

parole.significato: An instance of descending; act of coming down.
parole.testo: From Middle English and Anglo-Norman descente, from Anglo-Norman descendre (“to descend”); see descend. Compare ascent, ascend. Doublet of desant.

parole.significato: To give up as beyond hope or expectation; to despair of.
parole.testo: From Middle English dispeir, from Anglo-Norman despeir and Old French desperer (from Latin dēspērō, dēspērāre), or desesperer, from des- (“dis-”) + esperer (“hope”). See also desperate. Displaced native Old English ormōdnes (“despair”) and Old English ortrīewan (“to despair”).

parole.significato: Full of contempt or ill will; opprobrious; insulting.
parole.testo: From Middle English despitous, from Anglo-Norman despitous.

parole.significato: To disport.
parole.testo: From Middle English disporten, from Anglo-Norman and Old French desporter, deporter (“to take pleasure”).

parole.significato: A large warhorse, especially of a medieval knight.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman destrer, destrier.

parole.significato: The right to keep a person, or a person's goods or property, against his will; a type of custody.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman detener, from Old French detenir. By surface analysis, detain + -er (action noun suffix). First attested in the 17th century.

parole.significato: A person who belittles the worth of another person or cause.
parole.testo: From Middle English detractor, dectractour, from Anglo-Norman detractour, from Old French detractor.

parole.significato: A card with two pips, one of four in a standard deck of playing cards.
parole.testo: From Middle English dewes (“two”), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French deus, from Latin duo. The word was used by Ford Motor Co. in 1932 to describe a two-seater car model.

parole.significato: A coin worth one-tenth of a dollar, that is, ten cents.
parole.testo: From Middle English dime, from Anglo-Norman disme (“one tenth, tithe”) (modern French dîme), from Medieval Latin decima, from Latin decima (pars) (“tenth (part)”). Doublet of decim, decima, and decime.

parole.significato: A lessening, decrease or reduction.
parole.testo: From Middle English diminucioun, from Anglo-Norman diminuciun, Old French diminucion, from Latin dīminūtiō.

parole.significato: The absence or reverse of accord.
parole.testo: From Middle English disacorden, from Anglo-Norman desacorder.

parole.significato: To deforest.
parole.testo: From Middle English disafforeten, from Anglo-Norman disaforester and its probable etymon Latin disafforestō. By surface analysis, dis- + afforest.

parole.significato: To fail to agree; to have a different opinion or belief.
parole.testo: From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”), from Old French desagreer, desagrëer (“to be disagreeable; to be unpleasant”) (modern French désagréer (“to displease”)); the English word is analysable as dis- + agree.

parole.significato: To refuse to allow.
parole.testo: From Middle English disallowen, desallowen, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman desalouer, Old French desalöer. By surface analysis, dis- + allow.

parole.significato: To deprive of weapons; to deprive of the means of attack or defense; to render defenseless.
parole.testo: From Middle English desarmen (“to divest of arms”), from Anglo-Norman desarmer.

parole.significato: A controlled behaviour; self-control.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Anglo-Norman, from Old French descipline, from Latin disciplina (“instruction”), from discipulus (“pupil”), influenced by disco (“to learn”), from Proto-Indo-European *dek- (“(cause to) accept”).

parole.significato: To completely renounce claims to; to deny ownership of or responsibility for
parole.testo: From Middle English disclaimen, from Anglo-Norman disclaimer, from Old French desclamer (French déclamer), des- + clamer.

parole.significato: One who disclaims, disowns, or renounces.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English discleymer, from Anglo-Norman desclamer; and partly from disclaim + -er.

parole.significato: Mental or bodily distress.
parole.testo: From Middle English discomforten, from Anglo-Norman descomforter, equivalent to dis- + comfort.

parole.significato: The occurrence of something being discontinued; a cessation; an incomplete ending.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French descontinuer.

parole.significato: Lack of concord, agreement, harmony; disaccord.
parole.testo: Circa 1230, Middle English descorde, discorde; from Anglo-Norman, Old French descort (derivative of descorder), descorde (“disagreement”); from Latin discordia, from discors (“disagreeing, disagreement”), from dis- (“apart”) + cor, cordis (“heart”). parole.significato: Not loyal, without loyalty.

parole.significato: Disastrous, calamitous.

parole.significato: To cause to feel apprehension; great sadness, or fear; to deprive of energy.

parole.significato: Something or someone that dispenses things.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman dispensour, from Old French despenseor, from Latin dispensator. By surface analysis, dispense + -er.

parole.significato: A show or spectacle.
parole.testo: From Middle English displayen, from Anglo-Norman despleier and Old French despleier, desploiier, from Medieval Latin displicare (“to unfold, display”), from Latin dis- (“apart”) + plicāre (“to fold”). Doublet of deploy.

parole.significato: To make not pleased; to cause a feeling of disapprobation or dislike in; to be disagreeable to; to vex slightly.
parole.testo: English dis- + please, from Middle English displesen, from Anglo-Norman despleisir, desplere, from Old French desplere (des- + plere).

parole.significato: To amuse oneself divertingly or playfully; in particular, to cavort or gambol.

parole.significato: The act of disseizing; an act of unlawful dispossessing, especially of someone's lands.
parole.testo: From Middle English disseisen, from Anglo-Norman disseisine; equivalent to dis- + seizin.

parole.significato: To separate (two or more things); to split apart (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English disseveren, from Anglo-Norman desevrer, Old French dessevrer, from Vulgar Latin *dissēperō, dissēperāre, from Latin dis- + sēparō.

parole.significato: Slander.
parole.testo: From Middle English disclaundre, disslaundre, from Anglo-Norman disclaundre, from sclandre, esclandre, from Old French esclandre. See slander and compare Middle English sclaundre. By surface analysis, dis- + slander.

parole.significato: The act of falling in drops, or the act of pouring out in drops.
parole.testo: From Middle English distillacioun, from Anglo-Norman distillacioun, from Latin distīllātiōnem, accusative of distīllātiō.

parole.significato: to confuse a quiet, constant state or a calm, continuous flow, in particular: thoughts, actions or liquids.
parole.testo: From Middle English destourben, from Anglo-Norman distourber and Old French destorber, from Latin disturbare, intensifying for turbare (“to throw into disorder”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH-, *(s)turH- (“to rotate, swirl, twirl, move around”).

parole.significato: A peppergrass of species Lepidium latifolium, native from Iberia to the Himalayas, introduced elsewhere.
parole.testo: From an Anglo-Norman or Middle English form ditaundere attested in a glossary ca. 1265 and by an obscure reason extended from the word underlying dittany.

parole.significato: A small ornamental piece of lace or linen or paper used to protect a surface from scratches by hard objects such as vas…
parole.testo: From Doiley, the name of a 17th-century London draper. The surname is Anglo-Norman, from d'Œuilly, name of several places in Calvados, from Old French oeil (“eye”).

parole.significato: One who makes a donation.
parole.testo: From Middle English donoure, donour; from Anglo-Norman donour, from Old French doneur (See French donneur).

parole.significato: One of the legendary “twelve peers” or renowned warriors of Charlemagne, the Emperor of the Romans from 800 to 814.
parole.testo: From Middle English dosse per, dousse-per (“one of Charlemagne’s twelve peers or paladins; one of the twelve great peers of France at later times; a famous knight or noble”) [and other forms], treated as a singular form of dosse pers, dousse pers [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman, Middle French d

parole.significato: Payment, such as property or money, paid by the bride's family to the groom or his family at the time of marriage.
parole.testo: From Middle English dowarye, dowerie, from Anglo-Norman dowarie, douarie, from Old French douaire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dower.

parole.significato: One who sells cloths; a dealer in cloths; a textile merchant.
parole.testo: From Middle English draper, from Anglo-Norman draper, from Old French drapier, from drap + -ier.

parole.significato: A kind of wood used especially in the handles of knives; the root of the box tree.
parole.testo: From Middle English dogeon, apparently from Anglo-Norman or Middle French, but the ultimate origin is obscure. Compare French douve (“stave”).

parole.significato: A legal concept where a person is ensured all legal rights when deprived of their liberty for a given reason.
parole.testo: From Middle English dewe processe, from Anglo-Norman due procés.

parole.significato: An underground prison or vault, typically built underneath a castle.
parole.testo: From Middle English dongeoun (“keep of a castle; dungeon; abyss, cave, den; whirlpool”), from Anglo-Norman donjun (“keep of a castle; keep used as a prison; dungeon”) and continental Old French donjon (“keep of a castle”), from Vulgar Latin *dominiōnem, seemingly derived from Latin dominus (“master,

parole.significato: Any of several large carnivorous and carrion-eating birds in the family Accipitridae, having a powerful hooked bill and…
parole.testo: From Middle English egle, from Anglo-Norman egle, from Old French aigle, from Latin aquila. Displaced native Middle English ern, earn, arn, from Old English earn (“eagle”). More at erne.

parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman aisement, easement, eisement, esament, esement, and Middle French aisement (“comfort, convenience, ease, facility, opportunity; a benefit, relief; a right to use land, a thing, etc.; a privy”), from aisier (“to put at ease; to facilitate”) + -ment (“-ment, suffix forming nouns, usu

parole.significato: Comfortable; at ease.
parole.testo: From Middle English esy, eesy, partly from Middle English ese (“ease”) + -y, equivalent to ease + -y, and partly from Anglo-Norman eisé from Old French aisié (“eased, at ease, at leisure”), past participle of aisier (“to put at ease”), from aise (“empty space, elbow room, opportunity”), of uncertain

parole.significato: Any of various wading birds of the genera Egretta or Ardea that includes herons, many of which are white or buff, and s…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman egret, aigrette (“egret”), from Old Occitan aigreta, diminutive of aigron (“heron”), from Medieval Latin hairo, from Frankish *haigro (“heron”). Cognate with Old High German heigaro (“heron”), Old English hrāgra (“heron”). Doublet of aigrette. More at heron.

parole.significato: A process of choosing a leader, members of parliament, councillors, or other representatives by popular vote.
parole.testo: From Middle English eleccioun, eleccion, from Anglo-Norman eleccioun, from Latin ēlectiōn-, stem of ēlectiō (“choice, selection”), from ēligō (“to pluck out, to choose”). Equivalent to elect + -ion. Displaced native Old English cyre (“choice, free will, election”).

parole.significato: To remove (something) to a distance.
parole.testo: From Middle English eloynen, from Anglo-Norman esloignier, Old French esloignier, from Vulgar Latin *exlongō, from Latin longe. Doublet of elongate.

parole.significato: Of a married or engaged person, to run away from home with a paramour.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman aloper (“to abduct, run away”), itself borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *andihlaupan (“to run away”). Equivalent to and- + lope as well as and- + leap (these being doublets). More at lope.

parole.significato: To steal or misappropriate money that one has been trusted with, especially to steal money from the organisation for wh…
parole.testo: From Middle English embesilen, from Anglo-Norman embesiler, embesillier, embeseillier (“to steal, cause to disappear”), from em- + Old French besillier (“to torment, destroy, gouge”), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: A list of jurors; a panel.
parole.testo: The verb is from Middle English empanellen, from Anglo-Norman and Old French empaneller.

parole.significato: The male monarch or ruler of an empire.
parole.testo: From Middle English emperour, from Anglo-Norman emperour, from Latin imperātorem, derived from imperō (“to command”). Doublet of imperator. Displaced earlier Old English casere, from Latin Caesar.

parole.significato: To retain (someone) as an employee.
parole.testo: From late Middle English emploien, imploien, emplien (“to apply to a specific purpose”), from Anglo-Norman emploier, Old French emploiier (“to entangle, fabricate, to make use of”), ultimately from Latin implicāre (“to infold, entangle, involve, engage”), from in- (“in”) + plicāre (“to fold”). Doubl

parole.significato: The female monarch (ruler) of an empire.
parole.testo: From Middle English emperice, emperesse, from Anglo-Norman and Old French empereriz, from Latin imperatrix, equivalent to emperor + -ess. Doublet of imperatrix. Compare modern French impératrice.

parole.significato: An opaque, glassy coating baked onto metal or ceramic objects.
parole.testo: From Middle English enamel, from Anglo-Norman enamailler, from en- (“in-”) + amailler (“to enamel”), variant of Old French esmailler (“to enamel”), from esmal (“enamel”), from Early Medieval Latin smaltum, from Frankish *smalt, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaną (“to melt, smelt”).

parole.significato: A cause, reason.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English enchesoun, from Anglo-Norman enchaisun, encheson, alteration of achaisun, acheison after the prefix en-.

parole.significato: To meet (someone) or find (something), especially unexpectedly.

parole.significato: To mentally support; to motivate, give courage, hope or spirit.
parole.testo: From Middle English encouragen, encoragen, from Anglo-Norman encoragier, from Old French encoragier. Displaced native Old English hiertan, tyhtan, and trymman. By surface analysis, en- + courage.

parole.significato: To famish; to starve.
parole.testo: From Middle English (verb forms) enfamecht, enfamyched, enfamyschist, enfamyscht, probably from Anglo-Norman; compare Old French afamer, enfaminer.

parole.significato: A large construction used in warfare, such as a battering ram, catapult etc.

parole.significato: A soldier engaged in designing or constructing military works for attack or defence, or other engineering works.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from: * Middle English enginour (“one who designs, constructs, or operates military works for attack or defence, etc.; machine designer”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman enginour, engigneour [and other forms], and Middle French and Old French engigneor, engigneour, engignier

parole.significato: Those people living in Ireland or in Wales who are of English descent (chiefly with definite article).
parole.testo: From English + -ry, in legal senses after Anglo-Norman englescherie, englecherie. Compare Late Latin Anglescheria, Englescheria (“the state of being English”).

parole.significato: To write (a document) in large, aesthetic, and legible lettering; to make a finalized copy of.
parole.testo: From Middle English engrossen, from Anglo-Norman engrosser (“to gather in large quantities, draft something in final form”); partly from the phrase en gros (“in bulk, in quantity, at wholesale”), from en- + gros; and partly from Medieval Latin ingrossō (“thicken, write something large and in bold le

parole.significato: To lift, raise up.
parole.testo: From Middle English enhauncen, anhaunsen, from Anglo-Norman anhauncer (“enhance, raise”), from Vulgar Latin *inaltiāre (“raise”), derived from Latin in + altus (“high”). The /h/ in Old French was taken from haut (“high”), where it resulted from Frankish influence.

parole.significato: To enhance.
parole.testo: From Middle English enrichen, from Anglo-Norman enrichir and Old French enrichier. By surface analysis, en- + rich.

parole.significato: To enter (a name, etc.) in a register, roll or list
parole.testo: From Middle English enrollen, from Anglo-Norman enroller; by surface analysis, en- + roll.

parole.significato: Ensuing; following as a consequence.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman ensuant, present participle of ensivre, itself from Latin īnsequor (“to follow, to pursue”).

parole.significato: To make sure or certain of something (usually some future event or condition).
parole.testo: From Middle English ensuren, from Anglo-Norman enseurer, from Old French seur (“sure”). Doublet of insure.

parole.significato: Whole; complete.
parole.testo: From Middle English entere, enter, borrowed from Anglo-Norman entier, from Latin integrum, accusative of integer (“whole”). Doublet of entier and integer.

parole.significato: To give a title to.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman entitler, from Old French entiteler, (French intituler), from Late Latin intitulāre.

parole.significato: Senses relating to asking or pleading.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English entreten (“to deal with (someone) in a specified way; to concern oneself with (something); to deal with or give an account of (a topic); to engage in negotiation; to intercede for (someone); to plead with (someone)”), from Anglo-Norman entraiter, entretie

parole.significato: Charged with animals.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman enorné, enourné, variant forms of aurné, aourné, from aurner (“to adorn, decorate, endow”); compare anorn, enorn from the same nasal variants.

parole.significato: Feeling or exhibiting envy; jealously desiring the excellence or good fortune of another; maliciously grudging.
parole.testo: From Middle English envious, from Anglo-Norman envious, from Old French envieus, envious (modern French envieux), from Latin invidiōsus; more at envy. Doublet of invidious, borrowed directly from Latin. Displaced native Old English æfestiġ.

parole.significato: To encircle or surround (someone or something).
parole.testo: From Middle English envirounen, enviroun (“to surround in a circle or ring, or on the perimeter; to beset, besiege; to cover, enclose, envelop; to provide a setting or surrounding to; to move in a circle; to move around the perimeter; to go, move, or wander about (a place); to fill or pervade (a pla

parole.significato: A surrounding area or place (especially of an urban settlement); an environment.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English invyroun, Middle English enuyroun, enuyrown, from Anglo-Norman enviroun, environ, envirun, and Middle French environ (“circumference; surroundings; (in the plural) boundaries, frontiers”) (chiefly in the plural) (modern French environ), a noun use of Old French environ (adve

parole.significato: A knight-errant.
parole.testo: From Middle English erraunt [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman erraunt, from Old French errant, the present participle of errer (“to walk (to); to wander (to); (figuratively) to travel, voyage”), and then: * from Vulgar Latin iterāre (compare Late Latin itinerāre, itinerāri (“to travel, voyage”)),

parole.significato: The state, quality, or condition of being wrong.
parole.testo: From Middle English errour, from Anglo-Norman errour, borrowed from Old French error, from Latin error (“wandering about”, noun), derived from the verb errō (“to wander, to err”).
