parole.significato: To get free; to free oneself.
parole.testo: From Middle English escapen, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French escaper ( = Old French eschaper, modern French échapper), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre (“to escape a garment, get out of one's clothing”, literally “to free oneself from one's cape”), from Latin ex- (“out”) + Late Latin cappa (“c

parole.significato: The return, conversion, or vesting of property of a deceased person or closed business to the government (originally to…
parole.testo: From Middle English escheat, achete, eschete (“the reversion or conversion of property to the government”), from Anglo-Norman eschete and Old French eschet, escheit, escheoit (“that which falls to one”), past participle of escheoir (“to fall”) (modern French échoir), from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall

parole.significato: A royal officer in medieval and early modern England, responsible for taking escheats from deceased subjects.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English eschetour, itself borrowed from Anglo-Norman eschetour; equivalent to escheat + -or.

parole.significato: The shield on which a coat of arms is displayed, or, by extension, the coat of arms itself.
parole.testo: From Middle English scochon, from Anglo-Norman escuchon, Old French escusson (French écusson), ultimately from Latin scutum (“shield”). Related to scutum, scute, scudo, escudo, and écu.

parole.significato: An act of finding out or observing by spying or looking; an espial or espying.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspie, espie (“covert investigation or observation, scouting, spying; information obtained through spying; secret and treacherous plan, plot; treachery; a scout or spy”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman espie, Old French espie, from espier (verb): see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: An attorney who sufficiently excuses the absence of another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman essoigniour, from Old French essoignier. By surface analysis, essoin + -er.

parole.significato: Previously owned; secondhand.
parole.testo: From Middle English estat, from Anglo-Norman estat and Old French estat (French: état), from Latin status. Doublet of state and status.

parole.significato: To impede or bar by estoppel.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English estoppen (“to prevent (conception)”), from Anglo-Norman and Old French estoper, from a Late Latin stuppō.

parole.significato: An animal that has escaped from its owner; a wandering animal whose owner is unknown. An animal cannot be an estray whe…
parole.testo: From Middle English astrai, from Anglo-Norman estray, from the Old French verb estraier. Etymological doublet with stray.

parole.significato: A kind of widemouthed pitcher or jug with a shape like a vase and a handle, and originally used for carrying water.
parole.testo: From Middle English ewer, from Anglo-Norman or Old French ewer, eawer (modern French évier), from Latin aquārium, from aqua (“water”). Doublet of aquarium.

parole.significato: The act of excepting or excluding; exclusion; restriction by taking out something which would otherwise be included, as…
parole.testo: From Middle English exception, excepcioun, from Anglo-Norman excepcioun, from Old French excepcion, from Latin exceptiō. Equivalent to except + -ion.

parole.significato: An office of revenue taxation; a treasury.
parole.testo: From Middle English escheker, from Anglo-Norman escheker (“chessboard”), from Medieval Latin scaccarium. This is because the cloth on which the treasurer counted money was chequered like a chessboard.

parole.significato: A person who carries out some task.
parole.testo: From Middle English executour, from Anglo-Norman executour, from Latin exsecūtor, agent noun of exsequor.

parole.significato: The act of exemplifying; a showing or illustrating by example.
parole.testo: From Middle English exemplificacion, exemplification, from Anglo-Norman exemplification, from Medieval Latin exemplificātiō.

parole.significato: To change (something) from a smaller form or size to a larger one; to spread out or lay open.
parole.testo: Recorded in Middle English since 1422 (as expanden, expaunden), from Anglo-Norman espaundre, from Latin expandō (“to spread out”), itself from ex- (“out, outwards”) + pandō (“to spread”). Doublet of spawn.

parole.significato: A spending or consuming, often a disbursement of funds.
parole.testo: From Middle English expense, from Anglo-Norman expense and Old French espense, from Late Latin expēnsa, from Latin expendō. See expend. Doublet of speso.

parole.significato: To increase in extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English extenden, from Anglo-Norman extendre, estendre, from Latin extendō (“to stretch out”).

parole.significato: State or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective, opposite of success.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman failer, from Old French faillir (“to fail”). Equivalent to fail + -ure.

parole.significato: A charlatan or imposter, especially one pretending to be ill, or to tell fortunes.
parole.testo: From Middle English faytour, from Anglo-Norman faitour (cognate with Old French faitor (“doer, maker”), from Latin factor, factōrem, from facere (“do, make”).

parole.significato: Well known.
parole.testo: From Middle English famous, from Anglo-Norman famous, from Latin fāmōsus, equivalent to fame + -ous. Displaced native Old English hlīsful.

parole.significato: To work on a farm, especially in the growing and harvesting of crops.
parole.testo: From Middle English fermen, from Anglo-Norman fermer (“to let out for a fixed payment, lease, rent”) ultimately from the same Old English source as Etymology 1. Compare Old English feormian (“to feed, supply with food, sustain”).

parole.significato: A current (constantly changing) trend, favored for frivolous rather than practical, logical, or intellectual reasons.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English facioun, from Anglo-Norman fechoun (compare Jersey Norman faichon), variant of Old French faceon, fazon, façon (“fashion, form, make, outward appearance”), from Latin factiō (“a making”), from faciō (“do, make”); see fact. Doublet of faction.

parole.significato: Culpability; the responsibility for a blameworthy event.
parole.testo: From Middle English faute, faulte, from Anglo-Norman faute, Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita (“shortcoming”), feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”). parole.significato: Fidelity to one's lord or master; the feudal obligation by which the tenant or vassal was bound to be faithful to his l…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English feaute, feute, from Anglo-Norman fëauté, fëuté, from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness”; “homage, fealty” in Medieval Latin), from fidēlis (“faithful”) + -tās (noun suffix); the modern form (for expected *feauty /ˈfjuːti/) is due to learned influence. Equivalent to obsolet

parole.significato: the performing of an act, especially out of one's duty.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman fesance, from Old French faisance (“action, deed, enactment”), from faisant, present participle of faire.

parole.significato: The state of being feasible or possible.
parole.testo: From Middle English faisible, from Anglo-Norman fesable + English suffix -ity.

parole.significato: Able to be done in practice.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman fesable, from Latin facere, Old French fesable, faisable (“doable”), from fere, faire (“to do”) + -able.

parole.significato: A relatively rare or difficult accomplishment.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Anglo-Norman fet (“action, deed”), from Old French fait, from Latin factum, from facere (“to do, to make”). Doublet of fact.

parole.significato: To ascribe the greatest importance to something within a certain context.
parole.testo: From Middle English feture, from Anglo-Norman feture, from Old French faiture, from Latin factūra, from Latin factus, from Latin faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place, set”). Doublet of facture.

parole.significato: An estate in land in common law in which the land is inherited, but cannot be sold, devised by will, or otherwise alien…
parole.testo: From Middle English fee taille, fetayll, from Anglo-Norman fee tailé, from Medieval Latin foedum talliātum.

parole.significato: Deficient in physical strength.
parole.testo: From Middle English feble, from Anglo-Norman feble (“weak, feeble”) (compare French faible), from Latin flēbilis (“tearful, mournful, lamentable”) by dissimilation, from fleō (“to weep, cry”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁-. Doublet of foible.

parole.significato: A woman.
parole.testo: From Middle English feme, from Anglo-Norman feme (“woman”), from Old French femme, from Latin fēmina. Doublet of femina, femme, and hembra.

parole.significato: A married woman.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman feme (“woman”) covert (“covered, protected”).

parole.significato: A single woman, whether unmarried, spinster, widow or divorcee.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman feme (“woman”) sole (“alone”).

parole.significato: A fief.
parole.testo: Alternative form of fief, related to Anglo-Norman feoffer. Compare Latin feodum.

parole.significato: Fierce.
parole.testo: From Middle English fer, from Anglo-Norman fer, from Old French fier. Compare Latin ferus (“wild”).

parole.significato: A receptacle that houses relics of saints.
parole.testo: From Middle English feretory, fertre, feretre, et al., from Anglo-Norman fertre, from Latin feretrum (“bier, funeral litter”), from Ancient Greek φέρετρον (phéretron), from the verb φέρω (phérō, “to carry”). Doublet of feretrum.

parole.significato: The fruit of the fig tree, pear-shaped and containing many small seeds.

parole.significato: The hazelnut.
parole.testo: Earlier filbert-nut, Philibert-nut, from Middle English filbert-note, from Anglo-Norman noix de filbert, so named because they are ripe near Saint Philibert’s Day.

parole.significato: The management of money and other assets.
parole.testo: From Middle English finaunce, fynaunce, from Anglo-Norman, Middle French finance, from finer (“to pay ransom”) (whence also English fine (“to pay a penalty”)), from fin (“end”), from Latin fīnis. parole.significato: Son of; especially used for the illegitimate sons of royalty.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman fitz, from Old French fiz (modern fils), from Latin fīlius (“son”).

parole.significato: The visible part of fire; a stream of burning vapour or gas, emitting light and heat.
parole.testo: From Middle English flawme, blend of Old French flame and flambe, flamble, the first from Latin flamma, the second from Latin flammula, diminutive of flamma, both from pre-Latin *fladma; Proto-Italic *flagmā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shimmer, gleam, shine”). parole.significato: A soft cloth material originally woven from wool, today often combined with cotton or synthetic fibers.
parole.testo: From Middle English flaunneol, from Anglo-Norman flanelle (compare Norman flianné), diminutive of Old French flaine, floene (“coarse wool”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *wlānos, *wlanā (“wool”) (compare Welsh gwlân, Breton gloan), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂. More at wool.

parole.significato: A design representing a flower whose three petals are joined together at the bottom (⚜, ⚜️), often used in heraldry, wh…
parole.testo: From earlier flower-de-luce, from Middle English flourdelis, from Anglo-Norman flour de lis (“lily flower”); later remodelled after modern French fleur de lis (“lily flower”).

parole.significato: Debris floating in a river or sea, in particular fragments from a shipwreck.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.

parole.significato: A European species of flatfish having dull brown colouring with reddish-brown blotches; fluke, European flounder (Plati…
parole.testo: From Middle English flowndre, from Anglo-Norman floundre, from Old Northern French flondre, from Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. Cognate with Danish flynder, German Flunder, Swedish flundra.

parole.testo: From Middle English flour, from Anglo-Norman flur, from Latin flōrem, accusative of flōs, from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“to thrive, bloom”). parole.significato: To shape a metal by heating and hammering.
parole.testo: From Middle English forgen, from Anglo-Norman forger and Old French forgier, from Latin fabrico (“to frame, construct, build”). Doublet of fabricate.

parole.significato: The act of forging metal into shape.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1574; from forge + -ery, from Middle English forgen, via Anglo-Norman forger, from Old French forgier, from Latin fabricārī (“to frame, construct, fabricate”), itself from fabrica (“workshop; construction”), from faber (“workman, smith”). parole.testo: From Middle English founderess, founderesse, foundress (“female founder or builder of a city; female founder or benefactor of a religious house; (figuratively) female inventor or originator; (figuratively) a source”) [and other forms]; from founder, foundere, foundour (“founder or builder of a build

parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman franc banc.

parole.testo: From Middle English frankelein (“freeholder”), from Anglo-Norman fraunclein (“a landowner of free, but not noble birth”), from Old French fraunc (“free”), from Frankish *Frankō (“Frank”, literally “freeman”) + Old French -lein (“-ling”), from Frankish *-ling (“-ling”). parole.significato: A noisy commotion, especially resulting from fighting; a brawl, a fight; also, a loud quarrel.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English frai (“an assault, attack; a brawl, fight; disturbance, uproar; fine for assault or breach of the peace”), an aphetic variant of affrai, effrai (“an assault, attack; a brawl, fight; disturbance, uproar; public disturbance, riot; dismay; fear; something frightening”), then: *

parole.significato: A married woman's entitlement to the use of her husband's lands or property after he dies; or the land and property its…
parole.testo: From free + bench, after Anglo-Norman franc banc (“frank bank”).

parole.significato: One who sells fruit.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English fruiterē̆r (“fruit grower; fruit dealer”), from fruitē̆r (“fruit dealer; household official having charge of fruit”) + -er (it is unclear why the second suffix was added). parole.significato: To make cloth denser and firmer by soaking, beating and pressing; to waulk or walk.
parole.testo: From Middle English fullen (“to full”), from Anglo-Norman fuller, fuler, Middle French foller, fouler, from Old French foler, fouler (“to tread, stamp, full”), from Medieval Latin fullāre, from Latin fullō (“a fuller”). Compare Old English fullian (“to full”).

parole.significato: The hairy coat of various mammal species, especially when fine, soft and thick.
parole.testo: From Middle English furre, forre, from Anglo-Norman forre, fuerre (“case; sheath”), from Frankish *fōdar, from Proto-West Germanic *fōdr, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“sheath”) (compare Old English fōdor (“sheaf”), Dutch voering (“lining”), German Futter (“lining”), Gothic 𐍆𐍉𐌳𐍂 (fōdr, “sheath”)), fro

parole.significato: A person who sells, makes, repairs, alters, cleans, or otherwise deals in pelts or in clothing made of fur.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French forreor, from fourrer (“to line or trim with fur”).

parole.significato: A saddle tree maker.
parole.testo: From Middle English fuster, fuystour, fuystor, from Anglo-Norman fuster, Old French fuyster, fust, ultimately from Latin fūstis. Compare French fût, Old French fustier.

parole.significato: Food waste material of any kind.
parole.testo: From late Middle English garbage (“the offal of a fowl, giblets, kitchen waste”, originally “refuse, what is purged away”), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French garber (“to refine, make neat or clean”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *garwijan (“to make ready”). parole.significato: To pick out such parts (of a text) as may serve a purpose not intended by the original author; to mutilate; to pervert.
parole.testo: From Middle English garbelen, from Anglo-Norman garbeler (“to sift”), from Medieval Latin garbellare (or a similar Italian word), from Arabic غَرْبَلَ (ḡarbala, “to sift”).

parole.significato: An outdoor area containing one or more types of plants, usually plants grown for food or ornamental purposes.
parole.testo: From Middle English gardyn, garden, from Anglo-Norman gardin, from Frankish *gardin-, oblique stem of *gardō (“enclosure, yard”), from Proto-Germanic *gardô (“enclosure, garden, house”), whence also inherited English yard. (compare Old French jart alongside jardin, Medieval Latin gardīnus). Doublet

parole.significato: Something that garnishes; a decoration, adornment or embellishment
parole.testo: From Middle English garnetture, from Anglo-Norman garniture, gerneiture, from Old French garneture (“accessory for a saddle”), from Old French garnir, guarnir, from Frankish *warnijan (“to prevent, deny”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Gascon.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Gascoyne, from Anglo-Norman Gascoigne, from Late Latin Wascōnia, from Wascōnēs, modification of Classical Latin Vasconēs (“Basques, Gascons”), from Ancient Greek Οὐάσκωνες (Ouáskōnes). Compare Gascon and Gascony.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Gascony, a region of southwest France.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Gascoun, from Anglo-Norman gascoun, gascun et al., Middle French gascon, from Latin plural Vascōnēs. Compare Basque. Doublet of Vascon.

parole.significato: To measure or determine with a gauge; to measure the capacity of.
parole.testo: From Middle English gauge, gaugen, from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French gauger (compare Modern French jauger from Old French jaugier), from gauge (“gauging rod”), from Frankish *galgā (“measuring rod, pole”), from Proto-Germanic *galgô (“pole, stake, cross”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰalgʰ-, *ǵʰ

parole.significato: Liable to the payment of taxes; subject to taxation.
parole.testo: From Middle English geldable, from Anglo-Norman gilable, guldable, equivalent to geld + -able, from geld (“money”).

parole.testo: From Middle English genet, ionet, from Anglo-Norman genette, Middle French genette, jenette et al., of uncertain origin.

parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English genetif (“pertaining to the genitive case; pertaining to the generation of offspring”) + English -ive (suffix meaning ‘relating or belonging to’ forming adjectives). parole.testo: The second element is -ly; the first element may be Anglo-Norman gençur or Old French gençor, gensor, comparative forms (also attested as positives) of gent (“beautiful, noble, pleasant, courteous”). parole.significato: To exalt, or give glory or praise to (something or someone).
parole.testo: From Middle English glorifien, from Anglo-Norman and Old French glorifier, from Late Latin glōrificō, from Latin glōria + -ficō (“to make”). By surface analysis, glory + -fy. parole.significato: Exhibiting attributes, qualities, or acts that are worthy of or receive glory.
parole.testo: From Middle English glorious, from Anglo-Norman glorius and Old French glorïos, from Latin glōriōsus. Displaced native Middle English wulderful, from Old English wuldorfull (“glorious”), among other terms. Equivalent to glory + -ous.

parole.significato: A glosser; one who covers things in gloss.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gloser, glosour, from Anglo-Norman glosor; by surface analysis, gloze + er.

parole.significato: Good, honest intentions.
parole.testo: Calque of Anglo-Norman bone fei, Middle French bonne foy and Old French bonne foy, en bone fei (“loyally, with honesty, with sincere intention”) (modern French bonne foi (“good faith”), de bonne foi (“in good faith, in earnest”)), from Latin bona fidēs (“good faith”).

parole.significato: Any of the trailing or climbing vines producing fruit with a hard rind or shell, from the genera Lagenaria and Cucurbit…
parole.testo: From Middle English gourde, from Anglo-Norman gurde, gourde, from Latin cucurbita. Doublet of cucurbit.

parole.significato: To make and administer the public policy and affairs of; to exercise sovereign authority in.
parole.testo: From Middle English governen, governe, from Anglo-Norman and Old French governer, guverner, from Latin gubernō, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, govern”). Displaced native Old English wealdan, whence modern dialectical English wald (“to govern”).

parole.significato: A killer whale (Orcinus orca).
parole.testo: From Middle English *grampas, grappays, grapas, graspeys, from Anglo-Norman grampais, Old French graspois, craspois (“whale, (salted) whale meat; blubber; seal”), from Medieval Latin craspicis (literally “fat fish”), from Latin crassus (“fat”) + piscis (“fish”).

parole.significato: Large, senior (high-ranking), intense, extreme, or exceptional
parole.testo: From Middle English grand, grond, graund, graunt, from Anglo-Norman graunt, from Old French grant, from Latin grandis. Doublet of grande and grandee.

parole.significato: A group of citizens assembled by the government to hear evidence against an accused, and determine whether an indictmen…
parole.testo: From Middle English graunde jurie, from Anglo-Norman graund juree. Named because it typically has more jurors than the petit jury.

parole.significato: A member of the Grange, National Grange of the Patrons of Husbandry, an association representing farmers.
parole.testo: From Middle English graunger, from Anglo-Norman granger, variant of Old French grangier, from grange, perhaps corresponding to Medieval Latin granicārium, from Vulgar Latin *granica, from Latin granum.

parole.significato: A person who grants something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman grantour.

parole.significato: A grapnel (small anchor).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French grapil, grapin. Compare modern French grappin.

parole.significato: A small anchor, having more than two flukes, used for anchoring a small vessel.
parole.testo: From Middle English grapnel, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French grapil, grapin. Compare modern French grappin.

parole.significato: Animal fat in a melted or soft state.
parole.testo: From Middle English grece, from Anglo-Norman grece, from Vulgar Latin *crassia, noun derived from Latin crassus (“fat, thick”). Doublet of crass.

parole.significato: A stone or metal flat plate or surface on which food is fried or baked.
parole.testo: From Middle English gridil, from Anglo-Norman gredil, variant of Old French greil, from Latin crāticulum, diminutive of crātis. Doublet of grill (“grid of wire”), from the same Old French and Latin sources, doublet of grate.

parole.significato: Causing grief, pain, or sorrow.
parole.testo: From Middle English grevous, from Anglo-Norman grevous, from Old French grever, from Latin gravō (“to burden”). Developed in the 13th century. Equivalent to grief + -ous.

parole.significato: Fragments; parings; scraps (especially of fish).
parole.testo: Ante 1553. From gobbin (“piece, portion, slice”), from Middle English goboun, from Anglo-Norman gobon. Compare with English gobony (“line of alternating squares”).

parole.significato: A breed of dairy cattle originally bred on Guernsey; any individual of this breed.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old Norse, compound of Grani (“Grani's”) and ey (“island”). Folk etymology points to a dialectal root for green.

parole.significato: Astuteness often marked by a certain sense of cunning or artful deception.
parole.testo: From Middle English gile, from Anglo-Norman gile, from Old French guile (“deception”), from Frankish *wīl (“ruse”), from Proto-Germanic *wīlą, from Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, bend”). Cognate via Proto-Germanic with wile.

parole.significato: A viscous water-soluble carbohydrate exudate of certain plants that hardens when it becomes dry, or such a substance as…
parole.testo: From Middle English gomme, gumme, borrowed from Anglo-Norman gome, from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”). Cognate with Spanish goma (“rubber”). Doublet of gumma.

parole.significato: A prepared channel in a surface, especially at the side of a road adjacent to a curb, intended for the drainage of wate…
parole.testo: From Middle English gutter, guttur, goter, from Anglo-Norman guttere, from Old French goutiere (French gouttière), ultimately from Latin gutta (“drop”).

parole.significato: A dealer in ribbons, buttons, thread, needles and similar sewing goods.
parole.testo: From Middle English, 13th century. Uncertain but may derive from Anglo-Norman habertas (“small goods”).

parole.significato: A saltwater fish, Melanogrammus aeglefinus, of the North Atlantic, important as a food fish.
parole.testo: From Middle English haddok. Compare Anglo-Norman hadoc from Old French hadot, probably from an English source. parole.significato: To drag or pull, especially forcibly.
parole.testo: From Middle English halen, from Anglo-Norman haler, from Old Dutch *halon (compare Dutch halen), from Proto-Germanic *halōną (compare Old English ġeholian, West Frisian helje, German holen), from Proto-Indo-European *kelH- (“to lift”) (compare Latin ex-cellō (“to surpass”), Tocharian B käly- (“to st

parole.significato: A Hammond organ.
parole.testo: A patronymic surname from the Anglo-Norman given name Hamo, Hamon, from Germanic names beginning with a derivative of Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home”), such as descendants of *Haimarīks (“Henry”). The river in New Brunswick is named after British politician and colonial governor Sir Andrew Hamond, 1s

parole.significato: A large basket, usually with a cover, used for the packing and carrying of articles or small animals.
parole.testo: From Middle English hamper, contracted from hanaper, hanypere, from Anglo-Norman hanaper, Old French hanapier, hanepier (“case for holding a large goblet or cup”), from hanap (“goblet, drinking cup”), from Frankish *hnapp (“cup, bowl, basin”), from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz (“cup, bowl”). Cognate with

parole.significato: A restraint or support, especially one consisting of a loop or network of rope or straps, and especially one worn by a…
parole.testo: From Middle English harneys, harnes, harneis, harnais, herneis, from Anglo-Norman harneis and Old French hernois (“equipment used in battle”), believed to be from Old Norse *hernest, from herr (“army”) + nest (“provisions”) (from Proto-Germanic *nesaną (“to heal, recover”)). More at harry.

parole.significato: The internal organs of an animal, especially the heart and liver of a pig.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hastelet, from Anglo-Norman hastilet (“roast meat”), diminutive of haste (“spear, spit, roast meat”), from Latin hasta (“spear”).

parole.significato: Demeanour, behaviour, comportment.
parole.testo: From Middle English havour, from Anglo-Norman aveyr, Old French aveir.

parole.significato: A thick or heavy-duty cable or rope used to tow or moor a ship.
parole.testo: From Middle English hauser, haucer, from Anglo-Norman haucer, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre (“to raise”), derived from Latin altus (“high”). Altered in English by mistaken association with hawse and perhaps haul. Compare French aussière, haussière.

parole.significato: Totally reprehensible.
parole.testo: From Middle English heynous, from Anglo-Norman hainous, heinous (compare French haineux) from Old French haïr, hadir (“to hate”) (compare Old French en-hadir (“to become filled with hate”)), from Frankish *hattjan (“to hate”) (compare Middle English hetien). More at hate. The fluctuation between pro

parole.significato: Someone who inherits, or is designated to inherit, the property of another.
parole.testo: From Middle English heir, from Anglo-Norman eir, heir, from Latin hērēs.

parole.significato: Property which can be inherited.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hereditament, from Anglo-Norman hereditament or its etymon Medieval Latin hērēditāmentum, from Late Latin hērēditō (“to inherit”), from hērēs (“heir”).

parole.significato: That can legally be inherited.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English heritable, from Anglo-Norman heritable; equivalent to herit + -able.

parole.significato: Inheritance; the act of inheriting or something inherited.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English heritaunce (“inheritance”), from Anglo-Norman heritance (“inheritance”); equivalent to herit + -ance.

parole.significato: A person who inherits; an heir or heiress.
parole.testo: From Middle English heriter, from Anglo-Norman heriter, Old French heritier, earlier eretier, eritier, from Late Latin hērēditārium (from the adjective hērēditārius (“hereditary”)), which took the place of hērēs (“heir”). In the 16th century conformed to agent nouns in -our, -or. By surface analysis

parole.significato: Any long-legged, long-necked wading bird of the family Ardeidae.
parole.testo: From Middle English heron, heroun, heiron, from Anglo-Norman heiron, from Medieval Latin hairō, from Frankish and Proto-West Germanic *hraigrō, from Proto-Germanic *haigrô (compare Swedish häger and Danish hejre), dissimilation of *hraigrô (compare Old English hrāgra, Dutch reiger, German Reiher), f

parole.significato: A hawk used in hunting herons.
parole.testo: From Middle English heroner, from Anglo-Norman heroner. By surface analysis, heron + -er.

parole.significato: Extremely or shockingly ugly.
parole.testo: From Middle English hidous, from Anglo-Norman hidous, from Old French hideus, hydus (“that which inspires terror”), from earlier hisdos, from Old French hisda (“horror, fear”), of uncertain and disputed origin. Probably from Proto-West Germanic *agisiþu (“horror, terror”), from Proto-West Germanic *

parole.significato: A hoarding (temporary structure used during construction).
parole.testo: From Middle English hord, whorde, from Anglo-Norman hurde and Old French hourd, hourt (“barrier, palisade”), from Middle Dutch horde, from Old Dutch *hurd, from Proto-West Germanic *hurdi (“wickerwork, braiding of branches, hurdle, scaffolding, military company”).

parole.significato: A three-sided box mounted on a pole for carrying bricks, mortar, or other construction materials over the shoulder.
parole.testo: Probably an alteration of hot (“(Northern England, Scotland) large basket for carrying earth, etc.”), from Middle English hott, hote, hotte (“large basket or pannier for carrying earth, etc.; unit of measure for grain; hut or shed (perhaps originally of wattlework); lump of dirt (?)”) [and other for

parole.significato: Any of various tools for scraping, scratching, digging, or stirring soil or other materials.
parole.testo: From Middle English howe, from Anglo-Norman houe, from Frankish *hauwā, derivative of Frankish *hauwan (“to hew”), from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną. More at hew.

parole.significato: A young sheep of either gender from about 9 to 18 months of age (until it cuts 2 teeth).
parole.testo: From Middle English hogget, from Anglo-Norman hoget and an Anglo-Latin hogettus.

parole.significato: To sacrifice (chiefly an animal) to be completely burned.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English holocaust (“burnt offering”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman holocauste, Old French holocauste, olocauste (modern French holocaust), from Late Latin holocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστον (holókauston), the neuter form of ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos, “who

parole.significato: Recognition of importance or value; respect; veneration (of someone, usually for being morally upright or successful).
parole.testo: From Middle English honour, honor, honur, from Anglo-Norman honour, honur, from Old French honor, from Latin honor. parole.significato: To move irregularly up and down.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman hocher, Middle French hocher, from a Germanic source (compare Dutch hutsen, hossen, German hotzen).

parole.significato: The public pursuit of a criminal, accompanied by shouts to warn others to give chase.
parole.testo: From Middle English heu and cri, from the Anglo-Norman legal phrase hu e cri.

parole.significato: A small, simple one-storey dwelling or shelter, often with just one room, and generally built of readily available loca…
parole.testo: From Middle English *hutte, hotte, from both Old English hōd and Old English hȳdan (“to hide”) and influenced by Anglo-Norman hute or hutte, from Middle French hutte, from Old French hute (“hut”), hute (“cottage”), from Old High German hutta (“hut, cottage”), from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ, *hudjō (“hut

parole.significato: The notional full-moon day of a Roman month, occurring on the 15th day of the four original 31-day months (March, May,…
parole.testo: From Middle English ides, idus, from Anglo-Norman and Old French ides, from Latin īdūs, a fourth-declension plurale tantum, from the Latin practice of treating most recurring calendrical days as plurals. The Latin term is cognate with Oscan eiduis, both perhaps deriving from an unknown Etruscan term

parole.significato: The result of being impaired.
parole.testo: From Middle English empeirement, empeyrement, emparement, from Anglo-Norman empairement, emperement, enpeirement, from Old French ampirement, anpirement, enperement, equivalent to impair + -ment.

parole.significato: To enrol (jurors), e.g. from a jury pool; to register (the names of jurors) on a "panel" or official list.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman empaneller.

parole.significato: Discussion, especially before some action is taken; conference, debate.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Anglo-Norman emparlance, from the verb Old French emparler.

parole.significato: To hinder, impede, or prevent.
parole.testo: From Middle English empechen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman empecher, from Old French empeechier (“to hinder”), from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”). Cognate with French empêcher (“to prevent”).

parole.significato: Constant and insistent demanding or proposing, especially if regarded as annoying or upsetting; also, the character of…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English importunitie, importunyte (“insistence, persistence; grievance; hardship, trouble; inappropriateness (?)”), from Anglo-Norman importunité, and Middle French importunité (“persistent demand; hardship, trouble; something difficult or troublesome; inappropriateness”) (modern Fr

parole.significato: To make poor.
parole.testo: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

parole.significato: The action of impoverishing someone.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman empoverissement, from the Old French verb empoverir. By surface analysis, impoverish + -ment.

parole.significato: A confinement in a place, especially a prison or a jail, especially as punishment for a crime.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman emprisonement, from Old French emprisonnement. See imprison + -ment.

parole.significato: To make (something) better; to increase the value or productivity (of something).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman emprouwer, from Old French en- + prou (“profit”), from Vulgar Latin prode (“advantageous, profitable”).

parole.significato: The act of improving; advancement or growth; a bettering
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman emprouwement. By surface analysis, improve + -ment.

parole.significato: (of a quantity, etc.) To become larger or greater, to greaten.
parole.testo: From Middle English encresen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman encreistre, from Latin increscere (“to increase”), from in (“in, on”) + crescō (“grow”). The noun is from Middle English encres, from the verb.

parole.significato: To bring upon oneself or expose oneself to, especially something inconvenient, harmful, or onerous; to become liable or…
parole.testo: From Middle English incurren, from Anglo-Norman encurir, Middle French encourir, from Old French encorre, from Latin incurrere.

parole.significato: A contract which binds a person to work for another, under specified conditions, for a specified time (often as an appr…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman endenture, from Old French endenteure, from endenter (“to dent”). The name of the contract derives from the irregular dent-shaped cut (indentation) used to prove the authenticity of the two parts, similar to a chirograph.

parole.significato: Of or relating to India or its people; or (formerly) of the East Indies.
parole.testo: From Middle English Indien, from Anglo-Norman indien, Middle French indien, corresponding to Ind + -ian or India + -an. Applied to inhabitants of the Americas due to an early misconception that the Americas were the eastern end of Asia / the Indies (hence also the designation of Caribbean islands as

parole.significato: An official formal accusation for a criminal offence, or the process by which it is brought to a jury.
parole.testo: 18th-century Latinized respelling of Middle English endytement (“action of accusing”), from Anglo-Norman enditement, from enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from Latin indictus.

parole.significato: One who informs someone else about something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English enformour, from Anglo-Norman enfourmour; equivalent to inform + -er.

parole.significato: That can be inherited.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English enheritable (“inheritable”), from Anglo-Norman enheritable; equivalent to inherit + -able.

parole.significato: The passing of title to an estate upon death.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English enheritaunce, inheritaunce, borrowed from Anglo-Norman, Old French enheritaunce, from enheriter. By surface analysis, inherit + -ance.

parole.significato: To wound or cause physical harm to a living creature.
parole.testo: A back-formation from injury, from Middle English injurie, from Anglo-Norman injurie, from Latin iniūria (“injustice; wrong; offense”), from in- (“not”) + iūs, iūris (“right, law”).

parole.significato: Causing physical harm or injury; harmful, hurtful.
parole.testo: From Middle English injurious, from Anglo-Norman enjurius, from Latin iniūriōsus; analysable as injury + -ous.

parole.significato: Damage to the body of a living thing.
parole.testo: From Middle English injurie, from Anglo-Norman injurie, from Latin iniūria (“injustice; wrong; offense”), from in- (“not”) + iūs, iūris (“right, law”). Doublet of injuria.

parole.significato: One of a series of parts, whether equal or unequal to the other parts of the series, of a given entity or a given proce…
parole.testo: A 1732 alteration of estallment, from Anglo-Norman estaler (“fix payments”), from Old French estal (“fixed position”), from Old High German stal (“stall", "standing place”) The sense of "part of a whole produced in advance of the rest" is from 1823.

parole.significato: A decorative element found especially in early medieval art
parole.testo: From Middle English entrelacen, from Anglo-Norman entrelacer, from Old French inter- + lacer (“weave”).

parole.significato: To mix, mingle together.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English entremedlen, entermedlen, from Anglo-Norman entremedler (= Old French entremesler), from inter- + medler.

parole.significato: To enthrone.
parole.testo: From Middle English intronizen, intronize, intronyce, intronyze, entronise, entronize, entronyce, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French inthronizer, introniser, intronizer, enthronizer, entronizer, from Old French entronisier (modern French introniser (“to induct; to introduce to”)), or directly from

parole.significato: To convert, convince, or win over with flattery or wiles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman enveugler, alteration of aveugler (“to blind, to delude”), from Old French avogle (“without eyes”), from Late Latin ab oculīs (“without eyes”, literally “away from the eyes”). parole.significato: The hard white form of dentin which forms the tusks of elephants, walruses and other animals.
parole.testo: From Middle English yvory, ivorie, from Anglo-Norman ivurie, from Latin eboreus (“in or of ivory”) adjective of ebur (“ivory”) (genitive eboris), from Demotic Egyptian yb (“ivory, Elephantine”) (compare Coptic ⲓⲏⲃ (iēb, “Elephantine”)), from Egyptian ꜣbw (“elephant, ivory, Elephantine”), from Proto-

parole.significato: A place or institution for the confinement of persons held against their will in lawful custody or detention, especiall…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gayole, borrowed from Anglo-Norman jaiole, from Late Latin caveola, from Latin cavea (“cage”) + -ola (diminutive ending). parole.significato: A piece of armour for the leg (especially below the knee), a greave.
parole.testo: From Middle English iambeau(s) (compare jamber), from an Anglo-Norman [Term?] derivative of Old French jambe (“leg”): compare Old French jambiere. See jamb (noun). Compare lamboy(s).

parole.significato: A rattling metallic sound; a clang.
parole.testo: From Middle English jangle (“gossip, idle talk; a dispute”), from Anglo-Norman jangle and Old French jangle (“gossip, idle talk; a dispute”), from Old French jangler (“to chatter, gossip; to argue noisily; to bawl”): see further at etymology 1. parole.significato: Danger of failure, harm, or loss.
parole.testo: From Middle English jupartie, jeupartie (“even chance”), from Anglo-Norman giu parti and Middle French jeu parti (“a divided game, i.e. an even game, an even chance”), from Medieval Latin iocus partītus (“an even chance, an alternative”), from Latin iocus (“jest, play, game”) + partītus, perfect pas

parole.significato: A breed of dairy cattle developed on Jersey.
parole.testo: From Middle English Gersey, from Anglo-Norman Gersui, further etymology disputed. Probably from Old Norse [Term?], compound of Geirs (“Geirr's”) + ey (“island”). parole.significato: Items thrown overboard from a ship or boat in distress in order to lighten its load.
parole.testo: From Middle English jetteson, from Anglo-Norman getteson. Doublet of jettison.

parole.significato: Items that have been or are about to be ejected from a boat or balloon to lighten the vessel.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman getteson, from Old French getaison, from geter, jeter (modern French: would be *jetaison like pendaison); possibly from a Vulgar Latin *iectātiō, from *iectātus < iectāre, from Latin iactō. Doublet of jetsam.

parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English gete, jette, jetti (“projecting upper storey of a building, overhang; breakwater, pier, jetty”), from Anglo-Norman geté, getee, getté, and Middle French geté, getee, jeté (“projecting upper storey of a building; breakwater, pier”) (modern French jetée), a

parole.significato: A precious or semi-precious stone; gem, gemstone.
parole.testo: From Middle English juel, jewel, juwel, jeuel, jowel, from Anglo-Norman juel, from Old French jouel, joel, joïel, hence French joyau, of uncertain origin. parole.significato: A person whose job is making, repairing or selling jewelry.
parole.testo: From Middle English jueler, from Anglo-Norman jueler, or Old French juelier. By surface analysis, jewel + -er.

parole.significato: A diary or daily record of a person, organization, vessel etc.; daybook.
parole.testo: From Middle English journal, from Anglo-Norman jurnal (“daily”), from Old French jornel (“day”) (whence modern French journal), from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus (“of the day”). Doublet of diurnal and the journal from French.

parole.significato: To sit in judgment on; to pass sentence on (a person or matter).
parole.testo: From Middle English jugen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman juger, from Old French jugier, from Latin iūdicāre. Doublet of judicate. Partly displaced native deem.

parole.significato: The administration of justice by judges and courts; judicial process.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman judicature, Middle French judicature, and their source, post-classical Latin iudicatura (12th century), from the participle stem of classical Latin iūdicāre (“to judge”).

parole.significato: An animal, especially a beast of burden.
parole.testo: From Middle English jument, from Anglo-Norman jument or directly from Latin iūmentum.

parole.significato: A group of individuals chosen from the general population to hear and decide a case in a court of law.
parole.testo: From Middle English jure, from Anglo-Norman juree, from Medieval Latin iūrāta, from Latin iūrō (“to swear or take an oath”).

parole.significato: A house or shelter for a dog.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱwṓ From Middle English kenel, kenell, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *kenil, northern variant of Old French chenil, from Vulgar Latin *canīle, from Latin canis.

parole.significato: A kind of fishweir resembling a wattle or fence.
parole.testo: From Middle English kidel, kedel, kydel, from Anglo-Norman quidel, quideau (“a wicker framework used to trap fish”), from Old Breton kidel (“a net at the mouth of a stream”).

parole.significato: A young cat, especially before sexual maturity (reached at about seven months).
parole.testo: From Middle English kitoun, kytton, kyton, keton (“kitten”), of obscure origin. parole.significato: Negligence in one's duty.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman laches, from Old French lachesse (“laxness”), from laschier, from Vulgar Latin laxico, frequentative of Latin laxo (“relax, moderate, weaken”).

parole.significato: People of a church who are not ordained clergy or clerics.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman laite, from Latin laitas, from Ancient Greek λαός (laós, “people”).

parole.significato: To lose strength and become weak; to be in a state of weakness or sickness.

parole.significato: The lowest junior commissioned officer rank(s) in many military forces, often Army and Marines.

parole.significato: A kind of dog kept on a lead; a bloodhound; a mongrel.

parole.significato: Straw, grass, and similar loose material used as bedding for people or animals.

parole.significato: Any distinctive identifying uniform worn by a group, such as the uniform worn by chauffeurs and male servants.
parole.testo: From Middle English livery, liveree, from Anglo-Norman liveree, from Old French livree. Compare modern French livrée.

parole.significato: Evil intent, bad intention; fraud, deceit.

parole.significato: A wrongdoer.

parole.significato: The criminal intent which precedes a crime, especially murder.

parole.significato: A self-evident axiom or premise; a pithy expression of a general principle or rule.

parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman medicinable, Middle French medicinable, or their source, Late Latin medicinabilis, from Latin medicīna.

parole.testo: From Late Middle English mesuage, messuage (“dwelling house, residence; farmstead; household”), from Anglo-Norman mesuage, messuage (“residence; holding”), probably from Late Latin mesuagium, messuagium, probably ultimately from Latin mānsiō (“abode, dwelling, habitation, home”) or its etymon mānsus

parole.significato: A prison, or other place of confinement.
parole.testo: From Middle English mewe, mue, mwe, from Anglo-Norman mue, muwe, and Middle French mue (“shedding feathers; cage for moulting birds; prison”), from muer (“to moult”).

parole.significato: The Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua).
parole.testo: From Middle English milwell (amid many other forms), from Anglo-Norman meluel (amid other forms) and Old French moluel, probably from moruel, from Old Breton mor (“sea”) (from Proto-Brythonic *mor) + Old French lus and luz (“pike, [as sea-luce] hake”) + -el (diminutive suffix). Cognate with modern F

parole.significato: Originally, an entertainer employed to juggle, play music, sing, tell stories, etc.; a buffoon, a fool, a jester; later…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English minstral, menestrel (“actor; juggler; mime; musician; singer; storyteller; (military) soldier playing a horn or trumpet as a signal”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman menestrel [and other forms] and Old French menestrel (“artisan; servant; itinerant musici

parole.significato: The musical and other art and craft of a minstrel.
parole.testo: From Middle English minstralcie, from 13th century Anglo-Norman menestralsie, menestralcie, from Old French menestrel (“minstrel”), itself from Medieval Latin ministralis (“servant, jester, singer”), from Late Latin ministerialis (“imperial household officer, one having an official duty”), from the

parole.significato: Bad luck, misfortune.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman meschance, Old French meschance, meschaunce.

parole.significato: Causing mischief; injurious.
parole.testo: From Middle English myschevous, mischevous, from Anglo-Norman meschevous, from Old French meschever, from mes- (“mis-”) + chever (“come to an end”) (from chef (“head”)). By surface analysis, mischief + -ous.

parole.significato: A mistake in the naming of a person or place; a misidentification.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English misnoumer (“(law) mistaken identification of a person; plea based on such misidentification”), from Anglo-Norman mesnomer, a noun use of Anglo-Norman mesnomer, mesnommer, and Old French mesnomer, mesnommer (“to name incorrectly”), from mes- (prefix meanin

parole.significato: Criminal neglect or wrongful execution of duty, especially by a public official; (countable) a specific instance of thi…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English misprision, mesprision (“criminal offence or illegal action, especially one committed by a public official”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman misprision, mesprision, mesprison (“criminal offence or illegal action; error, mistake, specifically an error by a court”) [and o

parole.significato: Despising or holding in contempt; disdain, scorn.
parole.testo: From misprize (“to despise or hold in contempt; to undervalue”) + -ion (suffix indicating a condition or state), probably influenced by misprision (etymology 1). Misprize is derived from Middle English mesprise, mespryse, from Anglo-Norman mespriser, Middle French mespriser, and Old French mesprisie

parole.significato: Someone's business or function; an occupation, employment, trade.
parole.testo: From Middle English mister, myster, from Anglo-Norman mester, meister (et al.), from Latin misterium, a medieval conflation of Latin ministerium (“ministry”) with Latin mysterium (“mystery”). Doublet of métier.

parole.significato: The result of mixing two or more substances; a mixture.
parole.testo: A merger of a nominal use of the verb and a borrowing from Anglo-Norman mixte, from Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (“mix”). Nowadays regarded automatically as the nominal form of the verb.

parole.significato: The action of mocking; ridicule, derision.
parole.testo: From Middle English mokkery, from Anglo-Norman mokerie, mokery and Middle French mocquerie, moquerie, from moquer, moker (“to mock”) + -erie (“-ery”), perhaps from Byzantine Greek μωκός (mōkós, “mocker”), perhaps from Arabic مَكْر (makr, “scheme, plot”). Equivalent to mock + -ery.

parole.significato: Characterized by the presence of moisture; not dry; slightly wet; damp.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English moist, moiste [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman moist, moiste, moste, Middle French moiste, and Old French moiste, muste (“damp, moist, wet”) (modern French moite); further etymology uncertain, perhaps a blend of a Late Latin variant of Latin mūcidus (

parole.significato: The crossed iron that supports the upper millstone by resting on the spindle; a millrind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman molin (“mill”), from Late Latin molinum (“mill”), from molere (“to grind”). Doublet of moulin and mill.

parole.significato: A generally accepted means of exchange.
parole.testo: From Middle English moneye, moneie, money, borrowed from Anglo-Norman muneie (“money”), from Latin monēta (“money, a place for coining money, coin, mint”), from the name of the temple of Juno Moneta in Rome, where a mint was. In this sense, displaced native Old English feoh, whence English fee. Doub

parole.significato: A minter: one who makes money, particularly (historical) the superintendent of a mint producing coinage.
parole.testo: From Middle English moneyour, partly from Middle English money + -our, and partly from Anglo-Norman monoiier, monneiere, monnier. Equivalent to money + -er.

parole.significato: A mullion.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French moinel, noun use of moienel (“middle”), from moien.

parole.significato: A nun, especially one dedicated to an enclosed order.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman monyale, Middle French monyalle, or their source, Late Latin monialis.

parole.significato: A caution or warning.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman monicion, Middle French monicion, and their source, Latin monitiō (“warning, admonition”).

parole.significato: Recognition of the distinction between good and evil or between right and wrong; respect for and obedience to the rules…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman moralité, Middle French moralité, from Late Latin mōrālitās (“manner, characteristic, character”), from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”), from mōs (“manner, custom”). equivalent to moral + -ity.

parole.significato: A case or writ relating to the recovery of an inherited estate that has been taken or occupied by another party followi…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman mordauncestre, from Old French mort d'ancestre (“death of ancestor”).

parole.significato: To discipline (one's body, appetites etc.) by suppressing desires; to practise abstinence on.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman mortifier, Middle French mortifier, from Late Latin mortificō (“cause death”), from Latin mors (“death”) + -ficō (“-fy”).

parole.significato: The perpetual, inalienable possession of lands by a corporation or non-personal entity such as a church.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman mortmayn, morte meyn, from Old French mortes meins, after Late Latin phrase mortua manus. See Latin mortuus (“dead”) + manus (“hand”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to death or a funeral; funereal.
parole.testo: From Middle English mortuary, from Anglo-Norman mortuarie (“gift to a parish priest from a deceased parishioner”), from Medieval Latin mortuārium (“receptacle for the dead; mortuary”), neuter form of mortuārius (“of or pertaining to the dead”), from Latin mortuus, perfect passive participle of morio

parole.significato: A change whereby something goes from one place to another; a state of progression from one place to another; a change o…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English mocioun, mocion, from Anglo-Norman motion, Middle French motion, and their etymon Latin mōtiō (“movement, motion”), related to movēre, from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move”).

parole.significato: To prompt or incite by a motive or motives; to move.
parole.testo: From Middle English motif, from Anglo-Norman motif, Middle French motif, and their source, Late Latin motivum (“motive, moving cause”), neuter of motivus.

parole.significato: Comprising greatly varied elements, to the point of incongruity.
parole.testo: From Middle English motle, from Anglo-Norman motteley (“parti-colored”), from Old English mot (“speck”). Doublet of mote. The English word can be analysed as mottle + -y.

parole.significato: An animal, usually a horse, used to ride on.
parole.testo: From Middle English mounten, from Anglo-Norman munter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre (“climb”), from Latin montem (“mountain”). Compare modern French monter.

parole.significato: An elevation of land of considerable dimensions rising more or less abruptly, forming a conspicuous figure in the lands…
parole.testo: From Middle English mountayne, mountain, montaigne, from Anglo-Norman muntaine, muntaigne, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem (“mountain”), from Proto-Indo-European *monti (compare Welsh mynydd (“mountain”), Albanian mat (“bank, shore”), Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬙𐬌 (mati, “promo

parole.significato: Anything that mutes or deadens sound.
parole.testo: From Middle English muflen (“to muffle”), aphetic alteration of Anglo-Norman amoufler, from Old French enmoufler (“to wrap up, muffle”), from moufle (“mitten”), from Medieval Latin muffula (“a muff”), of Germanic origin (—first recorded in the Capitulary of Aachen in 817 C.E.), from Frankish *muffël

parole.significato: A child born lawfully in wedlock, in distinction from an elder sibling born of the same parents before their marriage (…
parole.testo: From Middle English mulier(e), moillere, muliery (“adj.: legitimate, both in wedlock; noun: wedlock”), from Anglo-Norman muil(l)eré, moil(l)eré (“legitimate; of legitimate birth”) or Old French moil(l)eré, ultimately from Latin mulier (“woman”).

parole.significato: A stone with a flat grinding surface, which is held in the hand and rubbed on a slab to grind paint pigments, medicinal…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English molour, moler; further origin uncertain, possibly: * from mull (“(Northern England) something reduced to fine particles”, noun) or mull (“(chiefly Northern England) to grind to powder, crumble, powder, pulverize”, verb) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns)

parole.significato: An embalmed human or non-human animal corpse wrapped in linen bandages for burial, especially as practised by the ancie…
parole.testo: From Middle English mummie, from Anglo-Norman mumie, from Middle French momie, from Medieval Latin mumia, from Arabic مُومِيَاء (mūmiyāʔ), from Persian مومیا (mumyâ), from موم (mum, “wax”). Doublet of mumijo.

parole.significato: A tax paid for building or repairing the walls of a fortified town.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English murage, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French murage, from murer (“to wall”), from mur (“wall”), Latin murus. See mure (“wall”).

parole.significato: Infectious disease; pestilence, plague; (countable) sometimes used in curses such as a murrain on someone: an outbreak…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English morein, morine, moreyn (“(widespread) death; widespread sickness, plague; fatal disease; carnage; carrion”), from Anglo-Norman morine, mourine, moreyn (“death; widespread sickness, plague; carrion; cattle disease”), Middle French morine, and Old French mo

parole.significato: A series of sounds organized in time, usually employing some combination of harmony, melody, rhythm, tempo, timbre, sou…
parole.testo: From Middle English musik, musike, borrowed from Anglo-Norman musik, musike, Old French musique, and their source Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ), from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”), an Ancient Greek deity of the arts. By surface analysis, muse + -ic (“pertaining to”). In th

parole.significato: A gathering.
parole.testo: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”). Cognate with French montrer (“to show”), Italian mostrare (“to show”), Spanish mostra

parole.significato: Affected by dampness or mould; damp, mildewed, mouldy.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English musty; further origin uncertain, possibly from one of the following: * From Anglo-Norman muste, moste, variants of moiste, muiste (“moist”), from Old French moiste (“clammy, damp, moist, wet”) (modern French moite (“muggy; sticky, sweaty”)), from a b

parole.significato: Not having the power of speech; dumb.
parole.testo: From Middle English muet, from Anglo-Norman muet, moet, Middle French muet, from mu (“dumb, mute”) + -et, remodelled after Latin mūtus.

parole.significato: Something secret or unexplainable; an unknown.
parole.testo: From Middle English mysterie, from Anglo-Norman misterie (Old French mistere), from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion, “a mystery, a secret, a secret rite”), from μύστης (mústēs, “initiated one”), from μυέω (muéō, “to initiate”), from μύω (múō, “to shut”). Displaced native Old

parole.significato: Household linen, especially table linen.
parole.testo: From Middle English naperie, from Anglo-Norman naperie, Middle French naperie, from Old French nape + -erie.

parole.significato: Someone's birth; the place, time and circumstances of a birth.
parole.testo: From Middle English nativite, from Anglo-Norman nativite, Middle French nativite, and their source, Latin nātīvitās (“birth”). By surface analysis, native + -ity. See also naïveté.

parole.significato: A country's entire maritime military force, including ships and personnel.
parole.testo: From Middle English nave, navye, from Anglo-Norman, Old French navie, from Latin nāvigia < nāvigium, from Latin nāvigō, nāvis (“boat”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Compare Ancient Greek ναῦς (naûs, “ship”), Persian ناو (nâv, “boat, warship”), Sanskrit नाव (nāva, “ship”), Old English nōwend (“m

parole.significato: Used to signify a job well done.
parole.testo: From Middle English nete, net, nette, from Anglo-Norman neit (“good, desirable, clean”), a variant of Old French net, nette (“clean, clear, pure”), from Latin nitidus (“gleaming”), derived from nitēre (“to shine”). Doublet of net and nitid. Cognate with German nett (“nice, kind”). Compare also nait.

parole.significato: A woman born in the state of serfdom; a female serf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman neif m, niefe f (“native, serf”), from Latin nātīvus m, nātīva f (“native”). Doublet of naïf and native.

parole.significato: A trifle; something small and insignificant.
parole.testo: From Middle English nifle, possibly from Anglo-Norman. Compare Scots niffle (“to trifle”).

parole.significato: The quality of being noble; nobleness.
parole.testo: From Middle English noblesse, from Anglo-Norman noblesse, noblesce et al., Old French noblace, nobleche et al., from noble (“noble”).

parole.significato: A kind of hymn, or canticle, of mediaeval origin, sung in honor of the birth of Christ; a Christmas carol.
parole.testo: From Middle English nowel, from Anglo-Norman noel, Middle French noel, a variant of nael, from Latin adjective nātālis (“natal, having to do with birth”).

parole.significato: Morally hurtful or noxious.
parole.testo: From Middle English noysom; equivalent to noy + -some (short for annoy, from an(n)oien, enoien from Anglo-Norman anuier, from Old French enuier (French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiare, from in- (intensive prefix) + odium (“hate”)).

parole.significato: The state of being under legal age; minority, the fact of being a minor.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman nounage, corresponding to non- + age.

parole.significato: Worthy of note; remarkable; memorable; noted or distinguished.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English notable (“worthy of note, profitable, useful”), in some senses from Anglo-Norman notable (“noteworthy”), from Latin notābilis (“noteworthy, extraordinary”), from notō (“to note, mark”); in some senses from Middle English note (“benefit, profit, use, advantage”), from Ol

parole.significato: An officer who can administer oaths and statutory declarations, witness and authenticate documents and perform certain…
parole.testo: Anglo-Norman/Law French, on model of notaire publique, hence the unusual order of adjective following noun, instead of idiomatic English *public notary. Compare attorney general, court martial, fee simple, secretary general, surgeon general.

parole.significato: A word that functions as the name of a specific object or set of objects, such as person, animal, place, word, thing, p…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English noun, from Anglo-Norman noun, non, nom, from Latin nōmen (“name; noun”). The grammatical sense in Latin was a semantic loan from Koine Greek ὄνομα (ónoma). Doublet of name and nomen.

parole.significato: A beginner; one who is not very familiar or experienced in a particular subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English novice, novys, from Anglo-Norman novice, Middle French novice, itself borrowed from Latin novīcius, later novitius (“new, newly arrived”) (in Late Latin as a noun, masculine novicius, feminine novicia (“one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent”)), from novus (“new”).

parole.significato: To annoy; to harm or injure.
parole.testo: From Middle English noyen, partly an aphetic form of anoyen and partly from Anglo-Norman noier, nuier.

parole.significato: Annoyance.
parole.testo: From Middle English noy, partly an aphetic form of anoy and partly from Anglo-Norman nui.

parole.significato: The state of being annoyed; distress, irritation.
parole.testo: From Middle English noyaunce, partly an aphetic form of anoyaunce, partly directly from Anglo-Norman noyaunce.

parole.significato: A minor annoyance or inconvenience.
parole.testo: From Middle English noysaunce, from Anglo-Norman nusaunce, nussance and Old French nuisance, from nuisir (“to harm”), from Latin nocēre. Doublet of nocence and nocency.

parole.significato: Quantity of countable things.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English number, nombre, numbre, noumbre, from Anglo-Norman noumbre, Old French nombre, from Latin numerus (“number”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to distribute, to give, to take”). Compare Saterland Frisian Nummer, Nuumer, West Frisian nûmer, Dutch nummer (“numb

parole.significato: The quality of being obedient.
parole.testo: From Middle English obedience, from Anglo-Norman obedience, from Old French obedience (modern French obédience), from Latin oboedientia. Displaced native Old English hīersumnes (compare modern English hearsomeness). Cognate with obeisance.

parole.significato: To do as ordered by (a person, institution etc), to act according to the bidding of.
parole.testo: From Middle English obeyen, from Anglo-Norman obeir, obeier et al., Old French obeir, from Latin oboediō (also obēdiō (“to listen to, harken, usually in extended sense, obey, be subject to, serve”)), from ob- (“before, near”) + audiō (“to hear”). Compare audient. In Latin, ob + audire would have bee

parole.significato: The death of a person.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman obit, Middle French obit, and their source, Latin obitus (“going down; death”), from obīre (“to go down, to die”).

parole.significato: A communion wafer.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman obblé, oblei et al., Old French oblee, obleie et al., from Late Latin oblata (“light pastry; communion wafer”), noun use of the feminine past participle of Latin offerre (“to offer”).

parole.significato: The state of forgetting completely, of being oblivious, unconscious, unaware, as when sleeping, drunk, or dead.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English oblivion, from Anglo-Norman oblivion, from Latin oblīviō (“forgetfulness”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

parole.significato: To get hold of; to gain possession of, to procure; to acquire, in any way.
parole.testo: From Middle English obteinen, from Anglo-Norman obtenir, optiner et al., and Middle French obtenir, from Latin obtinēre (“to gain, achieve, succeed, possess”), from ob- + tenēre (“to hold”).

parole.significato: Any smell, whether fragrant or offensive.
parole.testo: From Middle English odour, borrowed from Anglo-Norman odour, from Old French odor, from Latin odor. Cognates * Swedish odör (“bad smell”)

parole.significato: One who has a position of authority in a hierarchical organization, especially in military, police or government organi…
parole.testo: From Middle English officer, from Anglo-Norman officer, officier, from Old French officer, Late Latin officiarius (“official”), from Latin officium (“office”) + -ārius (“-er”). By surface analysis, office + -er.

parole.significato: To anoint.
parole.testo: From Middle English ointen, from Anglo-Norman oint or Old French oint, past participle of oindre, from Latin unguere.

parole.significato: An elephant.
parole.testo: From Middle English olifaunt, from Anglo-Norman oliphant (“ivory, elephant”) and Old French oliphant (“ivory, elephant, musical horn of ivory”), from Latin elephantus (“elephant”), from Ancient Greek ἐλέφας (eléphas, “ivory, elephant”).

parole.significato: The Asiatic wild ass or hemione (Equus hemionus), an animal of the horse family native to Asia; specifically, the Persi…
parole.testo: From Middle English onager, onagir (“wild ass; military catapult”), from Anglo-Norman onager, Middle French onager, onagre, Old French onager, onagre (“wild ass; military catapult”) (modern French onagre), from Late Latin onager (“large siege engine”), Latin onager (“wild ass”), from Hellenistic Anc

parole.significato: A belief, judgment or perspective that a person has formed, either through objective or subjective reasoning, about a t…
parole.testo: From English opine + -ion, from Middle English opinion, opinioun, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French opinion, from Latin opīniō, from opīnor (“to opine”). Displaced native Old English wēna.

parole.significato: The saltbush: any of several plants of the genus Atriplex
parole.testo: From Middle English arage, from Anglo-Norman arace, arache; apparently an irregular derivation from Old French arepe, from classical Latin atriplex, from Ancient Greek ἀτράφαξυς (atráphaxus), of unknown origin (probably loaned).

parole.significato: Someone who orates or delivers an oration.
parole.testo: From Middle English oratour, from Anglo-Norman oratour, from Latin ōrātor.

parole.significato: A private chapel or prayer room.
parole.testo: From Middle English oratorie, from Anglo-Norman oratorie, Middle French oratoire, and their source, Late Latin ōrātōrium. Doublet of oratorio. Displaced native Old English bēdhūs.

parole.significato: Having regular jurisdiction; now only used in certain phrases.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman ordenarie, ordenaire et al., Middle French ordinaire, and their source, Medieval Latin ordinarius, noun use of Latin ōrdinārius (“regular, orderly”), from ōrdō (“order”).

parole.significato: The part of the horizon where the sun first appears in the morning; the east.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English orient, oriente, oryent, oryente, oryentte (“the east direction; eastern horizon or sky; eastern regions of the world, Asia, Orient; eastern edge of the world”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman orient, oriente, and Old French orient (“east direction; Asia, Orient”)

parole.significato: Of a pearl or other precious stone: having a superior lustre.
parole.testo: From Middle English oriental, from Anglo-Norman oriental, Middle French oriental, from Latin orientālis (“eastern”), from oriēns (“rising (of the Sun)”), present active participle of orior (“to rise”).

parole.significato: A prayer.
parole.testo: From Middle English orisoun, from Anglo-Norman oreison, oresoun etc. and Old French oraisun etc., from Latin ōrātiō, ōrātiōnem (“discourse, prayer”) (whence also English oration).

parole.significato: Any elaborate embroidery, especially when made of gold thread; an object (such as clothing or fabric) adorned with such…
parole.testo: From Middle English orfray, orfrei, orefreys (“elaborate (especially gold) embroidery; fabric adorned with such embroidery; embroidered ornamental band or border; decorative elements”), from Anglo-Norman and Middle French orfrais, orfreis, orfrois, and other forms, from Late Latin aurifrasium, aurif

parole.significato: A bird of prey of genus Pandion that feeds on fish and has white underparts and long, narrow wings each ending in four…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ospray, from Anglo-Norman ospriet, from Medieval Latin avis praedae (“bird of prey”), a generic term apparently confused with this specific bird in Old French on its similarity to ossifrage.

parole.significato: A large flightless bird of the order Struthioniformes.
parole.testo: From Middle English ostrich, ostriche, ostryche, ostrige, borrowed from Anglo-Norman ostrige and Old French ostruce, from Vulgar Latin *austruthio, from Latin avis (“bird”) + strūthiō (“ostrich”), from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn), or shortened from strūthiocamēlus, from Ancient Greek στρουθ

parole.significato: A brooch or clasp for fastening a piece of clothing together, especially when set with jewels or valuable.
parole.testo: From Middle English ouche, from nouche, which in phrases like a nouche was re-analyzed as an ouche (rebracketing). From Anglo-Norman nusche and Old French nusche (with metanalysis), from a Germanic source; compare German Nusche, Proto-Germanic *hnuts.

parole.significato: To expel; to remove.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman ouster, oustier, from Old French oster (modern French ôter), from post-classical Latin obstare (“to remove”), classical obstāre (“to obstruct, stand in the way of”). Not related to out.

parole.significato: A declaration that an individual cannot benefit from the protection of law in a jurisdiction.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English outlawerie (equivalent to outlawe + -erie), after Anglo-Norman utlagarie /utlarie and Medieval Latin utlagaria, both from Old English utlagu + Latin -aria (suffix that forms abstract nouns from other nouns). By surface analysis, outlaw + -ry.

parole.significato: Violating morality or decency; provoking indignation or affront.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman outrageus, Middle French outrageus, from outrage; equivalent to outrage + -ous.

parole.significato: That which remains beyond what is necessary or required; a surplus.
parole.testo: From over- + Anglo-Norman plus, Middle French plus.

parole.significato: Open and not concealed or secret.
parole.testo: From Middle English overt, uverte (“open, uncovered; unfastened; accessible, unobstructed; clear, manifest”), from Anglo-Norman overt, Middle French ouvert, Old French overt, ouvert, uvert (“opened”) (modern French ouvert), past participle of Anglo-Norman, Old French ovrir, ouvrir, uvrir (“to open”)

parole.significato: An opening; a recess or chamber.
parole.testo: From Middle English overture, from Anglo-Norman, Middle French overture, from Old French overture, from Latin apertūra. Doublet of aperture.

parole.significato: A hearing in a civil case which is based on the content of a document, in which the plaintiff is required to produce th…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman oyer (“hear”).

parole.significato: A commission under which a court is empowered to hear and determine a criminal case.
parole.testo: From Middle English oier and terminer, oyer and termyner, from Anglo-Norman oyer (“hear”) and terminer (“determine”).

parole.significato: Of a pale beige colour tinted with grey or pink, like that of an oyster.
parole.testo: From Middle English oystre, from Old English ostre, reinforced or superseded by Anglo-Norman oistre, which is from Old French oistre, uistre (compare modern French huître); both lines (Old English and Old French) from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon). Doublet of ostro (“a purple dy

parole.significato: A step.
parole.testo: From Middle English pase, from Anglo-Norman pas, Old French pas, and their source, Latin passus. Doublet of pas and fathom; compare also pass. Cognate with pass, Spanish pasear, paso.

parole.significato: A small horse with a smooth, ambling gait, popular in the Middle Ages with nobles and women for riding (contrasted with…
parole.testo: From Middle English palfrey, from Anglo-Norman palefrei (“steed”), from Old French palefroi, palefreid, from Late Latin paraverēdus (“post horse, spare horse”), from Ancient Greek παρά (pará) + Latin verēdus (“post horse”), from Gaulish *werēdos (“horse”) (compare Welsh gorwydd (“horse”)), from Prot

parole.significato: A bed of loose straw.
parole.testo: From Middle English paillet, from Anglo-Norman paillete (“bundle of straw”), from Old French paille (“straw, chaff”), from Latin palea (“chaff”).

parole.significato: Complete or partial muscle paralysis of a body part, often accompanied by a loss of feeling and uncontrolled body movem…
parole.testo: From Middle English palesie, from Anglo-Norman paralisie, parleisie et al., from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”), from παρα- (para-, “beside”) + λύω (lúō, “loosen”). Doublet of paralysis.

parole.significato: A marsh or swamp.
parole.testo: From Middle English palude, from Anglo-Norman palude, palud, palu, from Old French palu, from Latin palūs, palūdem. Reinforced (and with pronunciation influenced) by French palude, palud and Italian palude.

parole.significato: A (usually) rectangular section of a surface, or of a covering or of a wall, fence etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English panel (“piece of cloth, saddle pad, pane of glass, piece of ice, part, division, jury list, jury members”), from Anglo-Norman panel, panelle (“piece of cloth, saddle cushion”), from Vulgar Latin *pannellus, diminutive of Latin pannus (“cloth, rag, garment”), from Proto-Indo-Europ

parole.significato: Made of paper.
parole.testo: From Middle English paper, from Anglo-Norman paper, from Old Catalan paper, borrowed from Latin papȳrus (and given the Catalan suffix -er), from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros).

parole.significato: A type of elaborate robe especially as worn by someone in power or a religious official.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman parement, Middle French parement, from Medieval Latin parāmentum, from parō (“adorn”) + -mentum.

parole.significato: Highest, supreme; also, chief, leading, pre-eminent.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂éd From Anglo-Norman paramont /paramount (“paramount, pre-eminent; above”), from Old French par /per (“by”) + amont /amunt (“upward”).
