parole.significato: A person who is the object of one's love, especially in an affair or romance; a lover; also, a sexual partner.
parole.testo: The adverb is derived from Middle English par amour, paramore, paramours (“with sexual desire or love, passionately; in a courteous or friendly manner”), from Anglo-Norman par amur (“in a friendly or willing manner”) and Old French par amur, par amour, paramours (“by or through love”) (modern French

parole.significato: coparcenary; coheirship.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman parcenerie, from parcener, from Old French parçon (“part, portion, share, division”), from Latin partītiō, partītiōnem (“division”), from partīre, from pars. By surface analysis, parcen + -ary.

parole.significato: By God!
parole.testo: From Middle English parde, from Anglo-Norman pardi, pardeu, and Old French pardeu, from par (“by”) + Deu (“God”).

parole.significato: A person who raises a child (which they have made, adopted, fostered, taken as their own, etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English parent, borrowed from Anglo-Norman parent, Middle French parent, from Latin parentem, accusative of parēns (“parent”), present participle of pariō (“to breed, bring forth”).

parole.significato: Any of several species of Parietaria.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English peritorie, from Anglo-Norman paritarie, peritorie, from Late Latin parietāria (“the herb pellitory (noun)”), from parietarius (“of or belonging to a wall (adjective)”), which the modern English form has been remodelled on. Compare pellitory, parietal.

parole.significato: A certain way of speaking, of using words; especially that associated with a particular job or interest.
parole.testo: From Middle English *parlaunce, from Anglo-Norman parlance, parlaunce, from parler (“to talk”) + -ance.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a parish.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman parochial and its source Late Latin parochialis, an alteration of paroecialis (“of a church province”), from paroecia, from Hellenistic Greek παροικία (paroikía, “stay in a foreign land”), later “community, diocese”, from Ancient Greek πάροικος (pároikos, “neighbouring, neighbour”)

parole.significato: An Anglican cleric having full legal control of a parish under ecclesiastical law.
parole.testo: From Middle English persoun, from Anglo-Norman, Old French persone (“parson, person”), from Medieval Latin persona (“parson, person”), from Latin persona (“person”). Doublet of person and persona.

parole.significato: Pertaining only to a part of something; partial.
parole.testo: From Middle English particuler, from Anglo-Norman particuler, Middle French particuler, particulier, from Late Latin particularis (“partial; separate, individual”), from Latin particula (“(small) part”). Equivalent to particle + -ar. Compare particle.

parole.significato: A person or group of people constituting one side in a legal proceeding, such as in a legal action or a contract.
parole.testo: From Middle English party, partye, partie, from Anglo-Norman partie, from Old French partie (“side, part; portion, share; separation, division”, literally “that which is divided”), noun use of feminine of past participle of Old French partir (“to divide, separate”), from Latin partire (“to share, pa

parole.significato: Land, specifically, an open field, on which livestock is kept for feeding.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pasture, borrowed from Anglo-Norman pastour, from Latin pastūra, from pāscor + -tūra.

parole.significato: A type of seasoned meat and vegetable hand pie, usually of a semicircular shape.
parole.testo: From Middle English paste, from Anglo-Norman paste and Old French pasté. Doublet of patty.

parole.significato: Conspicuous; open; unconcealed.
parole.testo: From Middle English patent, patente (“wide open; clear, unobstructed; unlimited; of a document: available for public inspection”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman and Middle French patent (modern French patent), and directly from their etymon Latin patēns (“open; accessible, passable; evident, m

parole.significato: A paved surface; a hard covering on the ground.
parole.testo: From Middle English pament, from Anglo-Norman pavement and reinforced by Middle French pavement; both from Latin pavīmentum (“paved surface or floor”), from pavīre (“to beat, to ram, to tread down”). Morphologically pave + -ment.

parole.significato: An ornate tent.
parole.testo: From Middle English pavilloun, from Anglo-Norman pavilloun, from Latin pāpiliōnem, form of pāpiliō (“butterfly, moth”) (due to resemblance of tent to a butterfly’s wings), of unknown origin. Doublet of papilio and papillon. Cognate to French pavillon (“pavilion”) and papillon (“butterfly”), and simi

parole.significato: A person who lays paving slabs.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman paviour, from pavier (“to pave”).

parole.significato: Most usually, a very large shield fitted with a stand, like a small moveable wall, carried in front to protect all or m…
parole.testo: From Middle English pavis(e) (paveis, pavas), from Anglo-Norman pavis (compare French pavois), from Latin pavensis, probably from Pavia in Italy. Compare Italian pavese.

parole.significato: The soft foot of a mammal or other animal, generally a quadruped, that has claws or nails; comparable to a human hand o…
parole.testo: From Middle English pawe, from Old French poue, poe, from Vulgar Latin *pauta. Further origin unknown, perhaps from Frankish *pōta, from Frankish *pōtōn (“to put, stick, plant”), from Proto-Germanic *putōną, whence also Old English potian (“to push”), pȳtan (“to put out, poke out”). See more at put.

parole.significato: The most numerous chess piece, or a similar piece in a similar game. In chess, each side starts with eight; moves are o…
parole.testo: From Middle English pown, from Anglo-Norman poun, paun (“footman”), from Late Latin pedōnem (“pedestrian”), derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Doublet of peon.

parole.significato: A pagan or heathen, especially a Muslim, or a Jew.
parole.testo: From Middle English paynym, paynyme, from Anglo-Norman paienime, peinime et al., from Late Latin paganismus (“paganism”), from Latin paganus (“pagan”). Doublet of paganism.

parole.significato: A state of tranquility, quiet, and harmony. For instance, a state free from civil disturbance.
parole.testo: From Middle English pees, pes, pais, borrowed from Anglo-Norman peis and Old French pais (“peace”), from Latin pāx (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to fasten, stick, place”), related to Latin pacīscor (“agree, stipulate”), Latin pangō (“fasten, fix”); see pact. Doublet of pax. Displaced

parole.significato: Favouring peace rather than conflict; not aggressive, tending to avoid violence (of people, actions etc.).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pesible, peisible, Middle French paisible, from pais (“peace”) + -ible; later remodelled after peace + -able.

parole.significato: To inform on someone; turn informer.
parole.testo: From Middle English pechen, from apechen (“to accuse”) and empechen (“to accuse”), possibly from Anglo-Norman anpecher, from Late Latin impedicō (“entangle”). See impeach.

parole.significato: A type of pear.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman parmain, peremain et al., Middle French parmain, permain (“type of pear or apple”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A member of the lowly social class that toils on the land, constituted by small farmers and tenants, sharecroppers, far…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English paissaunt, from Anglo-Norman paisant, from Old French païsant, païsan (“countryman, peasant”), from païs (“country”), from Latin pāgus (“countryside”) + Old French -enc (“member of”), from Frankish -inc, -ing "-ing"; which was an alteration of earlier Late Latin pāgēnsis (“i

parole.significato: To make peace between (conflicting people, states etc.); to reconcile.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman paiser, pesser et al., Old French paisier, aphetic form of apaisier (“to appease”). Probably also partly from aphetic use of appease.

parole.significato: One quarter of a bushel; a dry measure of eight quarts; equal to approximately 9092 cubic centimeters in the imperial s…
parole.testo: Probably from Anglo-Norman pek, pekke, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Pecuniary.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pecunier, Middle French pécunier, alteration of pecuniaire, from Latin pecūniārius.

parole.significato: A chart, list, or record of ancestors, to show breeding, especially distinguished breeding.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pé de grue, a variant of Old French pié de gru (“foot of a crane”), from Latin pes (“foot”) + grus (“crane”).

parole.significato: A stake.
parole.testo: From Middle English peel, pele, from Anglo-Norman pel (compare modern French pieu), from Latin pālus (“stake”). Doublet of pole and pale.

parole.significato: Somebody who is, or something that is, at a level or of a value equal (to that of something else).
parole.testo: From Middle English per, pere, from Anglo-Norman peir, Old French per, from Latin pār. Doublet of pair and par.

parole.significato: To weigh or measure the weight of; to poise.
parole.testo: From Middle English peysen, from Anglo-Norman peiser, peser and Middle French peser, from Latin pēnsāre (literally “weigh”). Doublet of poise.

parole.significato: Money, riches; gain, especially when dishonestly acquired; lucre, mammon.

parole.significato: Hairy.
parole.testo: Coined by Irish novelist and poet James Joyce in his novel Ulysses. From Anglo-Norman pelure (“pelt, fur, animal skin”) + -ious.

parole.significato: To write (an article, a book, etc.).

parole.significato: A voluntary self-imposed punishment for a sinful act or wrongdoing. It may be intended to serve as reparation for the a…
parole.testo: From Middle English penaunce, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French peneance, from Latin paenitentia (“repentance, penitence”). Doublet of penitence.

parole.significato: A small pennon; a little banner, flag, or streamer.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pencel, reduced form of penuncel. See pennoncel. By surface analysis, pen + Old French -cel.

parole.significato: A supporting post attached to the main rafter.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pendaunt, Middle French pendant, noun use of adjective.

parole.significato: Dangling, drooping, hanging down or suspended.
parole.testo: From Middle English pendaunt, Anglo-Norman pendaunt, pendant, respelled to reflect Latin pendēns, pendentis, present participle of pendere (“to hang, to be suspended”). Compare pendant, which retained the spelling.

parole.testo: From Late Middle English pennon, penoun (“long narrow flag attached to a lance or used in other contexts; one who bears a pennon, knight bachelor; plume of feathers; strip around the edge of a shield”), from Anglo-Norman penun (“feather of an arrow”), penoun (“flag attached to a lance”), Middle Fren

parole.significato: Mentha pulegium, a plant of the mint family, formerly much used in various medicinal treatments and as a flea repellent.
parole.testo: Apparently an alteration (after penny) of Anglo-Norman puliol royal, from Latin pūlegium.

parole.significato: An annuity paid regularly as benefit due to a retired employee, serviceman etc. in consideration of past services, orig…
parole.testo: From Middle English pencioun, pensioun, from Anglo-Norman pencione, Old French pencion, and their source, Latin pēnsiō (“payment, weight, rent, compensation”), from the participle stem of pendō (“to weigh”). Doublet of pensione.

parole.significato: Someone who lives on a pension, especially the retirement or old age pension.
parole.testo: From Middle English pensioner, from Anglo-Norman pensionner and Old French pensionnier, from Medieval Latin pēnsiōnārius. By surface analysis, pension + -er.

parole.significato: A structure or annexe (especially one with a sloping roof) extending from the side of a building, sometimes as protecti…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pentiz (“pentice”), from apendiz (“appentice”), ultimately from a suffixed form of Latin appendō (“to append”). Altered by folk etymology to appear to be a compound of house. Doublet of appentice and pentice.

parole.significato: An extension of a building's roof and the protected area beneath.
parole.testo: From Middle English pentis, pendize, and other spellings; from Anglo-Norman pentiz, aphetic of Old French apentis (“appendage, attached building”), from Medieval Latin appendicium, from Latin appendo (“to hang”). Doublet of appentice and penthouse.

parole.significato: To interact with people; to socialize.
parole.testo: From Middle English puple, peple, peeple, from Anglo-Norman people, from Old French pueple, peuple, pople, from Latin populus (“a people, nation”), from Old Latin populus, from earlier poplus, from even earlier poplos, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”) of unknown origin. parole.significato: A survey, a tour; an instance of walking around.
parole.testo: From Middle English perambulacioun, from Anglo-Norman and Latin. By surface analysis, perambulate + -ation, or, by surface analysis, per- + ambulate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person's life regarded as a temporary stay on earth and a journey to the afterlife.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English peregrinacioun, peregrinacion (“journey; pilgrimage; (figuratively) human journey through life”), from Anglo-Norman peregrinaciun (“human journey through life”), peregrination (“pilgrimage; overseas travel”), and Old French peregrinacion, peregrination (“pilgrimage; overseas

parole.significato: Precluding debate or expostulation; not admitting of question or appeal.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman peremptorie, parentorie et al. (Modern French péremptoire), and its source, Latin peremptōrius (“deadly; precluding debate, decisive”), from perimō (“destroy, thwart”), from per- (“thorough”) + emō (“to obtain, buy”).

parole.significato: By constraint of circumstances; of necessity; as a matter of course.
parole.testo: From Middle English par force, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French par force (“by force”).

parole.significato: To do (something); to execute.
parole.testo: From Middle English parformen, performen (“to perform”), from Anglo-Norman performer, parfourmer, alteration of Old French parfornir, parfurnir (“to complete, accomplish, perform”), from par- + fornir, furnir (“to accomplish, furnish”), from Frankish *frummjan (“to accomplish, furnish”), from Proto-

parole.significato: A transparent olive green form of olivine, used as a gem.
parole.testo: From Middle English peritot, from Anglo-Norman peridou, peridout, Middle French perido, peridon, of uncertain origin; later reborrowed from modern French péridot.

parole.significato: The deliberate giving of false or misleading testimony under oath.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman perjurie, from Latin perjūrāre (“swear falsely”), from per- + jūrāre. Displaced native Old English mānāþ (literally “false oath”).

parole.significato: A taking or reception, as the receiving of rents or tithes in kind, the receiving of profits.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pernance, from Old French prenance, from prendre, prenre, penre (“to take”), from Latin prendere, prehendere.

parole.significato: An individual who has been granted personhood; usually a human being.
parole.testo: From Middle English persoun, personne et al., from Anglo-Norman parsone, persoun et al. (Old French persone (“human being”), French personne), and its source Latin persōna (“mask used by actor; role, part, character”), perhaps a loanword from Etruscan 𐌘𐌄𐌓𐌔𐌖 (φersu, “mask”). parole.significato: Pertaining to persons (human beings as opposed to things or animals).
parole.testo: From Middle English personal, personele, from Anglo-Norman personel, personal, personell, Old French personal, personel, from Late Latin persōnālis (“of a person, personly”), equivalent to person + -al. Doublet of personnel.

parole.significato: A regular trial jury, assembled to determine criminal or civil liability.
parole.testo: From Middle English petite jury, petit jury, from Anglo-Norman [Term?].

parole.significato: Having little or no importance.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English peti, pety (“little, small; minor”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman petit, Middle French petit, and Old French peti, petit, pitet (“young; little, small; inferior; insignificant”) (modern French petit), ultimately of imitative origin. It is no longer

parole.significato: A lover of wisdom.
parole.testo: From Middle English philosophre, from Anglo-Norman or Middle French philosophe, from Latin philosophus, from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos, literally “lover of wisdom”) + -er. Credited as having been coined by Pythagoras to describe himself. Displaced native Old English ūþwita.

parole.significato: A wasting illness of the lungs, such as asthma or tuberculosis; consumption; phthisis.
parole.testo: From Middle English tisike, from Anglo-Norman, from Latin phthisicus (“suffering from tuberculosis”), from Ancient Greek φθισικός (phthisikós, “consumptive”), from φθίσις (phthísis, “tuberculosis, consumption”).

parole.significato: The art or pseudoscience of deducing the predominant temper and other characteristic qualities of the mind from the out…

parole.significato: A heavy iron tool with a wooden handle; one end of the head is pointed, the other has a chisel edge.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pykeaxe, pecaxe, pyke exe (“pickaxe”), an alteration (due to folk etymology association with pick and axe) of Middle English pikeyse, pikeys, pykois, from Anglo-Norman *pikeis, Old French picois, pecois, from Latin picōsa (“pickaxe”), from picca, ultimately from Proto-W

parole.significato: Hair, especially when very fine or short; the fine underfur of certain animals. (Formerly countable, now treated as a c…
parole.testo: From Middle English pile, partly from Anglo-Norman pil (a variant of peil, poil (“hair”)) and partly from its source, Latin pilus (“hair”). Doublet of pilus.

parole.significato: A plunderer or thief.
parole.testo: Partly from Anglo-Norman pilour, from Old French piller (“to plunder”) (more at pillage)

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Pimpinella, especially burnet saxifrage (Pimpinella saxifraga).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pimpernele et al., Middle French pimpinelle (“burnet saxifrage”) et al., from Medieval Latin pimpinella, pipinella, most likely from piper (“pepper”) because its fruit resembled peppercorns, although variants may suggest other derivations, bipinnella the bipennis (“two-winged”).

parole.significato: A feeling of sympathy at the misfortune or suffering of someone or something.
parole.testo: From Middle English pitye, pitie, pittye, pitee, pite, from Anglo-Norman pité, pittee etc., from Old French pitet, pitié, from Latin pietās. See also the doublets pietà and piety.

parole.significato: Flat, level.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman pleyn, playn, Middle French plain, plein, and Old French plain, from Latin plānus (“flat, even, level, plain”). Doublet of llano, piano, plane, and plan.

parole.significato: A lamentation.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman plainer, pleiner, variant of Anglo-Norman and Old French pleindre, plaindre, from Latin plangere.

parole.significato: A complaint.
parole.testo: From Middle English plainte, borrowed from Anglo-Norman plainte (“lamentation”), plaint (“lament”), and Old French pleinte (“lamentation”), pleint (“lament”) (modern French plainte), from Medieval Latin plancta (“plaint”), from Latin planctus (“a beating of the breast in lamentation, beating, lament

parole.significato: A party bringing a suit in civil law against a defendant; accuser.
parole.testo: From Middle English plaintif, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French plaintif (“complaining”; as a noun, “one who complains, a plaintiff”) from the verb plaindre. Doublet of plaintive.

parole.significato: A flat fold; a doubling, as of cloth; a pleat.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleit, from Anglo-Norman pleit (compare Old French ploit), from Latin plectō, which is akin to Old Norse flétta (Danish flette), Russian плести́ (plestí) and also to Old English fleohtan, which it displaced. Doublet of plight (“plait, fold”) and pleat.

parole.significato: A tool for smoothing wood by removing thin layers from the surface.
parole.testo: From Middle English plane, plaine, from Anglo-Norman plaine, from Late Latin plāna (“planing tool”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Plantago, with a rosette of sessile leaves about 10 cm (4") long with a narrow part instead of a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English planteyne, planteyn, from Anglo-Norman plainteine et al., Old French plaintain, from Latin plantāgō, from planta (“sole of the foot”), a nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“flat; to spread”), because of the broad, flat shape of the plantain leaves.

parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English *plashen (attested by the present participle form plashynge), from Anglo-Norman plaissier, plaisser, Old French plaissier, plaisser, and Old French plaissier (“to bend; to interlace”) (modern French plaisser (regional)), from Late Latin *plaxus, a variant

parole.significato: A plot of land; a lot.

parole.significato: Flat; level; (by extension) frank, on the level.
parole.testo: From Middle English plat, plate, platte (“flat; smooth; blunt, plain”), from Anglo-Norman, Middle French, and Old French plat (“(adjective) flat, level; calm; blunt, plain; (adverb) in a flat position; directly, straight; bluntly, plainly”), from Vulgar Latin *plattus (“flat; smooth”); further etymo

parole.significato: Precious metal, especially silver.
parole.testo: From Middle English, partly from Anglo-Norman plate (“plate, bullion”) and partly from Latin plata (“silver”), from Vulgar Latin *platta (“metal plate”), from feminine of Latin *plattus (“flat”).

parole.significato: A tray for serving foods.
parole.testo: From Middle English plater, from Anglo-Norman plater, dissimilatory variant of platel, from Old French plate (“metal plate”) (see plate). Doublet of plateau.

parole.significato: To unite by interweaving, as (horticulture) branches of shrubs, trees, etc., to create a hedge; to interlock, to plash.
parole.testo: The verb is from Late Middle English pleshe, Middle English plechen, pleche (“to layer; to propagate (a plant) by layering, to pleach”), possibly from Anglo-Norman and Middle French plesser, plessier, Middle French plescer, variants of Middle French, Old French plaissier, plessier (“to plash”), from

parole.significato: a person who pleads in court; an advocate
parole.testo: Partly from Middle English pleder, pledere, equivalent to plead + -er; and partly from Middle English pledour, plaidour, from Anglo-Norman plaidur, pledour, Old French plaidëor, pledëor.

parole.significato: To make a solemn promise (to do something).
parole.testo: From Middle English plege, from Anglo-Norman plege, from Old French plege (Modern French pleige) from Medieval Latin plevium, plebium, from plebiō (“to pledge”), from Frankish *plehan (“to pledge; to support; to guarantee”). Akin to Old High German pflegan (“to take care of, be accustomed to”), Old

parole.significato: Fullness; completeness.
parole.testo: From Middle English plenitude, that borrowed from Anglo-Norman plenitude, Middle French plenitude, and their source, Latin plēnitūdō.

parole.significato: A more-than-adequate amount; plenitude; a great deal.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman plent(é) + -y, from Middle English plentie, plentee, plente, from Anglo-Norman plenté, from Old French plenté, from Latin plēnitātem, accusative of plēnitās (“fullness”), from plenus (“complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”), from which English full also comes

parole.significato: A dire or unfortunate situation.
parole.testo: From Middle English plit (“fold, wrinkle, bad situation”), conflation of Middle English pliht, plight (“risky promise, peril”) (from Old English pliht "danger, risk"; see Etymology 2) and Anglo-Norman plit, plyte (“fold, condition”), from Old French pleit (“condition, manner of folding”) (from Vulga

parole.significato: A network; a plait; a fold; rarely a garment.
parole.testo: From Middle English pliȝt, plight, plyt, pleit, from Anglo-Norman pleit (“pleat, fold”). More at plait.

parole.significato: Any of various wading birds of the subfamily Charadriinae.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English plover, from Anglo-Norman plover, plovier, from Medieval Latin plovarius, pluviārius, of disputed origin; perhaps from Latin pluvia (“rain”).

parole.significato: To adorn, cover, or furnish with feathers or plumes, or as if with feathers or plumes.
parole.testo: Sense 1 (“to adorn, cover, or furnish with feathers or plumes”) is derived from Anglo-Norman plumer (“to cover with or provide with feathers”), or its etymon Latin plūmāre, the present active infinitive of plūmō (“to grow feathers, to fledge; to cover with feathers, to feather; to embroider with a f

parole.significato: To thrust into liquid, or into any penetrable substance; to immerse.
parole.testo: From Middle English plungen, ploungen, Anglo-Norman plungier, from Old French plongier, (Modern French plonger), from unattested Late Latin frequentative *plumbicō (“to throw a leaded line”), from plumbum (“lead”). Compare plumb, plounce.

parole.significato: To bend; to fold; to mould; (figuratively) to adapt, to modify; to change (a person's) mind, to cause (a person) to sub…
parole.testo: From Middle English plīen, pli, plie (“to bend, fold, mould, shape; to be flexible; to be submissive, humble oneself; to compel someone to submit”), from Anglo-Norman plier, plaier, pleier, ploier, and Middle French plier, ployer (“to bend, fold; to be submissive; to compel someone to submit”) (mode

parole.significato: A bag stitched to an item of clothing, used for carrying small items.
parole.testo: From Middle English pocket (“bag, sack”), from Anglo-Norman poket, Old Northern French poquet, poquete, diminutive of poque, poke (“bag, sack”) (compare modern Norman pouquette and modern French pochette from Old French pochete, from puche), from Frankish *pokō (“pouch”), from Proto-Germanic *puhô (

parole.significato: Sharp-pointed; keen.
parole.testo: From Middle English poynaunt, poynant, borrowed from Anglo-Norman puignant, poynaunt etc., present participle of poindre (“to prick”), from Latin pungō (“prick”). Doublet of pungent.

parole.significato: A state of balance, equilibrium or stability.
parole.testo: From Middle English poys, poyse, from Anglo-Norman pois, Middle French pois (“weight”) and Anglo-Norman poise, Middle French poise (“measure of weight”), from Latin pendere (“to weigh, ponder, think”). Doublet of peise.

parole.significato: A sack or bag, especially a paper bag.
parole.testo: From Middle English poke, from Anglo-Norman poke (whence pocket), from Frankish *poka. More at pocket. Doublet of pouch. First attested in the early 13th c.

parole.significato: Physical contamination, now especially the contamination of the environment by harmful substances, or by disruptive lev…
parole.testo: From Middle English pollucioun, pollucion (“desecration, impurity”), from Anglo-Norman pollutiun, Middle French pollution, pollucion, and their source, post-classical Latin pollūtiō (“defilement, desecration; nocturnal emission”) (4th century), from the participial stem of polluō (“to soil, defile,

parole.significato: Any of many ferns of the genus Polypodium, especially common polypody.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman polypodie, from Late Latin polypodium, q.v.

parole.significato: A writ in law used by the superior courts to remove cases from inferior courts.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pone, from Anglo-Norman pone, from Late Latin pone, from Latin pōne, imperative of pōnere (“to place”).

parole.significato: A parrot.
parole.testo: From Middle English popinjay, popyngeay, popingay, popejay, from Anglo-Norman papegai, papejoie et al., (northern) Old French papejai (“parrot”), probably from Old Occitan papagay (compare Occitan papagai, Catalan papagai), ultimately from Arabic بَبْغَاء (babḡāʔ, “parrot”), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Any of various deciduous trees of the genus Populus.
parole.testo: From Middle English popler, from Anglo-Norman popler and Old French poplier (compare French peuplier), from Latin pōpulus, with a suffix later added.

parole.significato: A small cetacean of the family Phocoenidae, related to dolphins and whales.
parole.testo: From Middle English porpeys, purpeys, borrowed from Anglo-Norman porpeis, purpeis, Old French pourpois, porpois, pourpais, porpeis (“porpoise”), from Vulgar Latin *porcopiscis (“porpoise”, literally “hog-fish”), taken from Latin porcus (“hog, pig”) + piscis (“fish”). Compare (in transposed order) ob

parole.significato: A portable breviary.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman porteose, portehos, Old French portehors, from porte + hors (“outside”).

parole.significato: A person who carries luggage and related objects; (historically) one who carried luggage or did manual labour in the tr…
parole.testo: From Middle English porter, portere, portier, borrowed from Anglo-Norman portour and Old French porteor, from Late Latin portātor, from past participle of Latin portāre (“to carry”). By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -er.

parole.significato: A person in control of the entrance to a building.
parole.testo: From Middle English porter, portere, portare, borrowed from Anglo-Norman portour and Old French portier, from Late Latin portarius (“gatekeeper”), from Latin porta (“gate”).

parole.significato: A thick soup or stew, made by boiling vegetables, grains, and sometimes meat or fish, a staple food throughout Europe i…
parole.testo: From Middle English pottage, from Anglo-Norman and Old French potage, equivalent to pot + -age.

parole.significato: A quilted military doublet or gambeson worn in the 14th and 15th centuries.
parole.testo: From Middle English purpoynt, from Anglo-Norman purpoint, alteration of perpoint, from Late Latin perpunctum, from per- + punctum (“pierced”). The modern spelling is influenced by French pourpoint.

parole.significato: Power, authority, strength, health.
parole.testo: From Middle English pouste, from Anglo-Norman pousté, Old French poesté, posté etc., from (the stem of) Latin potestās (“power”). Doublet of podesta.

parole.significato: The ability to do or undergo something.
parole.testo: From Middle English power, poer, from Old French poeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse, whence English potent. Compare French pouvoir. Displaced the native Old English anweald.

parole.significato: The title designating a Roman administrative official whose role changed over time:
parole.testo: From Middle English pretour, pretor, from the Anglo-Norman pretour, pretore, the Middle French preteur (from the Old French pretor; compare the Modern French préteur), and their etymon, the Classical Latin praetor (“leader”, “commander”, “magistrate”); the Latin praetor being contracted from *praeit

parole.significato: To direct words, thoughts, or one's attention to a deity or any higher being, for the sake of adoration, thanks, petiti…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English preien, borrowed from Anglo-Norman preier, from Old French proiier, from Late Latin precāre, from Latin precārī, from prex (“request, petition, prayer”), from Proto-Italic *preks, from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ- (“to request, ask”). Displaced native Old English gebiddan

parole.significato: Preaching; sermonizing.
parole.testo: Partly from preach + -ment, partly after Anglo-Norman prechement.

parole.significato: A proclamation, announcement or preaching.
parole.testo: From Middle English predicacion, from Anglo-Norman predicaciun, from Latin praedicātiō, from praedicō.

parole.significato: To be in the habit of choosing something rather than something else; to favor; to like better.
parole.testo: From Middle English preferren, from Anglo-Norman preferer, from Latin praeferō. Displaced native Old English foresettan and foreberan. Doublet of prelate. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as collate and confer among others.

parole.significato: A clairvoyant or clairaudient experience, such as a dream, which resonates with some event in the future.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1533. From Anglo-Norman premunition, from Ecclesiastical Latin praemonitiōnem (“a forewarning”), form of praemonitiō, from Latin praemonitus, past participle of praemoneō, from prae (“before”) (English pre-) + moneō (“to warn”) (from which English monitor). Compare Germanic fore

parole.significato: Devised, contrived, or planned beforehand; preconceived, premeditated.
parole.testo: Back-formation from prepensed, probably from Anglo-Norman prepenser.

parole.significato: A right, especially when due to one's position or role.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman prerogative (noun), from Latin praerogātīva (“previous verdict; claim, privilege”), noun use of the feminine singular of praerogātīvus (“having first vote; privileged”).

parole.significato: A statement made on oath by a jury.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman presentment, presentement, Middle French presentement, corresponding to present + -ment.

parole.significato: To be so presumptuous as (to do something) without proper authority or permission [with to (+ infinitive)].
parole.testo: From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).

parole.significato: To speak or behave so as to give a false or simulated appearance.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pretendre, Middle French pretendre (French prétendre (“to claim, demand”)), from Latin praetendere (“to put forward, hold out, pretend”), from prae- (“pre-”) + tendō (“stretch”); see tend.

parole.significato: That which is or may be seized by animals to be devoured.
parole.testo: From Middle English preye, prei, preyȝe, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French preie, one of the variants of proie, from Latin praeda. Compare predator. Doublet of prede.

parole.significato: First in time, initial, early.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman primer (“first”), from Latin prīmārius (“first”).

parole.significato: A (male) ruler, a sovereign; a king, monarch.
parole.testo: From Middle English prince, from Anglo-Norman prince, from Latin prī̆nceps (“first head”), from prīmus (“first”) + capiō (“seize, take”). Cognate with Old English fruma (“prince, ruler”). Doublet of princeps and principe. Displaced English atheling (“prince”), from Middle English, from Old English æ

parole.significato: A female member of a royal family other than a queen, especially a daughter or granddaughter of a monarch.
parole.testo: From Middle English princesse, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman princesse, Old French princesse. By surface analysis, prince + -ess.

parole.significato: A region or sovereign nation headed by a prince or princess.
parole.testo: From Middle English principalte, principalite, from Anglo-Norman principalté, Middle French principalté, from Late Latin prīncipālitās, from Latin prīncipālis (“principal”) + -tās. Equivalent to principal + -ity.

parole.significato: A high-ranking member of a religious house or religious order.
parole.testo: From Middle English priour, prior (“head or deputy head of a monastery or other religious house; predecessor; superior”), from Old English prior, from Anglo-Norman priour, prior, priur, and Old French prior, priur (modern French prieur), and directly from their etymon Latin prior (“ancestor; predece

parole.significato: A monastery or convent governed by a prior or prioress.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman priorie.

parole.significato: An exemption from certain laws granted by the Pope.
parole.testo: From Middle English privilege, from Anglo-Norman privilege and Old French privilege, from Latin prīvilēgium (“ordinance or law against or in favor of an individual”), from prīvus (“private”) + lēx, lēg- (“law”). Displaced native Old English frēols (“privilege, immunity”).

parole.significato: A divine mystery; something known only to God, or revealed only in holy scriptures.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman priveté, privitee et al., Old French priveté, from privé + -té.

parole.significato: An outhouse: an outbuilding used for urination and defecation.
parole.testo: From privy (“outhouse”) to clarify the intended sense, likely under the influence of Anglo-Norman privé hostel (attested in an 1139 British source) and Latin domus privata (1141).

parole.significato: Next; nearest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman prochein, from Old French prochain, from Vulgar Latin propeānus, from Latin prope (“near”).

parole.significato: Next friend.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French prochain (“next”) + ami (“friend”); now sometimes spelt prochain ami following the French spelling.

parole.significato: A statement which is proclaimed; formal a public announcement.
parole.testo: From Middle English proclamacion, from Anglo-Norman and Old French proclamacion, from Late Latin proclāmātiō, from the verb Latin prōclāmō.

parole.significato: The office of a procurator.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procuracie, from Anglo-Norman procuracie, from Latin prōcūrātia, analyzed as procure + -cy (“office of”). Doublet of proxy.

parole.significato: A tax collector.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procuratour, from Anglo-Norman procuratour, from Latin prōcūrātor, from prōcūrō (“to procure”) (English procure). Equivalent to procure + -ator and a doublet of proctor and procurer.

parole.significato: A person who procures or obtains things
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procurour, from Anglo-Norman procurour and continental Old French procureor, from Latin prōcūrātor; by surface analysis, procure + er. Doublet of proctor and procurator.

parole.significato: A declaration of faith.
parole.testo: From Middle English professioun, from Anglo-Norman professioun, Old French profession (“declaration of faith, religious vows, occupation”), from Latin professiō (“avowal, public declaration”), from the participle stem of profitērī (“to profess”). By surface analysis, profess + -ion.

parole.significato: The most senior rank for an academic at a university or similar institution.
parole.testo: From Middle English professor, professour, from Anglo-Norman proffessur and its etymon Latin professor (“declarer, person who claims knowledge”), from the past participle stem of profiteor (“profess”). By surface analysis, profess + -or.

parole.significato: Descending far below the surface; opening or reaching to great depth; deep.
parole.testo: From Middle English profound, profounde, from Anglo-Norman profound, from Old French profont, profonde, from Latin profundus (“deep, profound”), from prō + fundus (“bottom; foundation”).

parole.significato: A forefather, any of a person's direct ancestors.
parole.testo: From Middle English progenitour, from Anglo-Norman progenitour, Middle French progeniteur (Modern French progéniteur), and their etymon Latin prōgenitor, from prōgenitus, perfect participle of prōgignere (“to beget”), itself from prō- (“forth”) + gignere (“to beget”). By surface analysis, pro- (“pri

parole.significato: An act of prohibiting, forbidding, disallowing, or proscribing something.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman and Old French prohibicion, from Latin prohibitiō. By surface analysis, prohibit + -ion.

parole.significato: An official public announcement.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman and Old French prononcement. By surface analysis, pronounce + -ment. Doublet of pronunciamento.

parole.significato: Suitable.
parole.testo: From Middle English propre, from Anglo-Norman proper, propre, Old French propre (French: propre), from Latin proprius.

parole.significato: Something that is owned.
parole.testo: From Middle English propertee, properte, propirte, proprete, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French propreté, proprieté (“propriety, fitness, property”), from Latin proprietās (“a peculiarity, one's peculiar nature or quality, right or fact of possession, property”), from proprius (“special, part

parole.significato: Someone who speaks by divine inspiration.
parole.testo: From Middle English prophete, from Anglo-Norman prophete, from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”). Displaced native Old English wītga.

parole.significato: The act of propitiating; placation, atonement, similar to expiation but also involving the appeasement of anger.
parole.testo: From Middle English propiciacion, propiciacioun, from Anglo-Norman propiciatiun, Middle French propiciation, propitiation, and their etymon Latin propitiātiō (stem propitiātiōn-). By surface analysis, propitiate + -ion.

parole.significato: Favorable; advantageous.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman and Old French propicius, from Latin propitius (“favorable, well-disposed, kind”). Compare French propice, Portuguese propício and Spanish propicio.

parole.significato: To suggest a plan, course of action, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English proposen, from Anglo-Norman proposer (verb), propos (noun), Middle French proposer (verb), propos (noun), from Latin prōpōnō, prōpōnere, with conjugation altered based on poser. Doublet of propound.

parole.significato: The particular character or essence of someone or something; individuality.
parole.testo: From late Middle English proprietee, propretee, propriete (“ownership”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman propreté, Middle French proprieté, from Latin proprietās. By surface analysis, prop(e)r + -iety. Doublet of property.

parole.significato: Causing something to last longer or remain in effect longer; prolongation, continuance.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman prorogation, Middle French prorogation, and their source, Latin prōrogātiō (“extension, postponement”).

parole.significato: Someone who protects or guards, by assignment or on their own initiative.
parole.testo: From Middle English protectour, from Anglo-Norman protectour, protector and its etymon Latin prōtēctor, from prōtegō (“shield, protect”). By surface analysis, protect + -or. Displaced native Old English sċildend.

parole.significato: Preparation for the future; good governance; foresight.
parole.testo: From Middle English providence, from Anglo-Norman providence, Middle French providence, and their source, Latin prōvidentia (“providence, foresight”), from the present participle of prōvidēre (“to provide”). By surface analysis, provide + -ence. Displaced native Old English foresċēawung.

parole.significato: A region of the earth or of a continent; a district or country.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English provynce, from Anglo-Norman province, Old French province, from Latin prōvincia, seemingly corresponding to prō- (“forward”) + vinciō (“to bind, bind about, fetter, tie, fasten, surround, encircle”). Displaced Old English boldġetæl.

parole.significato: The office or remit of a provost, especially with reference to French history.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman provosté.

parole.significato: Used as a proxy or acting as a proxy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procucie, contraction of procuracie, from Anglo-Norman procuracie, from Medieval Latin procuratia, from Latin prōcūrātiō, from Latin prōcūrō (“to manage, administer”) (English procure). Compare proctor.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being prudent: circumspection and good judgment in knowing how best to act; (countable, archaic…
parole.testo: From Middle English prudence (“discretion; foresight; knowledge; intelligence, wisdom; act of good judgment; wisdom to see what is virtuous”), from Anglo-Norman prudence, Middle French prudence, and Old French prudence (“common sense; wisdom”) (modern French prudence), and from their etymon Latin pr

parole.significato: A tax collector, especially one working in Judea and Galilee during New Testament times (1st century C.E.) who was gene…
parole.testo: From Middle English publican [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman publican, pupplican, Middle French publicain, and Old French publican, publicain, pupplican (“tax collector”) (modern French publicain), and from their etymon Latin pūblicānus (“tax collector”), from pūblicum (“state revenue”) + -ānus

parole.significato: A girl, a maiden; a virgin (often with reference to Joan of Arc).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pucele, Middle French pucele, perhaps from a Late Latin *pullicella, but the further etymology is disputed. Compare Sicilian pulla.

parole.significato: power, might or potency
parole.testo: From Middle English puissaunce, from Anglo-Norman puissance, pusaunce, and other forms, from Old French puissant (“powerful”).

parole.significato: A young hen, especially one less than a year old.
parole.testo: From Middle English polet, pulet, from Anglo-Norman pullet, Old French poulet (“young chicken”); polette (“young hen”), from poule (“hen”), from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of pullus. Doublet of poult. Compare also Middle English pulle. By surface analysis, pull(us) + -et.

parole.significato: A normally regular beat felt when arteries near the skin (for example, at the neck or wrist) are depressed, caused by t…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English pulse, Middle English pous, pouse (“regular beat of arteries, pulse; heartbeat; place on the body where a pulse is detectable; beat (of a musical instrument); energy, vitality”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman puls, pous, pus, and Middle French pouls, poulz, pous [and o

parole.significato: Annual leguminous plants (such as beans, lentils, and peas) yielding grains or seeds used as food for humans or animals…
parole.testo: From Middle English puls (“(collectively) seeds of a leguminous plant used as food; leguminous plants collectively; a species of leguminous plant”), Early Middle English pols (in compounds), possibly from Anglo-Norman pus, puz, Middle French pouls, pols, pous, and Old French pous, pou (“gruel, mash,

parole.significato: A light, porous type of pyroclastic igneous rock, formed during explosive volcanic eruptions when liquid lava is ejecte…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman and Old French pomis (“pumice stone”), from Latin pūmex (“pumice stone”). Doublet of pounce.

parole.significato: A figured stamp, die, or punch, used by goldsmiths, cutlers, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English punchoun, from Anglo-Norman ponchon, pounceon et al., and Middle French ponçon, poinchon et al., from Old French ponchon, from Latin pūnctiōnem (“act of piercing”). Doublet of punction. Related to Middle High German punze (“chisel; burin, graver”), ponze (“puncheon, standardized

parole.significato: To cause (a child, student, or someone else being looked after, or a suspect or criminal) to suffer for crime or miscon…
parole.testo: From Middle English punischen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French puniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of punir, from Latin puniō (“to inflict punishment upon”), from poena (“punishment, penalty”); see pain. Displaced Old English wītnian and (mostly, in this sense) wrecan.

parole.significato: Of inferior significance, size, or strength; ineffective, small, weak.
parole.testo: PIE word  *pós A respelling of puisne, from Anglo-Norman puisné (“later, more recent; junior; weakly”) [and other forms] and Middle French puisné (“born after (a specified person); younger, youngest; one who is born after (a specified person)”) (modern French puîné (“cadet (born after a sibling); a

parole.significato: A learner at a school under the supervision of a teacher.
parole.testo: From Middle English pupille, from Anglo-Norman pupille (“orphan”), from Latin pūpillus (“orphan, minor”), variant of pūpulus (“little boy”), from pūpus (“child, boy”).

parole.significato: In words borrowed through Anglo-Norman: involving forward movement or completeness.
parole.testo: From Middle English pur-, from Anglo-Norman pur- (compare modern French pour), from Latin prō- (“forward direction, forward movement”). Doublet of pro-.

parole.significato: The acquisition of title to, or property in, anything for a price; buying for money or its equivalent.
parole.testo: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (from Latin pro-) + chac(i)er (“to chase, pursue”). Compare Old French porchacier (“to follow, to chase”), which has given French pourchasser (“to chase without relent”).

parole.significato: The process or act of purging, such as by the use of a purgative.
parole.testo: From Middle English purgacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman purgacion, itself borrowed from Latin pūrgātiō; equivalent to purge + -ation.

parole.significato: To take the property of another, often in breach of trust; to appropriate wrongfully; to steal.
parole.testo: From Middle English purloynen (“to remove”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman purloigner (“to put far away”), one of the variants of Old French porloignier. Doublet of prolong.

parole.significato: To convey, imply, or profess (often falsely or inaccurately).
parole.testo: From Middle English purporten, from Anglo-Norman purporter and Old French porporter (“convey, contain, carry”), from pur-, from Latin pro (“forth”) + Old French porter (“carry”), from Latin portō (“carry”).

parole.significato: The unlawful personal appropriation of public lands; wrongful encroachment on, or enclosure of properties belonging to…

parole.significato: That pursues.
parole.testo: Anglo-Norman pursuant, present participle of pursure. Doublet of pursuivant.

parole.significato: To follow urgently, originally with intent to capture or harm; to chase.
parole.testo: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor). Doublet of prosecute.

parole.significato: To prepare in advance (for or to do something); to plan, make provision.
parole.testo: From Middle English purveyen, from Anglo-Norman purveer, purveir et al., Old French porveeir, porveoir, from Latin prōvidēre (“to provide”). Doublet of provide; compare prudent.

parole.significato: The act of purveying.
parole.testo: From Middle English purveiaunce et al., from Anglo-Norman purveaunce.

parole.significato: The enacting part of a statute.
parole.testo: From Middle English purveu (“proviso”), from Anglo-Norman purveu est (“it is provided”), or purveu que (“provided that”) (statutory language), from Old French porveü (“provided”), past participle of porveoir (“to provide”), from Latin prōvideō (see provide). parole.significato: Any of various small game birds of the genera Coturnix, Anurophasis or Perdicula in the Old World family Phasianidae or…
parole.testo: From Middle English quayle, quaile, quaille, from Anglo-Norman quaille, from Late Latin quaccola (“quail”). (prostitute): So called because the quail was thought to be a very amorous bird.

parole.significato: Of a person: cunning, crafty.
parole.testo: From Middle English queynte, quoynte, from Anglo-Norman cointe, queinte and Old French cointe (“pretty, clever, knowing”), from Latin cognitus, past participle of cognōscō (“to know”).

parole.significato: A dispute or heated argument (especially one that is verbal).
parole.testo: From Middle English querele (“altercation, dispute; argument, debate; armed combat; trial by combat; basis for dispute, complaint; claim, legal suit; a lament; illness”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman querele [and other forms] and Middle French querele, querelle (“altercation, dispute; basis f

parole.significato: A part of the entrails of a hunted animal, given to the hounds as a reward.

parole.significato: A fever whose symptoms recur every four days.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman quartaine, Old French quartaine, from Latin quartāna (short for febris quartana), noun use of feminine form of quartānus (“recurring every four days”), from quartus (“fourth”).

parole.significato: A fourth part of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English quarter, from Anglo-Norman quarter, from Latin quartarius, from quartus. Compare Spanish cuarto (“room, quarters; quarter”). Doublet of quartier.

parole.significato: A quarter part; one fourth.
parole.testo: From Middle English quartern, quarteroun, quartroun, from Anglo-Norman quatroun (“quarter of a hundred”), from Old French quarter (“fourth”).

parole.testo: From Middle English questioun, from Anglo-Norman questiun, from Old French question, from Latin quaestiōnem, accusative of quaestiō (“a seeking, investigation, inquiry, question”), from quaerere (“to seek, ask, inquire”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-

parole.significato: A line of people, vehicles or other objects, usually one to be dealt with in sequence (i.e., the one at the front end i…
parole.testo: From Middle English queue, quew, qwew, couwe, from Anglo-Norman queue, keu and Old French cöe, cue, coe (“tail”), from Vulgar Latin cōda, from Latin cauda. See also Middle French queu, cueue. Doublet of coda and cola.

parole.significato: A small plot of land; historically: a strip of land that together with others like it formed a larger field.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Anglo-Norman/Old French cueillette (“uncultivated strip of land for the gathering of herbs, berries, snails, etc.”).

parole.significato: A bed covering consisting of two layers of fabric stitched together, with insulation between, often having a decorative…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English quilte, quylte, from Anglo-Norman quilte and Old French coilte, cuilte (compare French couette), from Latin culcita. Doublet of quoit.

parole.significato: An object (generally a post or plank on a support) set up as a target to be tilted at in jousting, or otherwise used as…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman quintaine, quinteine, Middle French quintaine, probably from Latin quīntāna (“street separating fifth and sixth maniples in a Roman camp”), feminine form of quīntānus (“pertaining to the fifth”).

parole.significato: Synonym of hundredweight, 100 or 112 English or American pounds.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Anglo-Norman quintal, from Middle French quintal, from Old French and Medieval Latin quintale and quintallus (“various medieval hundredweights”), from Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār, “100 rottols”), from Classical Syriac ܩܰܢܛܺܝܪܳܐ (qanṭīrā) and ܩܰܢܛܺܝܢܳܪܳܐ (qanṭīnārā), from Byzant

parole.significato: One-twentieth of a ream of paper; a collection of twenty-four or twenty-five sheets of paper of the same size and quali…
parole.testo: From Middle English quayer, from Anglo-Norman quaier and Old French quaer, from Latin quaternus (“fourfold”), from quater (“four times”). Doublet of cahier.

parole.significato: Released from obligation, penalty, etc; free, clear, or rid.
parole.testo: From Middle English quiten, quyten, from Anglo-Norman quitter, Old French quitter, from quitte (“acquitted, quit”), ultimately from Latin quietus, which itself derives from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyéh₁-ti-s, from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”). parole.significato: To relinquish or release (a claim, title, etc.); to transfer (an interest in property).
parole.testo: From Middle English quiteclaymen, from Anglo-Norman quiteclamer, from clamer quite (“to claim quit”). Compare claim quit.

parole.significato: To the greatest extent or degree; completely, entirely.
parole.testo: A development of quit, influence by Anglo-Norman quite. Doublet of coy, quit, quiet, and quietus. For an analogous semantic development from the same root, compare Armenian շատ (šat).

parole.significato: A container for arrows, crossbow bolts or darts, such as those fired from a bow, crossbow or blowgun.
parole.testo: From Middle English quiver, from Anglo-Norman quivre, from Old Dutch cocare (source of Dutch koker, and cognate to Old English cocer (“quiver, case”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kokar (“container”), said to be from Hunnic, possibly from Proto-Mongolic *kökexür (“leather vessel for liquids”); see the

parole.significato: A select body of (usually eminent) justices of the peace, every member of which had to be present to constitute a decid…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English quorum (c. 1426), from Anglo-Norman quorum, clipped from the Anglo-Latin wording of commissions in which certain persons were specially designated as members of a body by the words quorum vos unum esse volumus ad etc. (“of whom we want you to be one assigned to etc.”).

parole.significato: Happening every day; daily.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman cotidian, cotidien, Middle French cotidian, cotidien, and their source, Latin cottīdiānus, quōtīdiānus (“happening every day”), from adverb cottīdiē, quōtīdiē (“every day, daily”), from an unattested adjective derived from quot (“how many”) + locative form of diēs (“day”).

parole.significato: To sharpen (a grindstone) by scraping its surface.

parole.significato: Violent uncontrolled anger.
parole.testo: From Middle English rage, from Anglo-Norman rage, from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs (“anger, fury”). Doublet of rabies. parole.significato: To gush; to flow.
parole.testo: Probably from Anglo-Norman raier, Middle French raier.

parole.significato: Clothing, garments, dress, material.
parole.testo: Aphetized from Middle English arayment, borrowed from Anglo-Norman arraiement and Old French areement, from areer (“to array”). See array.

parole.significato: A type of fine linen once imported from France.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman Reins, Middle French Reins, variant of Reims, the French town where the fabric was originally produced.

parole.significato: A dried grape.
parole.testo: From Middle English raysyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman reysin (“grape, raisin”), from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus. Possibly a distant cognate of Persian رز (raz, “vine”). Doublet of raceme.

parole.significato: To hack, slash, or slice (something).
parole.testo: Probably a variant of race, raze (“to demolish; to destroy, obliterate; to scrape as if with a razor”), possibly modelled after rash (etymology 5 or etymology 6). parole.significato: Scraping the surface of a parchment etc. in order to erase something from the document; erasure, more generally.
parole.testo: From Middle English rasure, from Anglo-Norman rasure, Middle French rasure, from Latin rāsūra (“scraping, shaving”), from the participle stem of rādō (“to scrape, shave”).

parole.significato: A rat.
parole.testo: From Middle English ratoun, from Anglo-Norman ratoun and Middle French raton, corresponding to rat + -oon.

parole.significato: Property obtained or seized by force or violence; booty, plunder, spoils.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English ravin, ravine, raven (“rapine, robbery; rape; force, violence; greed, rapacity; stolen goods, booty, plunder; prey, quarry; pursuit of prey; predatoriness, voracity”), from Anglo-Norman ravein, raveine, ravine (“rapine, robbery; rape; force, violence; greed, r

parole.significato: To seize and carry away by violence; to snatch by force.
parole.testo: From Middle English ravyschen, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French ravis-, present participle stem of ravir (“to seize; to take away hastily”), from Vulgar Latin *rapire, from Latin rapere. See also rape.

parole.testo: The verb is derived from Middle English rasen, racen, rase (“to scrape; to shave; to erase; to pull; to strip off; to pluck or tear out; to root out (a tree, etc.); to pull away, snatch; to pull down; to knock down; to rend, tear apart; to pick clean, strip; to cleave, slice; to sever; to lacerate;

parole.significato: Being behind, or in the hindmost part; hindmost.
parole.testo: From Middle English rere, from Anglo-Norman rere, ultimately from Latin retro. Compare arrear. Doublet of retro.

parole.significato: The rearmost part of a force, especially a detachment of troops that protect the rear of a retreating force.
parole.testo: From Middle English rier garde, from Anglo-Norman reregard, reregarde, rereguarde and Middle French rieregarde, from Old French rereguarde (attested in The Song of Roland, c. 1150), from rere (“after; behind”) + guarde (“guard”). parole.significato: A harsh criticism.

parole.significato: A subsequent brief recitement or enumeration of the major points in a narrative, article, or book.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman recapitulaciun et al., Middle French recapitulacion et al., or their source, from Late Latin recapitulatio (“summing up, summary”), from the participle stem of recapitulare (“recapitulate”), from re- + capitulum (“chapter, section”), diminutive of caput (“head”).

parole.significato: A person who receives.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English receyvour, from Anglo-Norman receverre, receivour et al., later also reformed as receive + -er. Compare recevor, rescaivour.

parole.significato: An officer who receives the public revenue; a treasurer.
parole.testo: From receiver + general, after Anglo-Norman receivur general.

parole.significato: A container.
parole.testo: From Middle English receptacle, from Anglo-Norman receptacle and Middle French receptacle (“organ containing a fluid; gathering place; water basin”) (modern French réceptacle), from Latin receptāculum (“animal enclosure, container, place of refuge, receptacle, repository, reservoir, shelter”), from

parole.significato: A series of notes blown on a horn as a signal in hunting to call back the hounds when they have lost track of the game.
parole.testo: Probably from Anglo-Norman; compare Old French racheter (“rally”).

parole.significato: To return land to a suitable condition for use.
parole.testo: From Middle English reclaymen, recleymen, reclamen, from Anglo-Norman reclamer (noun reclaim and Middle French reclamer (noun reclaim), from Latin reclāmō, reclāmāre. Equivalent to re- + claim.

parole.significato: To console (someone); to comfort, look after.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman reconforter, Middle French reconforter, from re- + conforter.

parole.significato: An act of recommending.
parole.testo: From Middle English recommendacioun, from Anglo-Norman recomendacion, from Medieval Latin recommendatio. By surface analysis, recommend + -ation.

parole.significato: To get back, to regain (a physical thing; in astronomy and navigation, sight of a thing or a signal).
parole.testo: From Middle English recoveren, rekeveren, from Anglo-Norman recoverer and Old French recovrer, from Latin recuperāre, alternative form of reciperāre. Doublet of recuperate. The noun is from Middle English recover, from the verb.

parole.significato: Having admitted defeat and surrendered; defeated.
parole.testo: From Middle English recreaunt, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French recreant (“defeated”), from recroire (“to yield in a trial by combat, surrender allegiance”). Compare miscreant.

parole.significato: To heal (an organ or part of the body).
parole.testo: From Middle English rectifien, from Anglo-Norman rectifiier, rectefier (“to make straight”), from Medieval Latin rēctificō (“to make right”), from Latin rēctus (“straight”).

parole.significato: To swell up (of water, waves etc.); to overflow, to surge (of bodily fluids).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman redunder, Middle French redonder, and their source, Latin redundō, from red- + undō (“surge”), from unda (“a wave”).

parole.significato: To put in order again; to set right; to revise.
parole.testo: From Middle English redressen, from Anglo-Norman radresser, redrescer, redrescier and Middle French redresser (“to stand (someone or something) up; to stand up again; to rebuild, to repair something damaged, to rectify, to restore; to obtain redress; to cure; (of hair) to stand on end; to revise a j

parole.significato: To hold back, to restrain (someone or something).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English refreynen, from Anglo-Norman refrener, Old French refrener, from Latin refrēnāre, from re- + frēnāre, from frēnum.

parole.significato: A refrain.
parole.testo: From Middle English refreit, from Anglo-Norman refreit (“response”), refraindre (“to sing a refrain”); also Old French refreit (“refrain”). parole.significato: A steady look, a gaze.

parole.significato: With the head turned toward the back of the body.
parole.testo: From Middle English regardant, from Anglo-Norman regardant, Middle French regardant.

parole.significato: One who rules in place of the monarch, especially because the monarch is too young, absent, or disabled.
parole.testo: From Middle English regent, from Anglo-Norman regent, Middle French regent, and their source, Latin regēns (“ruling; ruler, governor, prince”), present participle of regō (“to govern, to steer”).

parole.significato: The act or practice of regrating; buying commodities in order to sell them.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman regraterie, corresponding to regrate + -ery.

parole.significato: To recompense or reward.

parole.significato: A recompense or reward.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman reguierdon, from re- + guerdon.

parole.significato: Bound by religious rule; belonging to a monastic or religious order (often as opposed to secular).
parole.testo: From Middle English reguler, from Anglo-Norman reguler, Middle French reguler, regulier, and their source, Latin rēgulāris (“continuing rules for guidance”), from rēgula (“rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“move in a straight line”).

parole.significato: To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite.
parole.testo: From Middle English rehersen, from Anglo-Norman reherser (“to repeat word-for-word”).

parole.significato: The exercise of sovereign power.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English regnen, from Old French reignier, from the Latin verb rēgnō, and the noun rēgnum. Doublet of regnum. Displaced native Old English rīċe (“a reign”) and ricsian (“to reign”).

parole.significato: A strap or rope attached to a bridle or bit, used to control a horse, other animal or young child.
parole.testo: From Middle English rein, reyne, from Anglo-Norman reyne, resne, from Early Medieval Latin retina, ultimately from Classical Latin retineō (“hold back”), from re- + teneō (“keep, hold”). parole.significato: A kidney.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman reines, Middle French reins, and their source, Latin rēnēs. Doublet of ren.

parole.significato: To give in or be swayed; to become less hard, harsh, or cruel; to show clemency.
parole.testo: From Middle English relenten, from Anglo-Norman relentir, from Latin re- + lentare (“to bend”), from lentus (“soft, pliant, slow”). Earliest recording dates to 1526. The noun is from the verb.

parole.significato: In a relentless manner.
parole.testo: From relentless + -ly (suffix forming abverbs from adjectives and nouns). parole.significato: Concerning religion.
parole.testo: From Middle English religiouse, religious, religius, religeous, from Anglo-Norman religieus, religius, from Old French religious, religieux, and their source, Latin religiōsus (“religious, superstitious, conscientious”), from religiō. Doublet of religieux.

parole.significato: A part or parts remaining after some has/have been removed or already occurred.
parole.testo: From Middle English remaindre, remeigner, from Anglo-Norman remaindre, with infinitive used as noun.

parole.significato: Remedy.
parole.testo: From Middle English remede, from Anglo-Norman and Old French remede. Doublet of remedy.

parole.significato: To send or give back.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman remis, Middle French remis, past participle of remettre (“to remit”); Middle French remise (noun), from feminine past participle of remettre (“to remit”).

parole.significato: A small portion remaining of a larger thing or group; part of a former whole.
parole.testo: From Middle English, contraction of remenant, from Anglo-Norman remanant, present participle of remaindre, from Latin remaneō.

parole.significato: To feel remorse.
parole.testo: From the Middle English remorden, from the Anglo-Norman and Middle French remordre and its etymon the Latin remordeō, from re- + mordeō; compare the Catalan remordir, remordre, the French remordre, the Italian rimordere, the Old Occitan remordre, the Portuguese remorder, and the Spanish remorder.

parole.significato: To go up again; to rise another time.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman remunter, Middle French remonter, later also reinforced by re- + mount.

parole.significato: To delete.
parole.testo: From Middle English removen, from Anglo-Norman remover, removeir, from Old French remouvoir, from Latin removēre, from re- + movēre (“to move”), equivalent to re- + move. Displaced native Old English āfierran.

parole.significato: A right to receive rent where the tenant's goods cannot be seized as security for the payment of rent.
parole.testo: From late Middle English rent sek, from Anglo-Norman rente sec; sec rente (literally “dry rent”), ultimately from Latin siccus. Compare Middle English secce (“dry”).

parole.significato: To pass (back) again, especially in the opposite direction; to return.
parole.testo: Partly from Anglo-Norman repasser, partly from re- + pass.

parole.significato: A meal.

parole.significato: To cancel, invalidate, annul.

parole.significato: An action to recover personal property unlawfully taken, especially that seized by way of distraint; the writ or proced…
parole.testo: Anglo-Norman, from Old French replevir (“recover”), from re- + plevir (apparently from a Germanic word which was also the source of English pledge).

parole.significato: The process by which an object, person, place or idea may be copied mimicked or reproduced.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English replicacioun, replicacion, from Anglo-Norman replicacioun and Old French replicacion (“reply, answer”), from Latin replicātiō, replicātiōnem. By surface analysis, replicate + -(at)ion.

parole.significato: To relate details of (an event or incident); to recount, describe (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English reporten, from Anglo-Norman reporter, from Latin reportāre (“to carry back, return, remit, refer”), from re- + portāre.
