parole.significato: Habitual moderation in regard to the indulgence of the natural appetites and passions; restrained or moderate indulgenc…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman temperance, from Latin temperantia (“moderation, sobriety, discretion, self-control”), from temperans, present participle of temperare (“to moderate”). See temper. English equivalent temper + -ance.

parole.significato: One who holds a lease (a tenancy).
parole.testo: From Middle English tenaunt, from Anglo-Norman tenaunt and Old French tenant, present participle of tenir (“to hold”), from Latin tenēre (“hold, keep”).

parole.significato: Sensitive or painful to the touch.
parole.testo: From Middle English tender, tendere, from Anglo-Norman tendre, Old French tendre, from Latin tener, tenerum (“soft, delicate”).

parole.significato: Dark and gloomy; obscure.
parole.testo: ] From Middle English tenebrose, from Anglo-Norman tenebrous (earlier tenebrus), from Latin tenebrōsus, itself from tenebrae (“darkness, shadows”).

parole.significato: A building that is rented to multiple tenants, especially a low-rent, run-down one.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenement, from Anglo-Norman tenement (“holding”), from Old French tenement, from Medieval Latin tenimentum, from Latin teneō (“hold”).

parole.significato: A projecting member left by cutting away the wood around it, and made to insert into a mortise, and in this way secure…
parole.testo: From Middle English tenoun, tenown, tenon, from Anglo-Norman tenoun, from Old French tenon.

parole.significato: A musical range or section higher than bass and lower than alto.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenour, from Anglo-Norman tenour, from Old French tenor (“substance, contents, meaning, sense; tenor part in music”), from Latin tenor (“course, continuance; holder”), from teneō (“to hold”). In music, from the notion of the one who holds the melody, as opposed to the counterteno

parole.significato: A status of possessing a thing or an office; an incumbency.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenure, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French tenure, from Vulgar Latin *tenitura, from *tenitus, from Latin tentus (from teneō) + -ura.

parole.significato: A brawling, boisterous, and turbulent person or thing.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes The noun is derived from Termagant (“fictitious deity with a violent temperament represented as being worshipped by Muslims or other non-Christians”), from Middle English Termagaunt (“fictitious deity represented as being worshipped by Muslims; any pagan god”), from Anglo-Norman Te

parole.significato: Pertaining to earth or the material world; earthly, terrestrial (as opposed to heavenly or marine).
parole.testo: From Middle English terrene, from Anglo-Norman terriene, feminine of terrien, from Latin terrēnus, from terra (“earth”).

parole.significato: One of the rings on the top of the harness saddle, through which the reins pass.
parole.testo: Alteration of Middle English toret, turret (“half-ring, eyelet”), from Anglo-Norman turette, diminutive of Old French tur (“circuit, ring”). More at turn.

parole.significato: A collection of acknowledgments of the vassals or tenants of a lordship, containing the rents and services they owed to…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman terrier, from Old French terrier (“of earth”, adjective), from Medieval Latin terrarius (“of earth”), from Latin terra (“earth”).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to a will or testament
parole.testo: From Middle English testamentarie, from Anglo-Norman testamentarie and Latin testāmentārius (“of or belonging to wills”).

parole.significato: An English measure of length for rope, perhaps equivalent to the fathom.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle English teies, teyse, taken as a plural, from Anglo-Norman teice, from Old French teise, toise.

parole.significato: A kind of gauze, or very thin silk.
parole.testo: From an Anglo-Norman common name for the festival of the Epiphany. See Tiffany.

parole.significato: The stock; a beam on a crossbow carved to fit the arrow, or the point of balance in a longbow.
parole.testo: From Middle English teler, from Anglo-Norman telier (“beam used in weaving”), from Medieval Latin telarium, from Latin tēla (“web”).

parole.significato: A shining fabric used for ornamental purposes.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English tinsel (“cloth containing gold or silver thread”) [and other forms], probably from Anglo-Norman tincel, tincelle, tencele, and then: * from Old French estincelle, estencele (“a spark”) (modern French étincelle), from Vulgar Latin *stincilla, a metathesis of La

parole.significato: A medicinal drink, originally made from barley soaked in water.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman tysanne, Middle French ptisane, tisane (“barley water, medicinal drink”), and their source, Latin tisana, variant of ptisana, from Ancient Greek πτισάνη (ptisánē, “peeled barley, barley gruel”), from πτίσσειν (ptíssein, “to peel, to crush”).

parole.significato: Any small dot, stroke, or diacritical mark, especially if part of a letter, or of a letter-like abbreviation; in partic…
parole.testo: From Middle English tytle, titel, titele, from Anglo-Norman titil, titule and Medieval Latin titulus (“small stroke, diacritical mark, accent”), from Latin titulus (“title”). Doublet of tilde, titer/titre, title, titlo, and titulus.

parole.significato: Labour, work, especially of a grueling nature.

catena.termine: tilyen, telien, teolien, tolen, tolien, tulien

parole.testo: From Middle English toilen, toylen, apparently a conflation of Anglo-Norman toiller (“to agitate, stir up, entangle”) (compare Old Northern French tooillier, tooullier (“to agitate, stir”); of unknown origin), and Middle English tilyen, telien, teolien, tolen, tolien, tulien (“to till, work, labour”

parole.significato: To shave the crown of the head of (a person) as a sign of humility and religious vocation.
parole.testo: From Middle English tonsure, from Anglo-Norman and Old French tonsure, from Latin tonsūra (“a clipping, trimming”), from tondeō (“shear, clip, trim”).

parole.significato: One who torments; a person, animal, or object that causes suffering.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman tourmentour, from Old French tormenteor.

parole.significato: The condition, or an act, of doing wrong; the act of committing a tort.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman tortfesance, from Old French tort (“a misdeed, a wrong”) + fesance (“act, action, deed”).

parole.significato: A person who commits a tort.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman tortfeasor, from Old French tortfesor, tort-faiseur, torfesor, torzfesor (“wrongdoer”), from tort (“a misdeed, a wrong”) + fesor, faiseur (“doer”).

parole.significato: Wrongful; harmful.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English torcious, from Anglo-Norman torcious. By surface analysis, tort + -ious.

parole.significato: Twisted; having many turns; convoluted.
parole.testo: From Middle English tortuous, tortuose, from Anglo-Norman and Old French tortuos, from Latin tortuōsus, from tortus (“a twisting, winding”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to torture.
parole.testo: From Middle English torterous, from Anglo-Norman torturous, from Old French tortureus, from Latin tortūra. By surface analysis, torture + -ous.

parole.significato: A circuit made by a medieval English sheriff to the courts of his shire.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman. Doublet of turn.

parole.significato: A tournament.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman turnei, from Old French tornei (“tournament”), from tornoier (“to joust, tilt”).

parole.significato: Treachery; deceit.
parole.testo: From Middle English trayne (“treachery”), from Anglo-Norman traine, Middle French traïne, from traïr (“to betray”).

parole.significato: Characteristic of a traitor; disloyal.
parole.testo: From Middle English trayterous, traytrous, (also Middle English traytours, treytours), from Anglo-Norman traiterous, traitourous and Old French traitros.

parole.significato: To (cause to) be in a trance; to entrance.
parole.testo: From Middle English traunce, from Anglo-Norman transe (“fear of coming evil; passage from life to death”), from transir (“to be numb with fear; to die, pass on”), from Latin trānseō (“to cross over”).

parole.significato: Someone who transgresses.
parole.testo: From Middle English transgressour, from Anglo-Norman transgressour, from Latin transgressor. Equivalent to transgress + -or.

parole.significato: Senses relating to the change of information, etc., from one form to another.
parole.testo: From Middle English translaten (“to transport, translate, transform”), from Anglo-Norman translater, from Latin trānslātus, perfect passive participle of trānsferō (“to transport, carry across, translate”). See also -ate (verb-forming suffix). Distant doublet of transfer, see collate and confer, del

parole.significato: The act of translating, in its various senses:
parole.testo: From Middle English translacioun (“transfer, translation”), from Anglo-Norman translacioun, from Latin trānslātiō, from trānslāt-, the supine stem of trānsferō (“to transfer, transport, transform, translate”). Equivalent to translate + -ion. Displaced native Old English wending.

parole.significato: An ornamental covering or harness for a horse; caparison.
parole.testo: From Middle English trappyng, trappynge, from trap, trappe (“personal belongings, owndom, household goods”) (compare Middle English trappen (“to deck, caparison”)), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Anglo-Norman, from Medieval Latin trapus (“cloth”), from Frankish *traba, *trapa (“cloth, thread, ra

parole.significato: One of a series of allotments (of funds for a certain purpose).
parole.testo: From Middle English *traunche, from Late Anglo-Norman traunche (Old French tranche). Doublet of tranche and trench.

parole.significato: Causing or involving travail; laborious; toilsome.
parole.testo: From Middle English travailous (“laborious, wearisome”), from Anglo-Norman travaillous, Old French travaillos (“tiring, painful”). Equivalent to travail + -ous.

parole.significato: A hidden treasure, subsequently discovered.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman tresor trové (“found treasure”), calque of Latin thesaurus inventus, where the past participle trové was interpreted in English as a noun. Perhaps related to trophy.

parole.significato: To negotiate, discuss terms, bargain (for or with).
parole.testo: From Middle English treten, from Anglo-Norman treter, Old French tretier, traiter, from Latin tractāre (“to pull", "to manage”), from the past participle stem of trahere (“to draw", "to pull”).

parole.significato: A formal, usually lengthy, systematic discourse on some subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English tretys, from Anglo-Norman tretiz and Old French traitis (“treatise, account”), from traitier (“to deal with, treat”).

parole.significato: A formal binding agreement concluded by subjects of international law, namely, states and international organizations;…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English trete, trety (“bargaining, negotiation; discussion; conference, meeting; entreaty, persuasion; agreement, contract, covenant; arrangement, settlement; agreement between two rulers, states, etc.; written work on a particular subject, treatise; subdivision of a

parole.significato: An outdoor garden frame that can be used for partitioning a common area.
parole.testo: From Middle English trelis, from Anglo-Norman treslis, from Old French treille (“arbor”), from Latin trichila (“arbor", "summer house”). However, see OED which claims another Old French form referring to sackcloth, from Vulgar Latin.

parole.significato: A shake, quiver, or vibration.
parole.testo: From Middle English tremour (“fright”), from Anglo-Norman tremour and Old French tremor, from Latin tremor.

parole.significato: A plate on which food is served or cut.
parole.testo: From Middle English trenchour, from Anglo-Norman trenchour and Old Northern French trencheor (French tranchoir), from trenchier (“to cut, to carve”). See trench (verb).

parole.significato: A playing card or die with the rank of three.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Middle English trey, from Anglo-Norman trei or treis, from Old French treis (“three”). Doublet of three and tres.

parole.significato: An occasion on which a person or thing is tested to find out how well they perform or how suitable they are.
parole.testo: From Middle English trial, triall, from Anglo-Norman trial, triel, from trier (“to pick out, cull”) + -al. More at English try.

parole.significato: One who tries; one who makes experiments or examines anything by a test or standard.
parole.testo: From Middle English triour, from Anglo-Norman triour and Middle English trien (equivalent to try + -er).

parole.significato: A group or set of three people or things; three things combined into one.
parole.testo: From Middle English trinite, from Anglo-Norman trinite and Old French ternite (modern French trinité), from Latin trīnitās, from trīnī (“three each”), from trēs (“three”). By surface analysis, trine + -ity. Displaced native Old English þrines (literally “threeness”).

parole.significato: A type of steelyard (weighing machine) for heavy wares, such as wool, consisting of two horizontal bars crossing each o…
parole.testo: From Middle English trone (“a wooden beam or post used in public weighing, scale, balance”), from Anglo-Norman trone, tron (whence also Anglo-Latin trona), from Old Norse trönur (“a frame or framework on which trunks of trees are laid to be cut by the saw”), plural of trana, trani (“trunk, snout, na

parole.significato: Of a liquid: thick, muddy, full of sediment.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English troublous, from Anglo-Norman troublous and Middle French troubleus, corresponding to trouble + -ous.

parole.significato: A treasure trove; a collection of treasure.
parole.testo: Originally in the phrase treasure trove, from Anglo-Norman tresor trouvé (“found treasure”), where the past participle trouvé (“found”) was interpreted in English as a noun. Doublet of trope.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, troy weight.
parole.testo: From Middle English troye, from Anglo-Norman. According to the American Heritage Dictionary, probably first used at a fair in Troyes, France.

parole.significato: To trade, exchange; barter.
parole.testo: From Middle English trukien, from unrecorded Anglo-Norman and Old French words, from Latin trocāre, from Frankish *trokan. Related to Etymology 2.

parole.significato: To roll or move upon truckles, or casters; to trundle.
parole.testo: From Middle English trokel, trocle, trookyl, from Anglo-Norman trocle, from Medieval Latin trochlea (“a block, sheaf containing one or more pulleys”); or from a diminutive of truck (“wheel”), formed with -le, equivalent to truck + -le.

parole.significato: An armor plate hanging down from the breastplate or fauld to cover the thigh, either below or as part of a tasse. (Poss…
parole.testo: From Middle English toile, from Anglo-Norman toille, tuille, taken to be variants of Old French tieulle (modern French tuile, from Latin tēgula, and thus a doublet of tile and tuile. The French term occurs in only one medieval work and the English term in only two (one a translation of the French wo

parole.significato: The training or instruction provided by a teacher or tutor.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman tuycioun, from Old French tuicion, from Latin tuitiō (“guard, protection, defense”), from tuēri (“to watch, guard, see, observe”). Compare intuition, tutor.

parole.significato: Peatland from which peat or turf may be cut for fuel; (countable) a piece of such land; a peat bog.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English turbarie (“place where peat is dug, peat bog; substance obtained from such a place, peat”), from Anglo-Norman turbarie, turberie, and Old French torberie, tourbarie, turbarie, from Medieval Latin turbāria, from turba (“turf”) (whence Old French tourbe) + Latin -āria (su

parole.significato: Any member of the species Scophthalmus maximus (syn. Psetta maxima) of flatfish native to Europe.
parole.testo: From Middle English turbot, turbut, from Anglo-Norman turbut, Old French turbot, torbot, from Old Swedish tornbut, from törn (“thorn”) + but (“butt, flatfish”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Turkey red (“a vibrant red dye or its color”).
parole.testo: From Middle English Turkye, from Anglo-Norman Turkye, Medieval Latin Turcia, from Turcus (“Turk”), from Byzantine Greek Τοῦρκος (Toûrkos), from Classical Persian تُرْک (turk), from Middle Persian [script needed] (twlk' /⁠turk⁠/), from Old Turkic 𐱅𐰇𐰼𐰜 (t²ẅr²ẅk²). By surface analysis, Turke + -y.

parole.significato: A change of direction or orientation.
parole.testo: Partly from Anglo-Norman *torn, from Latin tornus, from Ancient Greek τόρνος (tórnos), and partly an action noun from the verb turn.

parole.significato: In a wine bottle, the empty space between the cork and the top of the wine.
parole.testo: From Middle English ulage, from Anglo-Norman ulliage, from *ullier (“to fill a partially empty cask”), from Old French oel (“bunghole”, literally “eye”), from Latin oculus (“eye”). See French ouillage.

parole.significato: An umbrere; the visor of a helmet
parole.testo: From Middle English umbrell, umbrel, probably from Anglo-Norman umbrail, from Old French ombrail, ombral, from ombrel (“shade”), from ombre + -el, from Latin umbra; compare French ombrelle. By surface analysis, umb(e)r + -el.

parole.significato: Oneness: the state or fact of being one undivided entity.
parole.testo: From Middle English unite, from Anglo-Norman, Old French unité, from Latin ūnitās, from ūnus (“one”) + noun of state suffix -itās, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one, single”), hence distantly related to one and an. By surface analysis, unite + -y. Displaced native Old English ānnes (l

parole.significato: An institution of higher education that provides facilities for teaching, research, and the conferral of academic degre…
parole.testo: From Middle English universite (“institution of higher learning, body of persons constituting a university”) from Anglo-Norman université, from Old French universitei, from Medieval Latin stem of universitas, in juridical and Late Latin "a number of persons associated into one body, a society, compa

parole.significato: Not mannerly (“polite; having good manners”).
parole.testo: From Middle English unmanerli (“of a person: disorderly, unruly; of conduct: inappropriate, improper”), from un- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + manerli, manerly (“well-mannered; modest; customary; moral”). Manerli is derived from maner (“kind, sort; form, nature; circumstances; method, manner; outward beh

parole.significato: Use, practise, exercise.
parole.testo: From Middle English ure, from Anglo-Norman *ure, Old French uevre (modern French œuvre), from Latin opera (“work, labor”). Doublet of oeuvre, opera, and opus.

parole.significato: Habit, practice.
parole.testo: From Middle English usage, from Anglo-Norman and Old French usage. By surface analysis, use + -age.

parole.significato: A person, in a church, cinema etc., who escorts people to their seats.
parole.testo: From Middle English ussher, uscher, usscher, from Anglo-Norman usser and Old French ussier, uissier (“porter, doorman”) (compare French huissier), from Vulgar Latin *ustiārius (“doorkeeper”), from Latin ōstiārius, from ōstium (“door”). Akin to ōs (“mouth”). Probably a doublet of ostiary and huissier

parole.significato: A person who loans money to others and charges interest, particularly at an exorbitant, exploitative, or illegal rate.
parole.testo: Anglo-Norman, from Old French usurier, Latin ūsūra (“interest”).

parole.significato: An extended trip or journey away from home for rest or pleasure.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English vacation, vacacion, vacacioun, from Anglo-Norman vacacioun, from Old French vacacion, vacation, from Latin vacātiō. Equivalent to vacate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person who wanders from place to place; a nomad, a wanderer.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English vagraunt (“person without proper employment; person without a fixed abode, tramp, vagabond”) [and other forms], probably from Anglo-Norman vagarant, wakerant, waucrant (“vagrant”) [and other forms] and Old French walcrant, waucrant (“roaming, wandering”) [and other forms], p

parole.significato: Wandering from place to place, particularly when without any settled employment or habitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English vagraunt, vagaraunt (“having no proper employment; having a tendency to go astray or wander; wayward”), from Anglo-Norman vagarant, wakerant, waucrant (“vagrant”) and Old French walcrant, waucrant (“roaming, wandering”); see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: A short curtain that usually hangs along the top edge of a window.
parole.testo: From Middle English valance, valans, valaunce, valence, valons. Origin uncertain. Probably from Anglo-Norman valaunce, valence, from valer (“go down, let down”), aphetic form of Old French avaler (“to descend, go down”).

parole.significato: The quality of being valiant; heroism, bravery or valour.
parole.testo: From Middle English valiaunce, from Anglo-Norman vaillaunce and Old French vaillance.

parole.significato: Possessing or showing courage or determination; brave, heroic.
parole.testo: From Middle English vailaunt (“having or showing courage or valour, valiant; characterized by valour; powerful, strong; person of valour or strength; excellent, worthy; beneficial, useful; valuable; legally valid, binding”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman vaillaunt, vaylant [and other forms], a

parole.significato: An elongated depression cast between hills or mountains, often with a river flowing through it.
parole.testo: From Middle English valeye, valey, from Anglo-Norman valey, Old French valee (compare French vallée), from Latin vallēs/vallis. Doublet of vlei and vly. Displaced native dene, from dene and partially displaced native dale, from dæl.

parole.significato: Individually sustained verve or passion.
parole.testo: From Middle English valour, from Anglo-Norman valour, from Latin valor. Doublet of valure.

parole.significato: The piece of armor designed to protect the arm from the elbow to the wrist.
parole.testo: From Middle English vambrace, vauntbras, from Anglo-Norman vambras, avantbras.

parole.significato: To speak boastfully.
parole.testo: From Middle English vaunten, from Anglo-Norman vaunter, variant of Old French vanter, from Latin vānus (“vain, boastful”).

parole.significato: The vanguard.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English vawarde, late form of vantwarde, aphetism of Anglo-Norman avantwarde, a variant of Old French avant-guarde. Doublet of avant-garde and vanguard.

parole.significato: The flesh of a calf (i.e. a young bovine) used for food.
parole.testo: From Middle English veel, from Anglo-Norman veel, from Latin vitellus, diminutive of vitulus (“calf”). Doublet of vitellus.

parole.significato: Something hung up or spread out to hide or protect the face, or hide an object from view; usually of gauze, crepe, or s…
parole.testo: From Middle English veil, veyl, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French veil (“sail, veil, shroud”) (Francien Old French voil, French voile), Latin vēlum (“cloth, covering”). Displaced Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyre (“veil”) (compare German Schleier). Doublet of velum and voile.

parole.significato: A person or a company that vends or sells.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman vendor (Old French vendeor), from Latin venditor (“seller”), from vendere (“to sell, cry up for sale, praise”), contraction of venundare, venumdare, also, as originally, two words venum dare (“to sell”), from venum (“sale, price”) + dare (“to give”).

parole.significato: Vengeful.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vengeable.

parole.significato: Revenge taken for an insult, injury, or other wrong.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vengeaunce, from Old French vengeance, venjance, from vengier (“to avenge”). Analysable as venge + -ance.

parole.significato: The meat of a deer, especially one that was hunted in its own natural habitat.
parole.testo: From Middle English venisoun, venesoun, from Anglo-Norman veneisun, venesoun, venesun (“meat of large game, particularly deer or boar; hunt”), from Latin vēnātiō, vēnātiōnem (“hunt; meat from a hunt”), formed on vēnātus, perfect participle of vēnor (“to hunt”). Doublet of venatio and venation.

parole.significato: A cupping glass.
parole.testo: Possibly continuing Middle English ventouse, ventuse, ventose, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman ventuse; or perhaps a reborrowing directly from French ventouse, or both.

parole.significato: A decision on an issue of fact in a civil or criminal case or an inquest.
parole.testo: From Middle English verdit, from Anglo-Norman verdit (> Medieval Latin veredictum), from veir (“true”) + dit (“saying”); possibly a calque of a Germanic term such as Old English sōþword, sōþsprǣċ, sōþspell, sōþsagu, or sōþcwide, all meaning "true story, statement of truth, account, history". Doublet

parole.significato: Truth, fact or reality, especially an enduring religious or ethical truth; veracity.
parole.testo: From Middle English verite, from Anglo-Norman verité or Middle French verité, from Old French verité, from Latin vēritās, from the adjective vērus (“true”). Doublet of veritas.

parole.significato: A sweet, white Italian wine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle English vernage, from Anglo-Norman vernage, from Old Italian Vernaccia.

parole.significato: A room in a church where the clergy put on their vestments and where these are stored; also used for meetings and class…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vesterie, from Old French vestiaire (“room for vestments, dressing room”), from Latin vestiarium (“wardrobe”). Doublet of vestiary.

parole.significato: A covering of, or like, clothing.
parole.testo: From Middle English vesture (noun) and vesturen (verb), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French vesteüre, from Vulgar Latin vestītūra (“clothing”), from Latin vestītus, perfect passive participle of vestiō (“to clothe”), from vestis (“garment”).

parole.significato: The action of vexing, annoying, or irritating someone or something; (countable) an instance of this.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English vexacioun, vexation (“physical suffering; act of inflicting trouble (specifically through unjustified legal action); anxiety, mental distress; mental disturbance”), from Anglo-Norman vexacion, vexation, Middle French vexacion, vexation (“distress, suffering; harassment (spec

parole.significato: An item of food.
parole.testo: From Middle English vyaund, from Anglo-Norman and Old French viande, from Late Latin *vivanda, from Latin vīvenda, from the verb vīvō (“to live”). Compare victual, viando. The Philippines usage is an anglicization of Spanish vianda (which is ultimately from Latin via French), which is used to transl

parole.significato: In the Church of England, the priest of a parish, receiving a salary or stipend but not tithes.
parole.testo: From Middle English vicar, viker, vikyr, vicaire, vicare, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman vikare, vicare, vikaire, vikere and Old French vicaire (“deputy, second in command”), from Latin vicārius (“vicarious, substitute”). Doublet of vicarious. Displaced native Old English ġespelia.

parole.significato: Violent, destructive and cruel.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English vicious, from Anglo-Norman vicious, (modern French vicieux), from Latin vitiōsus, from vitium (“fault, vice”). Equivalent to vice + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the viscount or sheriff of a county.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vicontiel, from Middle French visconte (“viscount”) + -iel. Equivalent to viscount + -ial.

parole.significato: Used to encourage someone to achieve success, or to celebrate a success or triumph.
